title: OCLDA-GS: Object-Centric Local Deformation-Aware Gaussian Streaming
summary: Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for online reconstruction of dynamic scenes from multi-view videos for Free Viewpoint Video (FVV). Current time and storage efficient methods rely on selecting a subset of anchor Gaussians and neighborhood interpolation for fast streamable 3DGS. However, these methods can overlook object-specific motion and introduce inconsistencies near object boundaries. We propose OCLDA-GS, an object-centric streaming framework that dynamically reallocates object and motion-aware Gaussian anchors to allocate anchor Gaussian support for objects undergoing large motion while at the same time, restricting the gaussian neighborhood within object groups for more precise object boundaries. Furthermore, it estimates object-wise rigid transformations (e.g. a hand moving) and leverages these estimates to learn per-anchor local deformation correction for small deformations (e.g. wrinkles on a shirt). Then, we conduct experiments on three dynamic multi-view video datasets and demonstrate improvements over the previous baselines alongside improved quality between refinement timesteps. Under matched refinement budgets, our method improves PSNR over Instant Gaussian Stream (IGS) by 0.169 dB on N3DV, 0.202 dB on Meeting Room and +0.199 on Google Immersive, while reducing the mean PSNR drop between refinement timesteps by 9.2% and 13.8% in N3DV and Meeting Room, respectively.

Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussians allows for photorealistic reconstruction from RGB images and camera poses using 3D Gaussians as primitives. 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) or Dynamic Gaussian Splatting . This enables realtime Free Viewpoint Video (FVV) for novel view synthesis~ wu2024gaussians,yang2024realtime4dgs,luiten2024dynamic . FVV has applications in VR, immersive communication and sports viewing~ broxton2020immersive,yan2025instantgaussianstreamfast . Current Dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods can be divided into two broad categories: offline and online~ wu2024gaussians,sun20243dgstream,girish2024queen . Offline methods optimize spatiotemporal deformation by learning the motion features throughout the entire video and emphasizes quality and refinement taking significant time and compute in the process~ yang2024deformable3dgs,yang2024realtime4dgs . In the online streaming setting, the scene representation is updated as each set of new multi-view frames arrive and the central concern is to make that update computationally cheap while maintaining image fidelity~ sun20243dgstream,girish2024queen . Recent time and storage-efficient Gaussian streaming methods rely on selection of subset of Gaussians called anchors, whose motion features are then interpolated to update the scene representation. Methods like IGS~ yan2025instantgaussianstreamfast and ReconGS fu2025recongs work under fixed computational budget controlled by the number of anchors and refinement per step or keyframes making them extremely effective for real-time dynamic scene streaming under limited computation bandwidth. IGS performs farthest point sampling (FPS) and periodic refinement on pre-specified timesteps called keyframes, while ReConGS~ fu2025recongs organizes anchors into an adaptive hierarchy for compact motion optimization and performs per-step refinements. ~ sumner2007embedded,huang2024scgs . For example, in the N3DV dataset (~ ), when the chef's hand moves near a stationary table, deformation via interpolated anchor neighborhood can induce incompatible motion in Gaussians belonging to the stationary table. Some related object and motion-aware control-point methods address parts of this challenge~ he2025h3ddgs,chen2025comgs , but maintaining accurate, object-consistent motion with limited refinement remains challenging. Furthermore, motion within an object often comprises a shared rigid component and local non-rigid deformations (e.g., a moving body with wrinkling clothes). Accounting for both components is important for accurate motion prediction under limited refinement budgets. We introduce Object-Centric Local Deformation-Aware Gaussian Streaming (OCLDA-GS) . OCLDA-GS jointly addresses anchor selection, object-aware motion propagation, and local deformation correction. First, OCLDA-GS uses optical flow~ teed2020raft observed over each completed keyframe interval to redistribute a fixed anchor budget across object groups, increasing support for groups with larger observed motion. Second, it restricts motion propagation to anchors within the same group, preventing cross-group interpolation for supported Gaussians. Finally, it fits a rigid transformation to the predicted anchor correspondences of each group and predicts an additional local deformation correction. More broadly, OCLDA-GS highlights object-aware motion modeling as a promising direction for improving the quality--efficiency trade-off in Gaussian streaming. Extensive experiments on datasets demonstrate competitive reconstruction quality and streaming efficiency in both in-domain and cross-domain settings. Temporal analyses against online streaming method like Instant Gaussian Stream (IGS) further show reduced quality degradation between keyframes. In summary, our contributions are: Related Work sec:related_work novel view synthesis. NeRF established neural radiance fields as a representation for novel view synthesis~ mildenhall2020nerf . Dynamic extensions model scene changes through deformation fields, scene flow, and higher-dimensional embeddings ~ pumarola2021dnerf,park2021nerfies,li2021nsff,park2021hypernerf . HexPlane and K-Planes improve efficiency through factorized spatiotemporal features ~ cao2023hexplane,fridovichkeil2023kplanes . With an explicit Gaussian representation and differentiable rasterization, 3DGS enables high-quality real-time rendering~ kerbl2023gaussians . Dynamic Gaussian methods extend this representation using learned deformation fields and spatiotemporal Gaussian formulations ~ yang2024deformable3dgs,wu2024gaussians,yang2024realtime4dgs,li2024spacetime . These advances improve dynamic scene representation and rendering, while online reconstruction additionally requires efficient updates as new observations arrive. Streaming. StreamRF and ReRF investigate incremental learning and residual representations for dynamic radiance fields ~ li2022streaming,wang2023rerf , while NeRFPlayer and VideoRF explore decomposed fields and feature streams for compact video representation and playback ~ song2023nerfplayer,wang2024videorf . For Gaussian-based online reconstruction, 3DGStream trains scene updates on the fly~ sun20243dgstream , and QUEEN uses sparse, quantized Gaussian attribute residuals~ girish2024queen . Complementary compression approaches, including 4DGC and GIFStream, target compact representations and efficient video delivery ~ hu20254dgc,li2025gifstream . HiCoM and ReCon-GS use hierarchical motion representations to reduce update and storage costs~ gao2024hicom,fu2025recongs . IGS instead employs a generalizable anchor-driven motion predictor with periodic Gaussian refinement at keyframes ~ yan2025instantgaussianstreamfast . OCLDA-GS builds on this inference-based setting to improve motion support and Gaussian deformation. motion and object-aware deformation. Embedded deformation represents motion through blended local transformations~ sumner2007embedded , and SC-GS uses sparse control points with learned interpolation and local rigidity regularization~ huang2024scgs . Dynamic 3D Gaussians encourage coherent tracking through local motion constraints~ luiten2024dynamic . MotionGS incorporates optical-flow-based motion guidance, while MoDec-GS uses global-to-local motion decomposition ~ zhu2024motiongs,kwak2025modec . Closer to object-aware streaming, H3D-DGS combines object-wise motion processing with flow-assisted control points~ he2025h3ddgs , and ComGS uses motion-sensitive keypoints and a motion-aware influence field~ chen2025comgs . Building on these ideas, OCLDA-GS combines motion-aware anchor allocation, explicit group-restricted propagation, and learned rigid-motion-conditioned correction within keyframe-based streaming. title: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization
summary: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language models to robot control~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,qu2025spatialvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,fang2026molmoact2 . A common design keeps the autoregressive next-token prediction of the backbone: an action tokenizer discretizes continuous action chunks into tokens, which the policy generates either one token at a time~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,qu2025spatialvla or in blocks of tokens predicted in parallel~ liu2026oat_rss,jawaid2026nac,dong2026actioncodec,liu2026faster . The action tokenizer thus determines what the policy learns to predict and how errors in those predictions affect the resulting robot motion~ pertsch2025fast,liu2026oat_rss,dong2026actioncodec . Existing tokenizers have explored frequency-domain compression~ pertsch2025fast , learned temporal abstraction~ mete2024quest , vector quantization~ vandenoord2017vqvae,lee2024vqbet,wang2025vqvla , and coarse-to-fine coding~ liu2026oat_rss,jawaid2026nac , but they treat an action chunk as a flat vector and do not model how its dimensions are organized across the arms of the robot. This limitation is especially consequential in bimanual manipulation, where successful execution depends on coordinated motion across both arms. Tasks such as handing over objects, folding fabric, and carrying large objects often require two arms~ smith2012dual,krebs2022bimanual , and VLAs are increasingly being applied to these tasks~ liu2024rdt,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t,chen2025robotwin2 . However, most general-purpose action tokenizers concatenate both arms' actions into a single vector, a formulation we call joint tokenization. Although this formulation can capture cross-arm dependencies, it leaves the structure of bimanual coordination to be learned implicitly. Human bimanual manipulation illustrates two useful aspects of this structure: the arms share a repertoire of movements, yet adapt their actions to complementary roles~ guiard1987asymmetric . During a handover, for example, one hand presents and releases the object while the other reaches to receive and secure it. For robots with matching arm kinematics, this suggests an action representation that captures both reusable motion patterns across arms and task-dependent coordination between them. Joint tokenization does not explicitly distinguish these two aspects, leaving the policy to learn both shared motion structure and cross-arm dependencies from the concatenated representation. Making this structure explicit raises a design question. One option, which we call per-arm tokenization, splits the action by arm and tokenizes each arm separately, as in Tok~ xu2026m2tok , leaving coordination to the policy. Per-arm tokenization yields arm-indexed tokens and lets both arms reuse one motion representation, but it removes partner context from each arm's codes; in our experiments, such a tokenizer performs no better than the strongest joint tokenizer (Sec.~ sec:simulation-control ). This paper therefore asks: once the arms are tokenized as separate streams, how should the streams interact to yield a better interface for bimanual policies? Our key insight is that arm-indexed tokens need not be arm-independent: each arm's tokens can be computed with access to its partner while the two streams remain separate. We build on this insight in Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), a per-arm tokenizer that restores partner context. Its design follows one principle: share the motion representation across arms while conditioning discretization on the partner arm. For the shared motion patterns, BiCAT exploits the mirror-image mounting of the arms: it maps the right arm into the left arm's convention, so that mirrored motions share one canonical trajectory, and encodes both arms with one shared causal temporal encoder. For the cross-arm coordination, symmetric cross-arm attention adds partner context to each stream before shared finite scalar quantization (FSQ)~ mentzer2024fsq , and a joint decoder reconstructs both trajectories from temporally paired codes. Trained by reconstruction alone, BiCAT produces separate tokens for each arm, which the VLA predicts in two successive blocks: the tokens of each arm are generated in parallel, and the right arm is conditioned on the left. We compare BiCAT with eight baselines from seven tokenizer families under a common VLA training protocol. On ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks~ chen2025robotwin2 , BiCAT improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest baseline, with a gain that grows from 1.5 points on single-arm tasks to 21.3 on tightly coupled ones, and on six real-world tasks across three embodiments it succeeds in 113 of 150 trials, compared with 74 for OAT~ liu2026oat_rss . Two-block prediction keeps policy latency at least lower than token-by-token decoding. Ablations show that the gain requires both the tokenizer and the prediction schedule: removing cross-arm interaction or predicting both arms in one block leaves BiCAT no better than the strongest baseline. Our contributions are threefold: BiCAT, a per-arm action tokenizer that shares one motion representation across mirrored arms and exchanges partner context on both sides of the discrete bottleneck. Improved bimanual VLA control over eight baselines from seven tokenizer families in simulation, and over FAST and OAT on three real embodiments. An analysis of per-arm tokenization showing that cross-arm interaction inside the tokenizer and arm-wise block prediction in the policy are jointly required for the gain over joint tokenization. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models sec:related-vla VLAs build on vision-language models pretrained on internet-scale image and text data~ beyer2024paligemma,steiner2024paligemma2 and are fine-tuned on large robot datasets~ oxe2024,khazatsky2024droid for control~ driess2023palme,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,lee2025molmoact,fang2026molmoact2 , inheriting the instruction following and generalization of their backbones~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi05 . Existing VLAs differ mainly in how they output actions. Continuous approaches regress actions from the backbone or attach a generative action expert, such as a diffusion or flow-matching model~ kim2025oft,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,shukor2025smolvla . Discrete approaches tokenize actions and keep the autoregressive next-token objective of the backbone~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,qu2025spatialvla,wang2025vqvla,goyal2025vla0,liu2026faster . Discrete prediction can incur higher inference latency~ pertsch2025fast,liu2026faster , but it trains the backbone with the same next-token objective as its pretraining, which better preserves its pretrained knowledge than propagating a continuous action-expert loss into it~ driess2025knowledge . Both the latency and the learnability of discrete prediction depend on the action tokenizer~ pertsch2025fast,liu2026oat_rss,dong2026actioncodec , which makes it a central design choice for VLAs; we study it in the bimanual setting. Action Tokenization sec:related-tokenization Early discrete-action VLAs such as RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA~ brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla discretize each action dimension into bins and predict the resulting symbols autoregressively, which yields long sequences as the action dimension and horizon grow. FAST~ pertsch2025fast shortens them with a discrete cosine transform (DCT) and byte-pair encoding (BPE), at the cost of variable-length sequences that can decode into invalid actions~ liu2026oat_rss . Learned tokenizers instead compress action chunks into fixed sets of latent symbols: VQ-BeT~ lee2024vqbet and VQ-VLA~ wang2025vqvla use vector quantization, QueST~ mete2024quest combines causal temporal encoding with finite scalar quantization~ mentzer2024fsq , and OAT~ liu2026oat_rss , NAC~ jawaid2026nac , and CATok~ zhang2026catok order their tokens from coarse to fine. Beyond compression and reconstruction fidelity, recent work has examined how action representations affect downstream policy learning. ActionCodec~ dong2026actioncodec investigates tokenizer properties associated with VLA optimization, while X-Tokenizer~ kang2026xtokenizer and ActionPiece~ lian2026actionpiece incorporate vision-language alignment and relational supervision between action chunks, respectively. When applied to bimanual robots, most existing discrete tokenizers operate on the concatenated action vector of both arms, the joint tokenization of Sec.~ sec:introduction . Tok~ xu2026m2tok expands quantization capacity through multiple codebooks and tokenizes each arm separately, but does not model cross-arm interaction within the tokenizer, leaving its role in discrete action representations largely unexplored. Bimanual Action Representations sec:related-bimanual Bimanual policies typically represent both arms as one concatenated action vector. ACT~ zhao2023act and ALOHA Unleashed~ zhao2024alohaunleashed learn bimanual skills through action-chunk prediction, RDT-1B~ liu2024rdt develops a large-scale diffusion policy for bimanual manipulation, and general-purpose VLAs have been applied to bimanual robots~ black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t and evaluated on bimanual manipulation benchmarks~ chen2025robotwin2,wang2026roboeval . Explicit inter-arm structure has mainly been introduced in the policy: InterACT~ lee2024interact adds synchronization blocks between arm decoders. In the tokenizer, Tok~ xu2026m2tok separates the arms but keeps them independent. BiCAT instead models cross-arm interaction within a learned discrete action tokenizer, producing arm-indexed tokens through cross-arm attention and joint reconstruction. Method sec:method BiCAT tokenizes a bimanual action chunk into two arm-indexed token streams that share one motion representation and are computed with access to each other (Fig.~ fig:bicat_overview ). Sec.~ sec:preliminaries introduces action tokenization in the bimanual setting, Sec.~ sec:bicat_tokenization describes the tokenizer, whose training is summarized in Algorithm~ alg:bicat_training , and Sec.~ sec:bicat_policy describes how a VLA predicts its tokens. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Action tokenization. A VLA policy maps an observation , comprising camera images, robot state, and a language instruction, to a chunk of future actions . To retain the next-token prediction of its backbone, an action tokenizer maps the chunk to discrete tokens from a vocabulary of size , and a detokenizer maps tokens back to an executable chunk . Grouping the tokens into blocks , the policy with parameters is trained on demonstrations to maximize where the tokens within a block are predicted in parallel. Token-wise autoregression uses blocks of one token~ kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast , and block-wise prediction~ stern2018blockwise,liu2026oat_rss,jawaid2026nac,dong2026actioncodec,liu2026faster reduces the number of sequential decoding steps to . Bimanual action chunks. A bimanual chunk concatenates the actions of the left and right arms, where is the per-arm action dimension and denotes feature concatenation. Joint tokenization applies one tokenizer to the whole chunk, , so that a token can mix both arms. Per-arm tokenization applies it to each arm separately, for , which yields arm-indexed tokens but computes each arm's tokens without its partner. BiCAT keeps arm-indexed token streams but computes them from both arms: where contains tokens for arm , and the policy predicts the two streams as successive blocks (Sec.~ sec:bicat_policy ). title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.
full_text: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, a veil of backscattered light, and scene light that was scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present (Sanskrit for ``without water''), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. has three parts. is a three-path image formation model that adds a range-saturating forward-scattering contribution to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and derive bounds on how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. is a reversible physics anchor that ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter global physical model in both the recovery and the re-formation direction, so scene content cannot quietly hide inside the water. collects the physics-informed objectives, including a colour prior that balances channels separately at each range. To score water removal against ground truth, we also built (``with water''), a 30-scene synthetic evaluation suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On , raises rendering PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76\,dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on the real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44\,FPS. We close with a discussion of where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and of the limits of our own evaluation. Introduction sec:intro Marine ecologists, archaeologists, and the engineers who run underwater robots all want the same thing from a camera survey: a 3D model of the reef, wreck, or pipeline whose colours belong to the object and whose shape can be measured~ Capra2015, Vogler2019, Anwar2020 . Neural radiance fields~ Mildenhall2020 and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl2023 have made such models routine in air. Under water, the camera never sees the scene directly. Every pixel blends light from the object, weakened by absorption, with light scattered by the water itself, and the blend depends on wavelength and distance~ McGlamery1980, Jaffe1990, Akkaynak2018 . A splatting model fitted naively to these images bakes the water into the scene: colours drift with distance, and the optimiser fills the water column with semi-transparent ``floaters'' to explain the haze. The usual fix is to place an underwater image formation model inside the renderer~ Levy2023, Li2025WaterSplatting, Yang2025SeaSplat, Yuan2026UIR . Nearly all of these methods build on the two-term model of Sea-thru~ Akkaynak2019 , , which keeps direct transmission and backscatter. Two problems remain. The first is physical: the model leaves out scene light that is scattered through small angles and still reaches the sensor, which softens texture and keeps distant objects faintly visible~ Jaffe1990, Yuan2022TEBCF . The second is numerical, and it matters more for 3D. Removing the water means dividing by , so the gain applied to the data grows exponentially with range. A small mistake in the estimated backscatter or attenuation at the far end of the scene turns into a large colour error in the water-free output, and the photometric loss then pushes that error back into the geometry. On top of this, scene and water are not identifiable from the images alone~ Akkaynak2017, Akkaynak2018 : a flexible neural water model can absorb scene texture and still match every observation. is built around these two failure modes. Its first ingredient, (Sanskrit/Hindi for the confluence of three rivers), is a three-path image formation model that adds a range-saturating forward-scattering contribution to the classical two terms ( ). We show that this single extra term keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range ( ), and we derive how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours under both models ( ). The second ingredient, (``reflection''), is a reversible physics anchor. We keep an expressive neural water model for rendering, but tie it to a compact physical model with only ten global parameters through a recover-then-re-form round trip. A model that small cannot reproduce scene-specific structure, so any texture the neural branch tries to hide in the water shows up as an inconsistency and is penalised. The third ingredient, (``harmony''), gathers the physics-informed objectives, most notably a grey-world prior applied separately inside range bins so that colour is balanced at each distance rather than on average. Judging water removal is itself hard. Real underwater datasets such as SeaThru-NeRF~ Levy2023 have no ground truth for the water-free scene or its depth, and a recent controlled study shows that appearance scores and geometric accuracy can move in opposite directions under water~ AlvarezTunon2026 . We therefore built (``with water''), a set of 30 synthetic scenes path-traced in Blender Cycles under controlled water colour and turbidity, each paired with water-free images, depth, and normals. Our contributions are: , a three-path underwater image formation model for Gaussian splatting, with a proof that its inversion gain is bounded at every range and explicit bounds on how backscatter and attenuation errors reach the recovered colours; under the two-term model both quantities grow exponentially with range. , a reversible physics anchor that couples a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both the recovery and the formation direction. , a set of physics-informed objectives that includes a range-binned colour prior and joint appearance--geometry supervision. , a 30-scene path-traced evaluation suite with water-free, depth, and normal ground truth under controlled water colour and turbidity. The best rendering quality on and SeaThru-NeRF and the best depth on among nine methods at 44\,FPS, followed by a frank discussion of what these numbers do and do not show. Related Work sec:related Neural scene representations. NeRF~ Mildenhall2020 renders a scene by integrating an MLP radiance field along camera rays. Mip-NeRF~ Barron2021 adds anti-aliasing, and NeRF-W~ MartinBrualla2021 handles changing appearance with per-image embeddings, an idea we reuse. 3DGS~ Kerbl2023 swaps the implicit field for explicit anisotropic Gaussians and tile-based rasterisation and renders in real time. Later work sharpens its geometry through surface alignment~ Guedon2024 and planar multi-view regularisation~ Chen2025PGSR . All of these assume clear air. Single-image underwater restoration. Physics-based restoration grew out of scattering models for haze~ Narasimhan2002, He2011 and their underwater counterparts~ McGlamery1980, Jaffe1990 . Learning-based methods range from CNNs~ Li2020WaterNet, Islam2020 and Transformers~ Peng2023 to physics-guided unsupervised models~ Yan2023UWCycleGAN, Pan2024LUIE ; see~ Anwar2020, Cong2026 for surveys. title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling.
  In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view.
  We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73.
  Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
full_text: : Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO ragento.ai\\ amrit@ragento.ai ragento.ai\\ smarak@ragento.ai Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding . With 0.21 billion parameters, sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28~cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where , run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105. vision-language-action models, imitation learning, data augmentation, robustness, LIBERO-PRO Introduction LIBERO~ liu2023libero has become the default benchmark for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, and its four evaluation suites are now saturated: recent models report average success well above 90 ~ kim2025oft,openpi2025,zheng2025xvla . LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro asks what these numbers measure. It keeps LIBERO's scenes and perturbs one factor at a time: object appearance (Obj), initial positions (Pos), instruction wording (Sem), the task itself (Task) and the table (Env). Strong LIBERO models collapse under two of these. On the LIBERO-PRO leaderboard, OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , ~ black2024pi0 , MolmoAct~ lee2025molmoact and NORA~ hung2025nora score zero on almost every Pos and Task cell, and the best model, ~ pi2025pi05 , averages 0.11 over them. The models have learned to replay trajectories. The benchmark's headline number hides this. LIBERO-PRO summarizes a model by its mean over all cells, but Obj and Sem leave both the layout and the task unchanged, so a model that replays its training trajectories still scores highly on them. OpenVLA, for example, has a total of 0.52 while solving none of the position-perturbed or task-changed tests. Fig.~ fig:teaser separates the two readings. This paper takes a simple position: these policies fail because what they do is coupled to things it should not depend on. Each LIBERO task is demonstrated 50 times in almost the same layout, so the identity of an object is tied to where it stands, the motion is tied to the scene around it, and the instruction is tied to one wording and one initial layout. A policy trained on such data has no reason to separate them, whatever its size. Robustness under perturbation requires decoupling these factors, and it has to happen in two places at once. The first is the data. We re-arrange LIBERO's demonstrations by general rules. Re-placing every object and fixture at a random position and orientation decouples what an object is from where it is. Carrying tasks into other environments and onto other surfaces decouples the manipulation from its background. Paraphrasing decouples the task from its wording. The second is the policy's input. Variation in the data helps only if the policy can read it, so a perception engine hands the action model the same factors in separated form: a list of objects with their classes and global positions, a wrist code of the surfaces and depths in front of the gripper, and one image and one instruction embedding. With accurate object positions as an input, the policy does not need to recall a trajectory; it can act on the scene in front of it. The two parts are designed for each other: without varied data the position input carries no information that the policy needs, and without the position input the variation has to be recovered from pixels. We call the resulting system , for Robust Augmentation with Grounded Encoding. Our contributions are as follows. A general augmentation pipeline for LIBERO-style demonstrations. Every object and fixture is re-placed at a random position and orientation, tasks are transplanted into LIBERO's other environments and onto its other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased (Sec.~ sec:aug ). The rules are general: no layout, object pair or instruction is taken from LIBERO-PRO. , an object-centric flow-matching policy. Small perception adapters on a frozen DINOv3 backbone~ simeoni2025dinov3 produce an object list and a wrist-view code, TinyCLIP~ wu2023tinyclip provides one image and one text embedding, and a diffusion transformer trained from scratch produces actions (Sec.~ sec:model ). State-of-the-art LIBERO-PRO results among VLA policies on the full protocol, with 0.21 billion parameters in total (Sec.~ sec:exp ). Direct evidence that the policy acts on perceived positions. Changing the object positions given to the policy at inference changes its behaviour even in LIBERO's original layouts, and under LIBERO-PRO's graded object displacement the policy degrades far more slowly than evaluated in the same harness (Sec.~ sec:probe ). Related Work OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft fine-tune a 7B vision-language model. and ~ black2024pi0,pi2025pi05 attach a flow-matching action expert to a 3B vision-language model. MolmoAct~ lee2025molmoact and NORA~ hung2025nora decode discrete action tokens autoregressively, and X-VLA~ zheng2025xvla pairs a Florence encoder with a flow-matching transformer. Smaller policies such as SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla and Octo~ octo2024 trade accuracy for size. All of these compute actions from the image tokens of one vision-language backbone. factorizes the input instead: explicit object positions and a wrist code come from small perception adapters, and the vision-language input comes from an aligned image-text encoder, TinyCLIP~ wu2023tinyclip , a distilled CLIP~ radford2021clip , as one image embedding and one instruction embedding. LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro and LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus perturb LIBERO's objects, layouts, language, cameras and scenes, and show that LIBERO success does not transfer. We evaluate on LIBERO-PRO with its released files and its own perturbation code, including its graded object-displacement suites, which no leaderboard entry reports. MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen re-targets object-centric segments of human demonstrations to new object poses and validates them in simulation. Our augmentation follows the same principle on LIBERO and extends it to full-scene re-layouts, fixtures, other environments and other surfaces. Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy and flow-matching action heads~ black2024pi0 model action chunks generatively. We use a diffusion transformer~ peebles2023dit trained with flow matching~ lipman2023flow,liu2023rectified and the parameter-efficient conditioning of PixArt- ~ chen2024pixart . Our object head follows CenterNet~ zhou2019centernet on DINOv3 features~ simeoni2025dinov3 . Code-as-policies~ liang2023cap and, recently, ASPIRE~ aspire2026 use a large language model to write robot programs on top of perception and motion-planning interfaces. ASPIRE reports high success on LIBERO-PRO's position and task perturbations. It is a different paradigm, in which a frontier language model writes and debugs a program for each task, and we discuss it separately from learned VLA policies (Sec.~ sec:aspire ). Decoupling in the Data: General Augmentation sec:aug All data starts from LIBERO's human demonstrations, 50 for each of its 130 tasks. Generation stores simulator states and actions only, and images are rendered afterwards. Like MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen , we generate new demonstrations by transforming segments of the human ones into new scenes. Each demonstration is cut into object-centric phases (approach, grasp, transport, place, fixture interaction), and each phase is assigned the entity it acts on. For a phase acting on entity , every end-effector pose of the source demonstration is first expressed in the frame of at its source pose , and then mapped back to the world through the entity's new pose : The relative motion between gripper and object is therefore preserved wherever the object is placed and however it is rotated. Consecutive phases are joined by interpolated transit motions, and the gripper commands are kept from the source. Every generated trajectory is re-simulated and kept only if the task's own success predicate holds at the end. Seeds depend only on the task, the demonstration, the generator and the round, so the data can be regenerated exactly. In every generated trajectory the scene is laid out anew. In most attempts the layout is uniform: every fixture is placed anywhere on the table with a yaw anywhere in , carrying its contents, and every free object is placed anywhere within the robot's reach with a yaw drawn according to its symmetry. The others use smaller random displacements of the object to be grasped, the destination and the distractors. Tasks whose instruction is relational (``the bowl next to the plate'') receive only the smaller displacements, so that the instruction remains true. Candidate layouts are filtered for workspace bounds, clearance, stability and reachability before re-simulation. No positions are exchanged between objects, and no layout is taken from any file other than LIBERO's own scene definitions. A task is carried into every other LIBERO environment that can host it, and the same random re-layout is applied on top. A transplant is valid when the task involves at most one fixture and at most three entities in total, and every object or fixture named in the instruction exists exactly once in the target environment, so that the instruction stays unambiguous. Objects are never inserted into a scene. Goal regions that are named after an entity, such as the front of the stove, move with that entity. The transplanted trajectory keeps the instruction of the task it carries. Every task is also moved onto each of LIBERO's other table surfaces, again with a random re-layout on top. A language model wrote 20 paraphrases for each instruction. During training the original instruction or one of its paraphrases is drawn at random. Each task receives a fixed quota of successful trajectories per round, split between its own environment, other environments and other surfaces (Appendix~ app:impl ). Data is generated in rounds with different seeds; all but one are used for training, and the last is held out as a test set and is used only to measure perception and action error (Table~ tab:data ). Each rule removes one correlation that LIBERO's demonstrations contain. Random re-layout decouples the identity of an object from its place: almost no training trajectory keeps an object or a fixture where LIBERO placed it, so the policy cannot succeed by recalling a path and has to read where the objects are from its inputs. Environment and surface transplants, each with a new layout on top, decouple the manipulation from its background: the room and the table change independently of where the objects stand, so neither can serve as a landmark for a stored motion. title: GRID-UAV: Geometry and Ray-depth Integrated Decision-making for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).

On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5 (seen), 17.1 (unseen objects) and 25.4 (unseen map). github.com/anas2908/GRID-UAV . Introduction sec:intro Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used for delivery and search-and-rescue operations, where an operator would state a goal in natural language, ``fly to your left and find the white truck parked on a residential street,'' and let the vehicle do the rest. In aerial vision-language navigation~ wang2025towards , the UAV must follow such an instruction through a large outdoor environment, flying hundreds of meters without collision and stopping at targets it has never seen before. Because UAVs are battery-powered and payload-limited, heavy sensors such as LiDAR shorten flight time~ abdilla2015power . Thus, at test time we use only forward- and downward-facing RGB cameras and must infer 3D structure from them~ sadeghi2016cad2rl,loquercio2018dronet . VLA models~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,team2024octo , now used across many robot embodiments and recently on UAVs~ xu2026aerovla,sun2026autofly , are a natural fit, but their 2D image encoders capture what is in an image rather than where it lies in 3D space~ el2024probing . This is a problem for a UAV, whose viewpoint changes rapidly in 3D, because a small tree nearby and a large tree far away can occupy the same part of the image. A common solution is to give the policy depth information. 3D-aware VLAs~ zhen20243d,qu2025spatialvla do this successfully in robot manipulation, where the relevant objects lie close to the camera. A UAV differs in three ways. First, it chooses its own altitude, so it must reason about what lies below as well as ahead. Second, the obstacles and targets that shape its route are often tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable~ yin2023metric3d . Third, near the target, the same object often appears in both cameras at once, e.g., its side in the forward view and its top in the downward one, so it must be matched across two very different views. Depth input helps UAV policies in compact, short-range settings~ sun2026autofly,loquercio2021learning , but on long outdoor flights ( wang2025towards ) we find that feeding depth features directly brings no gain ( w/ depth vs.\ w/o depth success), whereas lifting the depth~ yang2024depthv2 into 3D~ wang2019pseudo,philion2020lift raises success to . Hence, we study how 3D information should be given to UAV. We compare two forms of 3D grounding. In explicit grounding, we estimate metric depth with a monocular model adapted to aerial viewpoints, use each pixel's viewing ray to place every image patch at its 3D position in the UAV's own body frame, for both the forward and downward cameras, and add these positions to the visual tokens. In implicit grounding, we align the policy's visual features during training with those of a frozen 3D geometry model~ wang2025vggt , so that it learns to represent geometry on its own. To compare the two, we look at how flights fail. A flight can fail in one of two ways: (T1)~the UAV never reaches the target (comes within 15\,m horizontally of it), usually because it crashes on the way; or (T2)~it reaches the target but fails to finish, for example by hovering high above it. The two forms fail at different stages ( ). Explicit grounding suffers less from T1: the UAV crashes less and reaches the target more often ( vs.\ ). But it suffers more from T2: once there, it finishes less often ( vs.\ ) and hovers above the target nearly twice as often. Implicit grounding shows the reverse. We attribute this to what each form provides. Avoiding T1 requires knowing how far away things are, which explicit grounding provides directly. Avoiding T2 requires recognizing that the object in the forward view and the one in the downward view are the same, that is, relating the two current views, which we hypothesize implicit grounding learns. Since the two are complementary, we propose (Geometry and Ray-depth Integrated Decision-making), a UAV VLA that combines both and needs only RGB cameras at test time. Unlike prior UAV VLAs, which either use no depth (AeroVLA~ xu2026aerovla ) or feed it through a Siamese projector without 3D lifting (AutoFly~ sun2026autofly ), grounds the policy in 3D both explicitly and implicitly. The explicit branch adds only M trainable parameters (2.2 of trainable and 0.07 of total parameters) on top of frozen depth estimator, the implicit branch adds no inference overhead. By combining the two ( ), has fewer en-route failures (T1) than the implicit-only policy (reach , ) and fewer at-goal failures (T2) than the explicit-only policy (completion , ). On TravelUAV benchmark, it raises overall success from to , is the best on every split, and gains most on the unseen map ( relative), which tests generalization to new environments. Our contributions are as follows: A failure analysis of UAV VLAs that separates failing to reach the target (T1) from failing to complete the task once there (T2). We also show that directly adding depth features brings no gain in long-horizon aerial navigation, and that explicit and implicit 3D grounding address different failures. We propose , a UAV VLA policy that needs only RGB cameras at test time and combines explicit 3D lifting across forward and downward cameras with implicit alignment to a frozen geometry model, where the alignment adds no cost at inference. achieves state-of-the-art success on all TravelUAV benchmark test splits, with the largest improvement on the unseen map. Related Work sec:related Aerial VLN benchmarks. Aerial VLN has been studied through dialog-guided (AVDN~ fan2023aerial ), route-following (AerialVLN~ liu2023aerialvln ) and map-assisted (CityNav~ lee2024citynav ) benchmarks, and at scale by OpenFly~ gao2026openfly and AutoFly~ sun2026autofly . OpenFly and AutoFly use short routes ( \,m and \,m, the latter in scenes); AerialVLN and CityNav have longer routes but discrete actions without flight kinematics. TravelUAV~ wang2025towards , which we use, combines long routes ( \,m on average, up to \,km) with continuous flight and only a coarse direction instruction with a target description, so the UAV must itself judge distances over hundreds of meters. VLAs for UAVs. VLAs~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 have been adapted to UAV racing~ serpiva2025racevla , cognitive tasks~ lykov2025cognitivedrone and navigation~ sun2026autofly,xu2026aerovla . On TravelUAV, the benchmark's own baseline pairs a navigation LLM that predicts hierarchical trajectories~ wang2025towards ; NavFoM~ zhang2026embodied trains a single navigation foundation model across robot embodiments, including UAVs; and AeroVLA~ xu2026aerovla , maps forward-downward views and a coarse directional prompt directly to flight commands. All of them rely on 2D image encoders without 3D grounding. 3D grounding in VLAs. Several works add 3D information to manipulation VLAs. One line provides 3D information as input: 3D-VLA~ zhen20243d builds on 3D scene features, SpatialVLA~ qu2025spatialvla adds egocentric 3D position encodings to visual tokens, and PointVLA~ li2026pointvla and GeoVLA~ sun2025geovla inject point-cloud features. Another line transfers geometric knowledge from a 3D foundation model~ wang2025vggt , either by fusing its features into the policy (Evo-0~ lin2025evo ) or by aligning the policy's internal representations~ yu2025repa with them during training (Spatial Forcing~ li2026spatial ). These works target tabletop scenes close to the camera and follow one line or the other. adapts both to long-range, two-camera aerial navigation and combines them. Depth for long-horizon UAV navigation. AutoFly~ sun2026autofly is the closest prior work: it feeds DAv2~ yang2024depthv2 to a UAV VLA through a shared (Siamese) projector and reports a -point gain in success, in a setting with short routes in scenes and a single forward camera, where nearby obstacles keep monocular depth reliable. The TravelUAV benchmark is more demanding: obstacles and targets lie tens to hundreds of meters away, long routes let depth errors accumulate, and the target must be matched across two cameras. Feeding depth through AutoFly's shared Siamese projector ( ) leaves success essentially unchanged ( ), whereas lifting the same depth into 3D improves it; builds on this and adds implicit geometric alignment. Methodology sec:method keeps a standard VLA policy and changes only what its visual tokens carry ( ). Explicit 3D lifting ( ) adds to each token the metric position of the surface it sees, and implicit geometric alignment ( ) aligns the same tokens inside the LLM with a frozen VGGT during training only. Both need only the RGB cameras at test time and leave the action interface unchanged. Task and Base Policy sec:base Task. At each step, the UAV observes a front image and a downward image . It is given a description of the target and, as in~ xu2026aerovla , a coarse bearing toward it (one of seven sectors, e.g.\ ``forward-left''), recomputed at every step from the target's true position, which makes it a coarse form of oracle guidance. The policy outputs forward, vertical and yaw commands, or LAND to end the episode; an episode succeeds if the UAV stops within 20\,m of the target~ wang2025towards . Base policy. We follow the formulation in~ xu2026aerovla on an OpenVLA backbone~ kim2024openvla . The frozen vision encoder (DINOv2~ oquab2023dinov2 and SigLIP~ zhai2023sigmoid ) encodes each view separately, with shared weights, into patch tokens~ dosovitskiy2020image , so every token covers part of exactly one camera. The concatenated tokens pass through a trainable projector into Llama-2 7B~ touvron2023llama , fine-tuned with LoRA~ hu2021lora . Each command is quantized into 99 uniform bins and written as a two-digit token, and training minimizes the cross-entropy of these action tokens. title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
summary: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

Johnson , John Lathrop , and Soon-Jo Chung These authors are with the Department of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125 USA (e-mail: \ jdibrahi, gxj, jlathrop, sjchung\ @caltech.edu). This author is with the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 USA (e-mail: berrueta@stanford.edu). Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance. Supplementary Video--- . Robot Safety, Formal Methods in Robotics and Automation, Optimization and Optimal Control, Contraction Theory. Introduction sec:introduction obots are increasingly asked to operate near the limits of their capabilities. Legged robots run and recover from falls using policies learned in simulation~ hwangbo2019learning . Learned controllers race drones past human champions and to the physical limits of the platform~ kaufmann2023champion,song2023reaching . Automated vehicles exploit tire saturation to avoid collisions and to drive at the limits of adhesion~ funke2017collision,kritayakirana2012autonomous,betz2022autonomous . In each case, the most valuable behaviors lie near the boundary of the operating envelope, and improving performance means operating closer to that boundary or expanding the envelope itself, a practice known as envelope expansion. However, conventional safety certification penalizes operation at the boundary, treating peak performance as a hazard to be avoided. Most formal safety frameworks are based on the principle of forward invariance~ blanchini1999set , in which a set of safe states is rendered invariant under the closed-loop dynamics. This principle underlies control barrier functions (CBFs)~ ames2017control,ames2019control , Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability~ mitchell2005time,bansal2017hamilton , viability theory~ aubin1991viability , and predictive safety filters~ wabersich2021predictive,hsu2024safety . However, establishing forward invariance of the deployed closed-loop system requires a dynamical model that can be trusted throughout the safe set. High-performance operation concentrates the robot in regimes such as tire saturation, contact, and degraded surfaces, where models are least reliable and data are scarce. As a result, these guarantees are weakest where they are needed most. Invariance-based frameworks also impose a direct cost on performance, since safety filters steer the system away from the boundary of the safe set even in minimally invasive formulations~ fisac2019general,hsu2024safety . Backup controller methods lighten the modeling burden by certifying a backup policy instead~ gurriet2018towards,chen2021backup , but they retain its filter and cost, and their membership certificates offer no convergence rate or notion of margin. In this work, we show that robots do not need certified behavior to be certifiably safe. We formalize safety as recoverability, the certified ability of a robot to fall back on a trusted recovery behavior. Recoverability moves the invariance requirement off the deployed controller and onto the recovery mode, so the deployed controller may be aggressive, learned, or experimental, with no contraction, invariance, or modeling requirement. Figure~ fig:architecture shows the resulting architecture, in which a recoverability monitor hands control from the deployed mode to the recovery mode at a certified time. Using contraction theory, we certify a tube around the recovery reference from which recovery converges exponentially. Monitoring safety then reduces to evaluating a closed-form Riemannian distance, and the guarantee degrades gracefully under perturbations. The contraction insertion gradient then tells the robot when to hand off, scheduling the switch through an optimization whose feasible solutions are all safe. As a result, robots can run behaviors that invariance-based safety cannot certify, requiring only that they are recoverable. The contributions of this article are as follows. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that certifies a trusted recovery mode instead of the deployed controller, and prove that switching within a tube yields robust exponential convergence. We derive the contraction insertion gradient and use it to schedule switches through an optimization in which feasibility alone certifies recovery, and we synthesize certified tubes by sequential convex programming, benchmarking them against exact HJ viability. We demonstrate recoverability in quadrotor flight past uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms CBFs and backup CBFs, and onboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar at the limits of handling in the rain. Our results and experiments are also shown and summarized in a supplementary video accompanying this manuscript. The rest of the manuscript is structured as follows: Section~ sec:related-works positions recoverability against invariance-based and fallback-based safety. Section~ sec:preliminaries defines the closed-loop modes and recovery tubes. Section~ sec:scheduling presents our main results, proving recoverability from the tube, turning the certificate into an optimal switching decision, and evaluating it in quadrotor flight. Section~ sec:certificate_synthesis grows certified tubes through convex synthesis and benchmarks them against exact HJ viability. Section~ sec:racecar deploys the framework onboard a full-scale autonomous racecar, and Section~ sec:discussion concludes. Related Work sec:related-works The largest family of certification methods rests on forward invariance. HJ reachability computes the maximal safe set and answers the safety question exactly, but it requires a trusted global model and offline computation that scales exponentially with state dimension~ mitchell2005time,bansal2017hamilton . Control barrier functions reduce the online burden to a quadratic program, but synthesizing a valid barrier function is itself a difficult problem that scales poorly beyond modest dimensions~ ames2017control,ames2019control . Predictive safety filters replace offline synthesis with online optimization over a receding horizon, and they inherit the model requirements of the underlying predictions~ wabersich2021predictive,hsu2024safety . In every case the certified object is the deployed closed-loop system, so the modeling burden grows with the aggressiveness of the deployed behavior, and the filter itself biases operation away from the envelope boundary~ fisac2019general . Our framework instead inherits its guarantee from the recovery mode's contraction certificate for as long as a certified switch remains within reach, so the modeling burden falls on the recovery mode alone and the deployed behavior is never filtered at the boundary. In our work, the certificate rests on contraction theory, which establishes incremental exponential convergence of trajectories under a Riemannian metric~ lohmiller1998contraction,tsukamoto2021contraction . Contraction-based tubes have been used for robust motion planning~ singh2023robust , and learned metrics extend these tools to data-driven settings~ tsukamoto2021neural , where contraction certifies the tracking performance of the deployed controller. Instead, we focus on certifying a recovery mode, and the minimizing geodesic of the metric supplies the gradient that drives the switching decision. Gradient formulas for switching times~ xu2004optimal,egerstedt2006transition and the mode insertion gradients behind sequential action control~ ansari2016sequential optimize performance objectives with the mode schedule as the design variable. The contraction insertion gradient is the insertion gradient of a safety certificate rather than a performance cost, so the resulting switching-time problem certifies safety through feasibility alone. Certificate synthesis has its own literature, from maximum-volume invariant ellipsoids~ boyd1994linear and sum-of-squares barrier certificates~ prajna2004safety to funnel libraries that precompute certified tubes for online composition~ majumdar2017funnels . Control contraction metrics make the search for a metric convex~ manchester2017control , but the geodesic distances their certificates require are rarely available in closed form. Our transport certificates combine the flexibility of these richer classes with the closed-form online test of an ellipsoid, and accepted sequential convex updates grow the tube monotonically while preserving certification. Recoverability shares its premise with simplex and runtime-assurance architectures, which separate an unverified performance controller from a verified backup controller~ seto1998simplex,hobbs2023runtime . Recent work optimizes the supervisor and automates recoverability proofs~ miller2024optimal,nigam2023recoverability . The closest works to ours are backup controller methods~ gurriet2018towards,gurriet2020scalable,chen2021backup and their disturbance-robust extensions~ vanwijk2024disturbance , which fix a trusted fallback policy and certify safety online by forward integrating its dynamics and checking membership in an implicitly defined invariant set, the rollout set . This shrinks the modeling burden to the fallback policy alone, the same relocation our framework performs, but the certificate is a binary membership test with no convergence rate~ chen2021backup , and evaluating it requires integrating the fallback flow and its sensitivity matrix at every step. A quadratic program then blends the nominal and backup commands, so the executed trajectory tracks neither the intended behavior nor a certified fallback and pays a performance cost whenever the constraint is active. Our certificate instead guarantees convergence at an explicit rate with robustness to disturbances and model error, accommodates time-varying references, and lets the switch be scheduled ahead of time. Figure~ fig:comparison_panel summarizes this landscape, with uncertified deployment on the left, a backup-CBF filter accumulating a performance penalty in the center, and our framework on the right, which executes the intended behavior untouched until a single certified switch.
