title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
summary: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Large robot foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), can perform a wide range of behaviors. For these models to reliably succeed on a particular task, they must learn to improve via interaction with their environment. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a way to improve their task performance through interaction, but updating large policies can be computationally expensive. Noise steering has emerged as an approach to guide the denoising process of diffusion and flow-matching policies by replacing the initial noise samples. However, these methods struggle to scale to high-dimensional noise inputs that are common in large policy classes such as VLAs and WAMs. This work develops a noise steering method that addresses this challenge, focusing primarily on WAMs. World-action models couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation. Their sampling inputs include initial source distribution noise associated with both video and actions, and changing the video noise can also change the actions the model produces. Existing action-noise steering methods do not exploit this input, and in the implementations and settings we evaluate they give no consistent improvement when applied to the substantially larger video-noise space. In this work, we find that WAMs' decoded actions are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, implying video noise may serve as a strong steering modality. We introduce ( ), a method to efficiently train noise steering policies for world-action models. Recent work has found that selecting the initial noise samples of diffusion or flow matching heads can effectively steer robot policies in a sample efficient manner without requiring any updates to the full model~ dsrl . We find that extending noise steering to large robot foundation models often fails, primarily because their noise inputs are high-dimensional and their sensitivity to it differs sharply between the video and action inputs. overcomes these challenges by steering a low-rank projection of the noise distribution. A steering actor outputs a low-dimensional vector that a fixed random projection lifts to the full noise dimension, which is then rescaled to resemble a Gaussian sample's norm. The frozen policy denoises this noise, and the actor is trained with reinforcement learning. This formulation scales to high-dimensional action spaces and, most surprisingly, enables the steerability of the video noise to improve denoised actions. Two design choices underlie our approach. First, the actor controls only a small, low-rank subspace of the noise regardless of the input dimension. We show that such a low-rank subspace contains directions that improve on the base policy with high probability. Second, mixing the actor's direction with a fresh Gaussian sample preserves the expected squared norm of the noise, so the steered noise stays near the typical norm that diffusion and flow-matching policies are trained to denoise. Because neither choice depends on the structure of the noise input, can be applied to either the video or the action noise of a WAM. This flexibility matters in practice: we find that a WAM's actions are far more sensitive to one noise input than the other, and a probe that needs no reward identifies that input before training. On the three models we evaluate, it is the video noise, which existing methods do not steer. We evaluate on three world-action models, on action-noise steering with , , and Diffusion Policy, and on a physical bimanual robot station. In aggregate across three WAMs and ten model--task pairs, DSRL on the action noise improves the base policies by 7.1 percentage points, while steers the more expressive video noise and improves them by 26.2 percentage points. We also evaluate on twelve action-policy simulation tasks, where it generally achieves higher early-training success against DSRL~ dsrl and LP-DS~ lpds . Finally, we demonstrate that trained in simulation transfers to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks on two base policies, the released GR00T N1.7 and a fine-tuned in simulation, without additional training on hardware. Our contributions are fourfold: We introduce , low-rank noise steering for robot foundation models: a fixed random subspace of the noise, mixed with a fresh Gaussian sample, independent of the actor's output, so that the expected squared noise norm is preserved. We identify noise-norm preservation as a key requirement for reliable steering, and measure the band of norms that each frozen policy tolerates. We prove that a random subspace of rank misses the high-advantage noise of a state with probability at most , where is that noise's share of the sphere, and that a policy which selects an improving direction in that subspace whenever one exists improves on the base policy. We provide a practical recipe for steering world-action models, with a reward-free probe that finds which noise input to steer, and evaluate it on three world-action models, twelve action-policy tasks, and a bimanual robot station with two base policies. Related Work sec:related_work Reinforcement learning for generative robot policies. Diffusion and flow-matching policies~ diffusionpolicy,pi0,flowmatching generate action chunks by iteratively denoising a Gaussian sample. The same principle underlies generalist models~ groot and world-action models, which jointly denoise future video and actions~ cosmospolicy,dreamzero . These policies are commonly improved by fine-tuning their weights with policy gradients~ dppo,reinflow or by learning residual corrections to their actions~ policydecorator . For models with billions of parameters, however, online weight updates are computationally expensive and risk eroding pretrained capabilities. In contrast, keeps the policy frozen and adapts only its initial noise. Steering frozen generative policies. DSRL~ dsrl showed that a frozen diffusion or flow policy can be adapted by training an RL agent in its noise space. Concurrent work~ nsl likewise trains a Gaussian actor over the action noise of a frozen flow-matching VLA. Subsequent work regularizes the learned noise with a budget on its deviation from a Gaussian sample~ lpds , or restricts the actor to the noise directions to which the decoder is most sensitive~ ni2026pss . Golden-ticket search~ goldenticket instead finds a single fixed noise that improves a policy across states. Latent policy steering~ lps fixes the norm of the steered noise at its typical value and trains the actor offline with gradients through a one-step policy. These methods were developed for policies with low-dimensional noise. They either do not explicitly control the norm of the steered noise~ dsrl,ni2026pss,nsl , control it only on average~ lpds , or require a sensitivity probe whose cost grows linearly with the noise dimension~ ni2026pss . Fixing the norm exactly~ lps still leaves the full noise dimension as the search space and requires a policy that is differentiable in one step. In contrast, steers a random low-rank slice that requires no probing or gradients through the policy and preserves the expected squared norm of the noise by construction, which allows it to scale to the video noise of world-action models. Noise geometry and low-rank adaptation. High-dimensional Gaussian noise concentrates near a fixed norm. Image generative models exploit this property by interpolating along the corresponding sphere~ white2016,ddim and regularizing the norm during noise optimization~ reno,samuel2023 , and their outputs degrade when sampling drifts from it~ ning2024 . Separately, LoRA~ lora and studies of intrinsic dimension~ intrinsicdim show that large networks can be adapted within low-rank or random subspaces of their parameters. Outside robotics, active-subspace noise steering~ asns searches the initial noise of a frozen flow model along a few objective-sensitive directions estimated from objective values alone. brings both ideas to policy adaptation: it applies a random low-rank subspace to the input of a frozen model rather than its weights, and keeps the result concentrated near the typical Gaussian norm. Preliminaries and Problem Statement sec:problem We consider adapting a pretrained robot policy to a target task through online interaction. Let denote a frozen diffusion or flow-matching policy that maps an observation and an initial noise to an action chunk . Typically, during training of a policy , is always drawn from the Gaussian source distribution, . We model the target task as a Markov decision process with observations , action chunks , transition dynamics , reward function , and discount factor . DSRL noise steering~ dsrl replaces the input Gaussian sample with the output of a learned actor and executes . Because is fixed, it can be absorbed into the environment, which produces an MDP whose action space is the noise space . The objective is to find an actor that maximizes the expected discounted return , where . DSRL instantiates this formulation with SAC~ sac , whose bounded output replaces the noise; for action-chunk policies such as , it tiles a low-dimensional output across the steps of the chunk. A standard Gaussian sample has norm close to , and by the Gaussian annulus theorem~ blum2020foundations nearly all samples lie in a thin shell around the sphere of that radius, whose width relative to the radius shrinks as grows. We express norms as multiples of the typical norm . On this scale, the norms of Gaussian samples vary by approximately : about 13 for the 28-dimensional action noise of a small diffusion policy, but only 0.1 for the 506 , 880-dimensional video noise of Cosmos3-Edge. A large policy is therefore pretrained only on noise from a very narrow range of norms. examines how it behaves outside this range. Why Noise Steering Fails on Large Policies sec:analysis Before introducing , we examine why noise steering, which is effective on small diffusion policies~ dsrl , fails on large robot foundation models. We study four frozen policies: a Robomimic diffusion policy~ diffusionpolicy,robomimic , ~ pi0 , and two world-action models, Cosmos3-Edge and DreamZero-14B~ dreamzero . Their noise dimensions range from 28 for the Robomimic action noise to 506 , 880 for the Cosmos3-Edge video noise. We identify two failure modes. Failure mode 1: the search space grows with the noise dimension. The action noise of a generalist policy spans an entire chunk of padded action channels, and the video noise of a world-action model spans every latent pixel of every predicted frame. A noise steering actor that sets each entry independently must search a space of dimension , which reaches around for the Cosmos video noise. Steering such large policies therefore motivates the need for a search space whose dimension is independent of . Failure mode 2: the tolerated band of noise norms is policy-dependent and can be very narrow. We analyze how different input noise samples change policy performance by scaling Gaussian samples by a factor and measure each policy's success ( ). This scaling also scales the norm of the sample. Every policy fails once moves far enough from . Cosmos3-Edge fails outside , whereas DreamZero-14B holds its success from to and fails only by . The noise-steering methods we compare against leave the norm uncontrolled or constrain it only on average, and often fall outside this band. For example, we find that DSRL's noise sampling applied to the Cosmos3-Edge video noise produces noise at 0.003 times the typical norm and achieves zero success. title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation at CoRL 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action models (VLA) black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2024openvla are largely pretrained on cross-embodiment corpora dominated by parallel-jaw grippers o2024openXembodiment,Khazatsky2024Droid . This confines them to tasks that a two-finger gripper can solve, which excludes many tasks involving tool use and reorientation of the hand zhang2025dexterousmanufacturing,an2025dexterousILsurvey . Because multi-fingered hands are scarce in existing pretraining data zhang2026dexora,luo2026being , deploying a VLA on a novel dexterous embodiment necessitates fine-tuning. Furthermore, this adaptation must succeed on a limited number of demonstrations due to the high data-collection cost associated with dexterous teleoperation TaoT-RSS-25,arcap2025,guzey2025dexteritysmartlensesmultifingered . In this work, we investigate how to adapt VLA models for tasks with multi-fingered hands on limited data. How to fine-tune a VLA, meaning which of its parameters to update and at what rate, is already contested: some report that freezing the language model or the vision encoder degrades adaptation ferchau2026efficiency,kim2024openvla , others keep action-pathway gradients out of the backbone by default nvidia2025gr00tn15,driess2025knowledge . These conclusions were reached by evaluating adaptation solely based on the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) checkpoint with the highest rollout success. When adaptation pipelines culminate in latent-noise steering wagenmaker2025DSRL,yu2026support , the SFT checkpoint merely serves as an initialization. The critical factor is instead whether the frozen model's noise space admits an actor that succeeds and generalizes beyond its training states. In this paper, we investigate five SFT recipes to determine which, if any, reliably supports dexterous manipulation transfer when followed by latent steering. Our recipes vary which parts of the VLA we train (action expert only, plus the vision pathway, or the full model) and whether we update the language model and action expert fully or via LoRA hu2022lora adapters. Our analysis applies these combinations to intelligence2025pi05 on a 16-DoF LEAP hand shaw2023leap across two simulation tasks. We first compare VLA fine-tuning recipes as initialization for latent steering. Based on our empirical analysis, we provide a concrete recommendation: when SFT is followed by latent steering, freeze the VLM, train the action expert in full, and avoid using SFT rollout success for recipe or checkpoint selection. Furthermore, the choice of checkpoint mattered less than the choice of recipe. Since steerability declines over the course of SFT while motion quality improves, we suggest selecting the earliest checkpoint that qualitatively reproduces the demonstrated skill as the initialization for steering. Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action models. VLAs adapt a pretrained vision-language model on robot data so that it emits low-level actions black2024pi0,kim2024openvla,octo_2023 . The prevailing design consists of: a VLM backbone encodes images and language, and a smaller generative action expert decodes a chunk of continuous actions from the backbone's features by diffusion or flow matching black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,fang2026molmoact2 . The VLA approach has been extended to dexterous manipulation by training from scratch on new data sources---egocentric human video and large multi-fingered corpora nvidia2026gr00tn17,luo2026being,li2025vitra . We take a complementary route: adapting an existing gripper-pretrained VLA to a multi-fingered hand from a few dozen demonstrations. Fine-tuning VLAs. How to fine-tune a VLA for a new setup is an open question, particularly as prior research shows mixed results. OpenVLA kim2024openvla and Ferchau et al.\ ferchau2026efficiency find rank-32 LoRA on the backbone and action expert competitive with full fine-tuning, but Ferchau et al.\ also find that freezing the VLM, or restricting the vision encoder to LoRA, degrades performance sharply. GR00T N1.5 nvidia2025gr00tn15 and knowledge insulation driess2025knowledge reach the opposite default, keeping action-pathway gradients out of the language model. OpenVLA-OFT kim2025fine studies the decoding scheme, action representation, and objective rather than deciding which parameters to update, and, like the others, selects the checkpoints by the success of the SFT rollout. Improving VLAs with reinforcement learning. Online improvement of a fine-tuned VLA takes two forms. One updates the model's weights, with stabilization against forgetting intelligence2025pi,guo2025conrft,lu2025irevla . Others leave the model frozen and learn a small policy over its generative latent: Diffusion Steering Reinforcement Learning (DSRL) wagenmaker2025DSRL steers the initial noise of a diffusion or flow policy. Residual flow steering RFS2026Su adds a learned action residual for dexterous tasks. We adopt DSRL as the endpoint because it needs no distillation and never touches the fine-tuned weights, so differences between recipes act only through the frozen model. These works take the base policy as given; none asks how to fine-tune it, or which checkpoint to steer from. The closest work to ours is SCORE yu2026support , which frames steering as support-constrained RL and uses it to improve real-world multi-fingered policies through simulation. SCORE's data ablation finds that retry and play data leave base-policy success unchanged but substantially raise post-steering success, suggesting the prior should be prepared for steering rather than zero-shot performance. SCORE establishes this along the data axis for a point-cloud flow policy trained from scratch; we establish it along the fine-tuning-recipe axis for an image-based VLA with large-scale pretraining. Studying VLA Adaptation Recipes for Steering sec:method Our goal is to determine which SFT recipe produces the best policy when adaptation of a dual-system VLA is followed by latent-noise steering. We first provide preliminary information to put our work into context, define the design decisions a recipe makes and the five recipes that isolate them ( ), and then describe how each recipe is executed on (App.~ app:recipes ) and how the resulting checkpoints are steered with DSRL and evaluated ( ). Preliminary sec:background The model. We study intelligence2025pi05 , a dual-system VLA in which a PaliGemma backbone beyer2024paligemma encodes images, language and the binned proprioceptive state, and a flow-matching action expert produces chunks of actions zhao2023act . A new embodiment affects the VLA's state through the language model, and its actions through the expert's linear projections (see App.~ app:model ). Diffusion steering RL. The expert maps Gaussian noise to an action chunk by integrating a learned velocity field conditioned on the observation lipman2023flow,black2024pi0 . SFT continues this training with gradients restricted to a subset of the weights. The chosen parameter subset and learning rate is how we define an SFT recipe. At inference, the chunk is a deterministic function . DSRL wagenmaker2025DSRL exploits this: treating the task as a with reward and discount , it leaves frozen and learns a policy over the noise , crediting each executed chunk's reward to the that produced it. Adaptation design decisions sec:method:decisions We investigate the adaptation of a pretrained VLA to an embodiment absent from its pretraining data, utilizing a few dozen teleoperated demonstrations per task. Our pipeline consists of SFT on the demonstration data, followed by online improvement via DSRL. We isolate four key design decisions: updating the language model (H1), updating the vision encoder (H2), and updating the backbone/action expert either fully or through low-rank adapters (H3, H4). We construct five distinct recipes to evaluate these axes: : The action expert and its interface to the backbone are trained; the entire VLM remains frozen. : Extends \ by unfreezing the vision encoder and multimodal projector, isolating the impact of the vision pathway (H2). : All parameters are trained end-to-end. Contrasting this with \ and \ isolates the effect of language model adaptation (H1). : Applies rank-32 LoRA hu2022lora to the language model and action expert, while fully training the vision encoder, multimodal projector, and action projections. : Matches , but adds rank-32 LoRA to the language model. This isolates language model adaptation with fixed representations (H1) and contrasts with \ regarding full vs. adapter-based expert training (H4). Comparing this against \ isolates the update parameterization (H3). title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.

Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation in practical manipulation settings. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation~ kim2025openvla, zitkovich2023rt, black2024pi_0 . By integrating visual perception, language conditioning, and action generation, they enable robots to interpret natural-language instructions and perform diverse manipulation tasks. As VLA-based robots show growing promise for real-world deployment, their reliability under adversarial conditions becomes a critical requirement for safe operation in physical environments. Recent studies have begun to examine this concern through adversarial attacks on robotic VLA systems. Existing attacks mainly optimize visual perturbations or adversarial patches to induce prediction-level discrepancies, semantic confusion, or rollout-level deviations~ wang2025exploring, sadeghi2023attacking, wu2024characterizing . Typical objectives enlarge the difference between clean and perturbed actions, drive the policy toward erroneous manipulation behaviors, or cause visible deviations over the rollout. Although effective at task disruption, these methods primarily treat the VLA output or rollout behavior as the attack target, while the physical realization of the predicted command remains less explored. However, VLA-controlled manipulation is not determined by prediction alone. A VLA model may output a semantically plausible command, yet this command must still be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:concept , embodied constraints such as position limits, force limits, and kinematic constraints can reshape or attenuate the task-space command before physical execution. This creates a command-execution gap: a command that appears reasonable at the prediction level may still be difficult to realize effectively, thereby reducing effective task progress and making task completion less reliable. Rather than directly maximizing prediction discrepancy or rollout-level deviation, our goal is to enlarge the mismatch between the VLA-predicted task-space command and the realized motion. To this end, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits the limited executability of robot motion. Specifically, ExecGap derives low-executability directions from two factors: kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. By biasing commands toward these hard-to-execute directions, ExecGap increases command-execution mismatch, weakens realized task progress, and degrades task completion. Extensive simulation experiments on LIBERO suites~ liu2023libero show that ExecGap effectively disrupts manipulation and induces larger command-execution mismatch with weaker realized execution across OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , and ~ black2024pi_0 . Real-robot validation further shows that physically deployed patches can induce execution degradation on robotic hardware. Overall, our contributions are three-fold: [topsep=0pt, itemsep=1pt, parsep=0pt, partopsep=0pt] We identify execution degradation as an execution-side VLA failure mode arising from degraded embodied realization rather than prediction-side discrepancy alone. We propose ExecGap, a robot-aware patch attack that exploits kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation to induce low-executability commands. We validate ExecGap in simulation and on real robots, showing stronger execution degradation in simulation and physical feasibility on real platforms. Related Work VLA models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation for robotic manipulation. Representative systems, including RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt , OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla , Octo~ team2024octo , and ~ black2024pi_0 , adapt large-scale pretrained representations to robot control and enable language-conditioned manipulation across diverse tasks~ o2024open,liu2023libero,mees2022calvin . Broader discussions of recent VLA models and deployment challenges can be found in surveys~ ma2026survey,kawaharazuka2025vision,wang2025vlatest . Recent studies show that VLA systems are vulnerable to visual perturbations, adversarial patches, object-level modifications, language prompts, and multimodal attacks~ wang2025exploring,xu2025model,lu2025robots,chen2026tex3d,jones2025adversarial,yan2025alignment,wang2026partially . Existing attacks induce erroneous actions, manipulation failures, or rollout-level deviations by corrupting observations or instructions. In contrast, ExecGap targets execution degradation by steering VLA-predicted commands toward low-executability directions, while considering how commands are physically realized. Execution difficulty has long been studied in robot control through manipulability, force capability, and dynamic constraints~ siciliano2009robotics,lynch2017modern,yoshikawa1985manipulability,yoshikawa1985dynamic,chardonnet2009force,asada1983geometrical . These analyses have been used for motion planning, redundancy resolution, singularity avoidance, grasping, contact-rich manipulation, and whole-body control~ nakamura1987task,rozo2017learning,chan1995weighted,chiaverini1997singularity,gravagne2001manipulability,khatib2004whole,sentis2005synthesis,khatib1987unified . While prior work uses executability analysis to improve feasibility and control performance, we use it adversarially to expose execution-side vulnerabilities in VLA-controlled robots. Problem Formulation sec:problem VLA Policy and Embodied Execution We consider a vision-language-action (VLA) policy . At step , given a visual observation , a language instruction , and an optional robot state , the policy outputs a model-specific command. Since VLA models may use different action parameterizations, such as continuous actions, tokenized actions, or flow-based actions, we compare commands and realized motions in a common task space: is the model-specific action space, and maps to a comparable task-space command, such as translational end-effector motion. The downstream controller and robot embodiment realize the command as a task-space motion over one control interval: where abstracts control, kinematics, dynamics, and physical constraints during execution. In general, , since embodiment constraints may reshape, attenuate, or redirect the commanded motion before it is physically realized. Adversarial Patch Attack Following the adversarial patch threat model~ brown2017adversarial , we apply a static visual patch to the VLA observation. Given a patch location , the adversarial observation, command, and task-space command are We consider a robot-aware white-box patch attack. The instruction, VLA parameters, downstream controller, robot state, and robot dynamics are not modified by the attacker. Conventional patch attacks optimize prediction-level or task-level objectives, where typically measures action discrepancy, targeted deviation, or task failure. Such objectives attack the prediction side of the VLA policy but do not explicitly model whether the predicted command can be effectively realized by the robot embodiment. Execution Degradation Objective Instead of directly optimizing rollout-level deviation, we formulate execution degradation through command-execution mismatch. Under attack, the realized task-space motion and the command-execution mismatch are A persistent mismatch indicates that the VLA command is not effectively realized by the robot, which can reduce effective task progress even when the command is valid in task space. The execution degradation objective seeks This objective captures an execution-side failure mode by enlarging the mismatch between the task-space command and the realized motion. Method sec:method In this section, we present ExecGap, a patch attack that exploits the command-execution gap to induce execution degradation in VLA-controlled robots, as shown in Fig.~ fig:overview . Directly optimizing the mismatch objective in Sec.~ sec:problem is challenging because it requires differentiating through downstream execution and closed-loop rollout dynamics. title: Improving While Deployed: Learning Proactive End-to-End Driving from Imperfect Human Takeover Data
summary: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs.
full_text: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs. Introduction sec:intro End-to-end (E2E) driving models can still encounter situations that require a driver to take control after deployment on real vehicles~ goff2025learning,li2026worldengine . When a driver intervenes, the resulting log records the vehicle's motion before takeover, the timing of the intervention, and the driver's subsequent response. These records provide feedback for post-training from the deployed model's own on-road experience~ yang2026human . A simple way to use these logs is to imitate the recorded trajectories. However, drivers may take over even when the original model plan is reasonable~ gershon2021driver, zhou2025drarl , and a necessary correction may begin only after undesirable behavior has emerged~ bi2020learning . Direct imitation can therefore discourage an appropriate maneuver or reinforce a delayed response. Trajectory post-optimization can refine the imitation target, but the result depends on predefined costs and constraints~ pulver2021pilot . The challenge is to infer from the driver's subsequent response whether an earlier plan needed revision and, if so, how it should have changed. One way to learn from on-road takeovers is to use driving simulators to recreate the traffic conditions that prompted them and train a model to handle similar situations~ cao2023autonomous,zhou2025drarl . For example, DRARL identifies likely causes of disengagement and evaluates the updated planner in simulated scenarios. However, the sim-to-real gap can limit how well improvements observed in these environments transfer to real vehicles~ yuan2024naturalistic . A second line of work reconstructs scenes from real driving logs at the sensor level. RAD trains E2E models through closed-loop interaction in scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian splatting~ gao2025rad , while SimScale combines real driving data with pseudo-expert demonstrations for synthetic variations of logged scenes~ tian2026simscale . World Engine uses fleet logs to generate safety-critical interactions for post-training and reports improvements in on-road tests~ li2026worldengine . While intervention signals help identify challenging scenarios, these methods primarily rely on simulated rewards or generated demonstrations, rather than directly leveraging human corrections from takeover logs. In this paper, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision for E2E driving models. For each driving scene, we construct diverse trajectory candidates by advancing recorded human corrections and augmenting the multimodal plans of the deployed model. A scene-conditioned trajectory scorer learns to rank these candidates through expert trajectory matching and unpaired preference supervision. Unlike prior methods that directly optimize discrete action choices or action likelihoods~ liu2026takead,xia2025apo , our scorer evaluates complete trajectories from their continuous waypoint coordinates. We selectively refine pre-takeover supervision targets using its scores and distill the refined targets into the deployed model. Our main contributions are threefold. Intervention-aware trajectory augmentation. We shift recorded human corrections earlier by different time offsets and randomly augment the deployed model's multimodal plans. The resulting candidates offer earlier responses while retaining alternatives when corrections are unnecessary or unsuitable. Trajectory-level preference learning. We train a scene-conditioned scorer using expert trajectory matching and unpaired desirability feedback from takeover logs. It evaluates continuous, long-horizon trajectories without requiring explicit trajectory likelihoods or preference pairs involving unexecuted model plans. Selective target refinement for offline post-training. We replace pre-takeover targets only when a candidate scores sufficiently higher than the recorded trajectory and distill the refined supervision into the E2E model. Using 11,162 real-world takeover segments, our method improves the overall closed-loop success rate from 70.87 to 81.60 , compared with 75.30 for direct imitation learning. Related Work sec:related_works Post-training for autonomous driving. Most E2E driving models are initially trained through imitation learning (IL) on expert demonstrations. However, optimizing trajectory similarity alone may not adequately capture safety and interaction requirements in challenging driving scenarios. Recent studies have explored reinforcement learning (RL) to further improve these models. WorldRFT yang2026worldrft employs collision-aware trajectory rewards and group relative policy optimization to enhance planning safety. DiffusionDriveV2 zou2025diffusiondrivev2 introduces trajectory exploration with intra- and inter-anchor optimization to improve trajectory diversity and quality. PaIR-Drive lian2026pairdrive integrates IL and RL through parallel optimization to mitigate policy drift. Another line of research explores closed-loop training through world models and reconstructed environments. Raw2Drive yang2025raw2drive aligns privileged and raw-sensor world models to enable RL-based training. RAD gao2025rad employs 3DGS-based closed-loop RL in reconstructed driving scenes, while RAD-2 gao2026rad2 introduces a generator-discriminator framework with temporally consistent policy optimization and efficient BEV-based simulation. World Engine li2026worldengine mines safety-critical scenarios from real-world driving logs and synthesizes diverse traffic interactions for post-training. from human interventions. Human feedback provides additional supervision for improving driving models beyond fixed expert demonstrations. DAgger~ ross2011reduction queries expert action labels for states visited by the model, while HG-DAgger~ kelly2019hgdagger collects corrective demonstrations through human takeovers. In robotic manipulation, human interventions have been used to reweight imitation data~ liu2025robot , derive rewards~ luo2024rlif , and learn action preferences~ xia2025apo . In autonomous driving, DICL~ cao2023autonomous constructs simulated training experiences from real-world intervention cases, while DRARL~ zhou2025drarl identifies takeover reasons and generates similar scenarios for model improvement. CAT~ zhang2023cat further augments log-replayed driving scenarios through adversarial traffic generation for closed-loop training. Recent E2E studies also exploit simulated takeover data. TakeAD~ liu2026takead and CoReVLA~ fang2025corevla collect takeover demonstrations from privileged experts and human drivers in simulated environments, respectively. TakeVLA~ gao2026learning incorporates pre-takeover language supervision and reinforcement finetuning through scenario dreaming. However, real-world interventions may occur without planning errors~ zhou2025drarl or after an appropriate corrective maneuver should have begun~ bi2020learning . Our method directly exploits these imperfect corrections to refine trajectory-level supervision offline, enabling efficient updates to deployed E2E models. learning for model refinement. Preference learning enables model improvement by distinguishing desirable from undesirable behaviors. Representative approaches, including DPO rafailov2023direct and SimPO meng2024simpo , optimize models using chosen-rejected response pairs obtained from human judgments or reward-based rankings. In contrast, KTO ethayarajh2024kto learns from unpaired binary desirability feedback without explicit preference pairs. In autonomous driving, TakeAD liu2026takead leverages takeover preferences to optimize distributions over discrete trajectory modes and control actions. DriveDPO shang2025drivedpo constructs trajectory preference pairs using imitation similarity and simulation-based safety scores, while EMPlan chen2026emplan employs reward-guided unpaired preference optimization for multimodal planning. In robotic manipulation, APO xia2025apo exploits binary desirability feedback from human interventions to refine vision-language models. These approaches primarily apply preference supervision directly to model optimization, often relying on action or trajectory likelihoods. Instead, we learn a scene-conditioned scorer from imperfect real-world takeover data to evaluate candidate coordinates directly and refine trajectory supervision for distillation without using the driving model's trajectory likelihoods. Methodology sec:method Overview We consider an E2E driving model trained on large-scale expert driving data. The model takes seven synchronized camera views and LiDAR point clouds as inputs. Image features are extracted using a ResNet-50 backbone he2016deep with a feature pyramid network lin2017feature , while point clouds are encoded using a PointPillars-based encoder lang2019pointpillars . Features from both modalities are fused into a unified bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation liu2022bevfusion . As shown in Figure~ fig:framework , multiple task-specific heads perform object detection zhang2023dino , motion prediction, online vectorized mapping liao2025maptrv2 , and trajectory planning liu2025hybrid . Conditioned on the BEV features and ego states, the planning head generates multimodal trajectories over a 6-second horizon, each containing waypoints. Each waypoint is parameterized by the mean and variance of its 2D position, yielding an output tensor of . A selection head assigns confidence scores to the trajectories, selecting the highest-ranked candidate for vehicle control. The model replans at 10 Hz, so only the initial portion of each selected 6-second trajectory is executed before the next planning cycle. The entire E2E model comprises approximately 140 million parameters. The trained E2E model is deployed as a TensorRT engine on the onboard computing platforms of production vehicles. Real-world driving data are collected from diverse urban environments across Chongqing, Beijing and Shanghai in China. The vehicles feature different sensor configurations, including single- and dual-LiDAR setups, with sensor inputs adapted to a unified representation for training and inference. The E2E driving system operates under human supervision, requiring drivers or safety testers to intervene when necessary. For each takeover event, the vehicle automatically records a 60-second driving segment spanning 30 seconds before and after the intervention. title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation
summary: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.

Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav’s effectiveness. Introduction sec:introduction Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) is a challenging task in Embodied AI, requiring an agent to navigate to target objects in unfamiliar environments without training. Unlike conventional object navigation methods that focus on a single target, we consider zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation, where a robot must search for and locate multiple language-specified targets in succession within the same environment~ onemap,wtrp_searcher . In this setting, agents can use experience from earlier searches to refine their navigation strategies and locate subsequent goals more efficiently. When agents autonomously reflect on past searches and revise their decision rules, this process constitutes policy self-improvement. Related work ~ evolvenav,retronav,slow4fast explores such self-improvement across navigation settings. However, their updates primarily concern navigation rules or decision guidance, while the procedures that generate these updates remain predefined. In multi-object navigation, subsequent searches can reveal whether earlier revisions resolved their intended problems. However, the observations needed to explain an ineffective revision may not yet be available, and acquiring them consumes the same movement budget as navigation. Later searches can therefore expose omissions in the diagnostic checks or observation requests that guided earlier repairs. If this feedback only triggers further policy updates, the rules producing these omissions may remain unchanged, even as the navigation policy evolves. Figure~ fig:motivation illustrates why improving navigation also calls for improving the revision process. An initial revision adds checks of neglected locations to , producing . Subsequent searches may still yield redundant observations, revealing that the repair addressed where to visit without adequately considering what each view would reveal. The improver uses this feedback to revise its own diagnosis and repair rules. The updated improver then revises into , which retains useful site checks and selects views that test multiple object hypotheses. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation. Its improvement program diagnoses search problems, gathers observations that distinguish competing explanations, and generates targeted revisions to the navigation program. For each revision, the system records its intended behavioral change and actual execution outcome. Subsequent goal searches test these revisions and provide feedback on the diagnosis and repair decisions behind them. When this feedback exposes limitations in its improvement rules, the current improver applies those rules to propose revisions to itself. These changes can alter which causes are considered, which observations are requested, and which navigation functions are revised. The accepted version then governs the next round of navigation revisions, whose outcomes drive further self-revision, closing the recursive loop. Conditional inheritance carries accepted updates into later searches where applicable. We evaluate RPSI-Nav on public open-vocabulary multi-object navigation benchmarks, complemented by qualitative real-robot experiments. Related Work sec:related_work Open-vocabulary and multi-object navigation. Zero-shot object navigation uses pretrained models for semantic grounding, commonsense reasoning, and relational search~ gadre2023cow,zhou2023esc,yokoyama2024vlfm,yin2024sgnav . OpenFMNav interprets free-form requests~ kuang2024openfmnav , while VoroNav combines topology and semantics for exploration~ wu2024voronav . MultiON studies semantic memory over object sequences~ wani2020multion ; OneMap and WTRP-Searcher support zero-shot multi-object search through persistent mapping and global planning~ onemap,wtrp_searcher . GOAT-Bench evaluates multimodal lifelong navigation, and 3D-Mem builds reusable scene memory for exploration and reasoning~ khanna2024goatbench,yang2025threedmem . Recent work further advances multimodal goal understanding and scene representations for navigation~ yin2025unigoal,huang2026msgnav,hu2026astranavmemory,raychaudhuri2025mlfm,ortegapeimbert2025divnav . These studies primarily improve environmental representations and search planning, while we use feedback from successive goal searches to revise both the navigation program and its improvement mechanism. Experience-driven navigation improvement. Navigation agents increasingly turn execution experience into reusable rules, memories, and reflective guidance. Recent methods improve navigation through rule evolution, memory updates, and reflective guidance~ evolvenav,ge2026evomemnav,li2026metanav,retronav,slow4fast,zhao2026navharness . Other approaches improve navigation models through self-reflective learning and recursive training loops~ lin2025evolvenav,li2026rsinav . RPSI-Nav instead studies program-level improvement with frozen foundation models: subsequent goals provide feedback on earlier revisions, which updates both the navigation program and the diagnosis, observation-acquisition, and revision rules that produce future changes. Agents and recursive self-improvement. Language feedback and failure analysis support behavioral revision~ shinn2023reflexion,liu2023reflect,madaan2023selfrefine . Programmatic approaches enable reusable skills and automated optimization of agent workflows and memory mechanisms~ liang2023codeaspolicies,wang2024voyager,hu2025adas,zhang2025aflow,xiong2026alma . Recursive self-improvement evolves agent code and its revision mechanisms~ zelikman2024stop,zhang2026dgm . Hyperagents and MetaSkill-Evolve explicitly make the improvement process itself editable~ hyperagents,wang2026metaskillevolve . In robotics, related work improves policy code, execution harnesses, and diagnostic resources through feedback, targeted experiments, or selective model updates~ elmaaroufi2026rho,wang2026harnesspai,physevo,song2026embodiedrsi,wang2026adarsi . RPSI-Nav studies recursive improvement in continuous visual search, where evidence for assessing a repair may arrive during later goals or require additional movement to obtain. Cross-goal feedback revises how the improver diagnoses failures, requests observations, and selects navigation changes. Accepted rules govern subsequent revisions under their applicable conditions. Method sec:method RPSI-Nav leverages sequential goal searches to improve navigation and its revision mechanism. Early searches supply policy-improvement experience, while later searches test whether prior revisions fix their target issues. We link these two feedback streams via recursive self-revision: the improver updates itself, and the updated improver shapes future navigation revisions. Accepted changes transfer across goals under applicable conditions.
