title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
summary: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
full_text: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM--VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently emerged as a dominant paradigm in embodied intelligence~ brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . By transferring the powerful semantic and scene-understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to robot control signals through discrete action tokens or dedicated action experts, VLAs achieve strong generalization. However, their reactive control paradigm cannot model the evolution of the physical world or predict the consequences of actions, both of which are essential capabilities for open-world manipulation agents. World Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by jointly modeling future visual-state transitions and action distributions~ li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel,yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels,li2026causalworldmodelingrobot . By conditioning action generation on learned world dynamics, WAMs provide a viable paradigm for pretraining on large-scale videos and make it possible to build manipulation agents capable of understanding the physical world. Despite their ability to predict state evolution, WAMs lack the open-world understanding, reasoning, and planning capabilities provided by a VLM backbone. Existing WAMs, such as Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels , LingBot-VA~ li2026causalworldmodelingrobot , and DreamZero~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot , typically rely on a separate frozen text encoder to provide language grounding. This design is often insufficient for tasks that require open-world scene understanding, semantic generalization and long-horizon planning. Recent works, such as ST-WAM~ wang2026stwamsemantictemporalworldaction and SG-WAM~ he2026sgwamtextgroundedspatialawaresemantic , incorporate VLMs to provide scene-aware semantic guidance for action generation. However, ST-WAM keeps its VLM frozen throughout training, so its semantic representations are not jointly optimized with the WAM. This limits the adaptation of the VLM's semantic knowledge to the needs of future-state prediction and action generation. SG-WAM jointly trains a VLM-based semantic planner with the WAM, but relies on additional frozen semantic and geometric teachers to supervise future feature prediction. To address these limitations, we propose CoT-WAM, a framework that seamlessly integrates the rich semantic prior of a VLM into a WAM, thereby equipping WAM prediction and decision-making with open-world understanding and planning capabilities. Building upon Fast-WAM, CoT-WAM replaces its conditioning input with a learnable hidden state produced by the VLM. The VLM is responsible for scene understanding or subtask planning, and conveys its planning intent to the WAM through the latent embedding. Conditioned on this compact yet semantically rich representation, the WAM predicts the corresponding future states and generates control signals. During training, we supervise the learnable embedding with two complementary signals: a discrete textual task signal and a continuous goal-image signal. Consequently, the information transmitted from the VLM to the WAM is no longer restricted to ``hard'' text, but can encode richer information about the predicted consequences of an intended action. Through a two-stage training strategy, we successfully endow the WAM with stronger understanding and planning capabilities, leading to improved closed-loop control performance. We evaluate CoT-WAM across six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. For control, CoT-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen without additional embodied pretraining. For zero-shot generalization, the same LIBERO-trained policy substantially outperforms Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with methods using additional embodied pretraining or supervision from external visual priors. For long-horizon planning, CoT-WAM outperforms baselines with and without external planners on RoboCasa365, a challenging benchmark for mobile manipulation. Beyond these simulation benchmarks, real-world experiments further validate the practicality of CoT-WAM. Together, these results demonstrate that integrating VLM semantic knowledge with world modeling through joint training improves scene understanding, semantic generalization, and long-horizon planning. In summary, our contributions are: We propose CoT-WAM, a joint WAM--VLM training framework that equips WAMs with scene understanding, semantic generalization, and long-horizon planning capabilities. We introduce dedicated latent tokens to enable richer and more flexible information exchange between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images. A staged training strategy enables joint learning and collaboration between the two models. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that CoT-WAM substantially improves long-horizon planning over the baseline, while achieving state-of-the-art control performance and stronger zero-shot generalization. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action models transfer semantic knowledge from pretrained VLMs to robot control. OpenVLA~ kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel learns manipulation policies from multi-robot demonstrations, while ~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel couples a VLM with flow-matching action generation. X-VLA~ zheng2025xvlasoftpromptedtransformerscalable studies scalable adaptation across embodiments. ~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld combines robot data, web data, and semantic subtask prediction to improve open-world generalization. These methods emphasize semantic understanding and action generation without explicitly supervising future visual-state prediction. We complement such semantic priors with WAM-based visual prediction, so that the representations used for control are also trained to capture task-relevant scene evolution. World Action Models World action models learn visual dynamics alongside robot actions. LingBot-VA~ li2026causalworldmodelingrobot couples video and action experts through causal modeling. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels retains future-video prediction as training supervision while omitting it at inference, and Faster-WAM~ ma2026fasterwamworldactionmodels further reduces computation with a lightweight action module. However, language conditioning in models such as Fast-WAM is encoded independently of the current observation, leaving scene-dependent task interpretation to the downstream video--action network. Building on Fast-WAM, we replace this conditioning interface with continuous intent representations produced by a VLM from both the observation and instruction, providing scene-aware semantic guidance for visual prediction and action generation. Integrating VLMs with World Action Models Recent work incorporates VLM priors into WAMs through different conditioning interfaces. DSWAM~ zhu2026dswamdualsystemworldaction introduces an optional VLM planner that supplies explicit subtask instructions to a WAM executor, but this discrete text interface does not provide a differentiable path from the executor to the planner. ST-WAM~ wang2026stwamsemantictemporalworldaction uses frozen VLM features to retrieve task-relevant semantic history for action generation, so WAM training cannot adapt the VLM itself. SG-WAM~ he2026sgwamtextgroundedspatialawaresemantic enables joint training of a VLM-based planner and the WAM, but requires additional frozen semantic and geometric teachers to supervise future feature prediction. Our approach jointly optimizes the VLM and video predictor through a continuous interface supervised by task text and future visual observations, without additional external priors. Predicted visual goals further ground the communicated intent in a future state that conditions both video and action generation. Overview We consider embodied policy learning from visual observations and language instructions. Given the current observation , robot proprioceptive state , and task instruction , the policy predicts an action sequence of length , . Following Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels , we use future video prediction as auxiliary supervision to shape visual representations during training, while omitting full video prediction at inference time to accelerate execution. As shown in Figure~ fig:architecture , our model consists of a world action model based on a MoT architecture~ liang2025mixtureoftransformerssparsescalablearchitecture and a VLM planner. Given the current observation and task, the VLM planner communicates its plan for the next step to the world action model through a latent interface. The world action model then generates the action chunk conditioned on the VLM's intent and the current observation. To make the intent signal transmitted from the VLM to the world model more concrete and continuous, we further introduce goal-image prediction on the video-model side, mapping the VLM's continuous hidden representations to a concrete target visual state. The predicted goal image then conditions both action and video generation, grounding the VLM's intent more directly in control. This grounds the WAM's control outputs in the VLM's strong semantic priors, improving closed-loop performance and generalization. Method sec:method Latent VLM--WAM Interface sec:latent-interface To better incorporate the VLM's understanding and planning of the current scene and task into action generation, we introduce a learnable latent embedding interface for communication between the VLM and the WAM. Specifically, we encode the current observation and task instruction , then append learnable intent tokens to form the VLM input sequence. Through the VLM's self-attention, these tokens aggregate scene and task information. Their final hidden states form a continuous representation of the VLM's intent, which is passed to the downstream WAM through a projection layer: where denotes the VLM and is an MLP projection layer. The downstream WAM adopts a MoT architecture similar to Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels , in which a video expert and an action expert are integrated through joint attention. Both experts access the intent information from the VLM through cross-attention to condition future-state and action

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce , a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of and in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ awomo2026awomo05, team2026xiaomi, intelligence2025pi_, nvidia2025gr00tn16, li2026trm, marmotlab2025falcon have made significant progress toward developing generalist robotic policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks. Despite their performance on short-horizon tasks (e.g. `Pick up the straw and place it in the cup.'), these models often struggle with reliable execution of long-horizon instructions (e.g. ``Open the drawer, pick up the straw, navigate to the cup, and place the straw in the cup''). This can be attributed to their inability to coordinate simultaneous progress tracking and execution of the long-horizon tasks, allowing small errors to propagate and cause downstream failures. Towards this end, we propose decoupling of long-horizon reasoning, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery from a single-VLA policy to a VLA-agnostic framework, retaining the VLA policy only as a reliable executor of short-horizon tasks. Recent approaches improve long-horizon manipulation through complementary mechanisms: leveraging future prediction~ huang2026long, zhang2026foreact, chen2026unified , persistent action memory~ marrie2026reki, wu2024unleashing, huang2026long , and action prediction~ liu2026neural . Progress-aware approaches~ zhang2026recurrent, Yan2026ProgressVLAPD, Li2026SentinelVLAAM , either leverage progress estimates as monotonically increasing rewards for computationally intensive policy training, do not consider explicit failure diagnosis and recovery, or overlook the compositional structure and interdependencies of long-horizon tasks by treating them as monolithic execution problems. Consequently, missed prerequisites and incorrectly assumed completions propagate through subsequent manipulations, motivating the need for an execution-grounded framework capable of handling task dependencies, progress monitoring, execution awareness, and failure-conditioned replanning. To address these challenges, we propose a VLA-agnostic framework for long-horizon task execution. Our approach integrates language-based task decomposition, visual progress monitoring, and failure-conditioned re-planning into a closed-loop execution pipeline. We evaluate our approach on the RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 composite-task benchmark and a focused subset of challenging CALVIN's~ mees2022calvin long-horizon task sequences. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: We introduce RePlan-VLA, a VLA-agnostic framework that enables policies to reliably execute long-horizon tasks without requiring further VLA fine-tuning. We develop a fine-tuned progress-monitoring VLM that grounds sub-task progress estimation and failure diagnosis via visual observations to guide adaptive re-planning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RePlan-VLA on challenging long-horizon manipulation benchmarks, improving average task success rate from to on RoboCasa365 composite tasks, and from to on CALVIN ABCD hardD. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Policies. Early mobile manipulation approaches typically trained separate policies for individual tasks or narrowly defined sets of manipulation skills, limiting their ability to generalize to new instructions and environments. RT-1~ brohan2022rt marked a shift toward generalist policies by learning multiple manipulation skills within a unified architecture, while RT-2~ brohan2023rt leveraged pretrained vision-language representations to improve semantic generalization. Building on these foundations, Octo~ team2024octo and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla scaled training across diverse robot embodiments, enabling broader skill transfer and efficient adaptation. Subsequent approaches like ~ intelligence2025pi_ , GR00T-N1.6~ nvidia2025gr00tn16 , Xiaomi-Robotics-1~ team2026xiaomi , RLDX-1~ kim2026rldx , and PRTS~ zhang2026prts further advanced generalist manipulation through larger and more diverse training datasets, improved action-generation architectures, and refined training strategies. More recently, recognizing the limitations of purely reactive action prediction, World-Action Models such as Awomo-0.5~ awomo2026awomo05 , PatchWAM~ wang2026action , and ABot-M0.5~ chen2026abot have explored coupling action generation with predictive visual world modeling to better capture environment dynamics and improve sequential decision-making. Despite these advances, reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging, as these approaches largely emphasize policy-level capabilities without explicitly accounting for sub-task dependencies, execution-grounded progress tracking, or recovery from intermediate failures. -Horizon Planning. Several approaches extend VLAs beyond reactive action prediction through hierarchical subgoals (LoHo-VLA~ yang2025lohovla ), temporal and motion reasoning (TRM-VLA~ li2026trm , HiF-VLA~ lin2026hif ), and persistent memory (REKI~ marrie2026reki , Long-WAM~ huang2026long ). Building on these advances, Foreact~ zhang2026foreact , GR-1~ wu2024unleashing , NIAF~ liu2026neural , and LoHo-Manip~ liu2026lohomanip incorporated future-state prediction and execution-aware planning. More recently, progress-aware methods (Progress-VLA~ Yan2026ProgressVLAPD , Sentinel-VLA~ Li2026SentinelVLAAM , SPR~ Dai2026SeePR , NeurVLA~ liu2026neurvla , R VLM~ zhang2026recurrent ) have sought to monitor execution and guide recovery through progress estimates, often derived from temporal advancement in demonstrations or used as monotonic rewards for policy optimization. However, elapsed-time supervision may not reflect actual task completion, while monotonic progress signals can obscure regressions caused by execution errors. Consequently, maintaining an accurate representation of completed and failed sub-tasks, and translating these observations into corrective plans, remains challenging. In contrast, our approach grounds progress estimation in the observed execution of individual manipulation primitives rather than elapsed time or monotonically increasing task-level progress. By explicitly tracking execution behavior, and using the diagnostic feedback to revise the remaining plan, our framework enables failure-aware recovery across interdependent sub-tasks without retraining or modifying the underlying VLA policy. Our Approach sec:approach Overview. Our framework, illustrated in~ , consists of three key components: (i) a few-shot planner VLM that decomposes long-horizon instructions into an ordered sequence of executable short-horizon subtasks and adaptively revises the plan during execution; (ii) a progress estimator VLM trained via supervised fine-tuning to monitor execution using temporal visual observations, task context, and sub-task completion history; and (iii) a frozen VLA policy that translates the active sub-task instruction into low-level robot control commands. To ensure compatibility with the underlying VLA, the planner generates sub-task instructions that align with the linguistic structure of instructions encountered during the VLA policy's training. During execution, the progress estimator periodically evaluates sub-task completion and advances the policy to the next sub-task upon successful execution. When progress stalls or execution deviates from the intended outcome, the estimator generates natural-language diagnostic feedback, allowing the planner to revise the remaining sub-tasks while preserving the history of completed actions. This closed-loop interaction between planning, progress estimation, and control enables RePlan-VLA to extend robust short-horizon policies to reliable long-horizon manipulation without re-training or modifying the underlying VLA. To monitor execution, a progress estimator VLM periodically evaluates the active manipulation primitive in context of the task instructions using a temporally sampled observation history , where is the temporal sampling stride and is the number of sampled observations. Given this input, the progress estimator outputs the estimated progress of the active primitive pertaining to the current sub-task , an indicator for whether re-planning is required, and a natural-language summarization of the observed execution sequence. A sub-task is considered complete when all its constituent primitives have been successfully completed, after which execution advances to the next sub-task . Decomposition and Replanning. The annotated observations are then provided to the planner and produce . title: GTI: Grounding Task Intent Throughout Long-Horizon VLA Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$π_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.

We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. On VLA-Arena, GTI+ reaches 47.6 overall success versus 45.2 for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support. INTRODUCTION Vision--language--action (VLA) models such as ~ black05 and GR00T N1.5~ groot map visual observations, language, and robot state to actions, enabling multi-task manipulation. However, a global instruction remains unchanged while the robot encounters different subtasks and interaction states. Successful long-horizon execution therefore requires identifying not only which subtask is currently active, but also which interaction phase should be executed. Without this distinction, the policy may skip or repeat subtasks, switch phases prematurely, or continue executing after a failure. Hierarchical methods narrow the gap between complex instructions and low-level actions. Hi Robot~ hirobot translates high-level reasoning into local language instructions, while ForeAct~ foreact , VISTA~ vista , and H-WM~ hwm use predicted future states as execution references. Language specifies what to do but leaves contact geometry to the executor, and a single completion state cannot represent the distinct interaction and completion relations within one subtask. For grasping or placing, establishing contact and reaching local completion require different visual targets within the same subtask. Phase therefore determines how intent should be concretized visually. We therefore view long-horizon manipulation as a continuous task-intent-grounding problem with three coupled questions: which part of the global intent should be executed now; what visual target should represent that local intent in the current phase; and how an executable context consistent with that intent should be restored after persistent anomalies. GTI addresses these questions through history-based intent localization, phase-conditioned visual grounding, and failure-triggered local recovery. GTI's planner localizes the active subtask and phase from current observations and execution history. A phase-conditioned visual predictor grounds the local instruction into an interaction/contact ( ) or completion ( ) target using the current observation, instruction, and phase. The target and instruction jointly condition the VLA. When an internal-feature monitor detects persistent anomalies, local rollback and re-observation are followed by phase re-evaluation to restore alignment with the current subtask and visual milestone. The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We introduce GTI, a continuous task-intent-grounding framework for long-horizon VLA manipulation that localizes the active subtask and phase from current observations and execution history, and re-establishes an intent-consistent context after persistent anomalies. We propose a high-level mechanism combining a structured planner with phase-conditioned visual grounding: the planner localizes local task intent, while the visual model generates a interaction/contact target or completion target according to phase; both language and phase-specific visual targets condition the VLA. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real PiPER tasks using complete-system comparisons, matched visual-grounding ablations, and deployment-sensitivity tests. RELATED WORK Generalist Robot Policies RT-2~ rt2 , Open X-Embodiment~ openx , OpenVLA~ openvla , OpenVLA-OFT~ oft , ~ pi0 , ~ black05 , and GR00T N1.5~ groot advance transfer, adaptation, and general-purpose action generation; feasible-action-neighborhood regularization improves VLA fine-tuning~ fan . RoboCasa365 provides a large-scale household benchmark~ robocasa . GTI adds long-horizon intent localization and phase-specific guidance. Hierarchical Task-Intent Localization Hi Robot~ hirobot , AtomicVLA~ atomic , hierarchical systems~ multitask , ReKep~ rekep , LoHo-Manip~ loho , LiLo-VLA~ lilo , and Long-VLA~ longvla provide high-level structure, relational constraints, progress-aware representations, or phase-aware perception. title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/

Introduction utonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been widely deployed in diverse applications including infrastructure inspection, search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and logistics delivery. In such scenarios, UAVs are often required to operate in unstructured and partially observable environments. Beyond reliable low-level flight control, these settings demand high-level intelligence, including the ability to comprehend natural-language instructions, reason about spatial semantics, and generate safe and dynamically feasible actions under strict onboard computational constraints. Enabling such capabilities is critical to advancing UAV systems from task-specific navigation toward general embodied autonomy. While Vision-Language-Navigation (VLN) zhang2025embodiednavigationfoundationmodel and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel, black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel paradigms have shown considerable potential for autonomous robots, such methods remain underexplored for agile, resource-constrained UAVs. Most existing UAV navigation methods follow modular perception–planning–control pipelines 9811688,9981489,10044964 , relying on predefined algorithms, hand-crafted policies, or explicit mapping strategies. While effective in well-defined tasks, they lack general task understanding and reasoning capabilities, particularly the ability to interpret open-vocabulary language instructions. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) liu2023visualinstructiontuning,openai2023gpt4,team2023gemini,bai2023qwenvl have enabled VLN and VLA systems for ground robots, allowing natural language to be grounded in visual observations and translated into executable commands within a unified framework. However, adapting these methods to agile aerial robots is non-trivial due to fundamental differences in system dynamics, action spaces, data distributions, safety constraints, and deployment requirements. In particular, several critical challenges are as follows: Scarcity of 3D navigation data and domain shift. Most navigation foundation models are pretrained on large-scale ground-view 2D navigation datasets, which differ drastically from UAV-centric views that exhibit large variations in pose and scale. Existing UAV navigation datasets are often limited to outdoor environments with coarse visual features and insufficient fine-grained structural details, resulting in sim-to-real domain gaps. Mismatch between 3D action representation and safety-aware control. UAV navigation requires safe and reliable control. End-to-end continuous commands derived from foundation models often fail to guarantee safety or satisfy dynamical constraints, while semantically discrete action representations offer limited maneuverability. Balancing 3D maneuverability, control stability, and collision avoidance remains a core challenge. Insufficient reasoning for long-horizon embodied navigation. Existing VLN/VLA methods typically rely on single-frame or short-term reasoning, making it difficult to integrate historical observations in complex indoor environments. Long-horizon aerial navigation requires spatial grounding, conditional inference, and sequential task decomposition, which cannot be sufficiently supported by single-step prediction schemes. Prohibitive onboard computational constraints. State-of-the-art foundation models are computationally intensive, making real-time deployment on small UAVs with strict size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints challenging ravichandran2025distillingondevicelanguagemodels . Practical onboard deployment therefore requires preserving strong inference capability while significantly reducing computational and memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical Vision Language Navigation framework for Aerial Robots in complex environments. The proposed system integrates data generation, multimodal learning, and onboard deployment into a unified closed-loop framework (Fig.~ fig:overview ). At its core, VLN-AR decomposes the navigation problem into two tightly coupled components: a navigation-oriented vision language model (VLM) that performs multimodal reasoning and predicts structured navigation intentions, and a lightweight action expert that translates these intentions into dynamically feasible control commands. Instead of directly generating low-level actions, the model generates diverse navigation representations tailored to different task requirements. Specifically, it outputs a structured representation comprising 3D pose commands, 2D bounding-box guidance, and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, establishing an effective interface between high-level cognition and low-level control. The proposed model achieves a maximum success rate of 98.1 on single navigation tasks and an overall aerial navigation success rate of 92.7 , . To mitigate flight data scarcity and sim-to-real domain gaps in UAV navigation, we develop a high-fidelity data generation pipeline based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl2023gaussiansplatting , a large-scale 3D aerial navigation dataset with approximately 4 million samples, covering navigation data, general visual question answering (VQA), grounding data, reasoning data, spatial VQA, and more. Building upon this data foundation, we introduce a progressive three-stage training strategy that sequentially enhances multimodal grounding, navigation-specific motion prediction, and reasoning-aware navigation, as shown in Fig.~ fig:overview (II). The first two stages perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale mixed datasets to improve scene understanding and spatial reasoning for navigation, while the third stage shao2024deepseekmathpushinglimitsmathematical . To support long-horizon and ambiguity-aware navigation, we incorporate a lightweight cognitive-driven agent that aggregates historical observations, task states, and action states into a unified temporal memory, enabling structured reasoning, task decomposition, intelligent exploration, and failure recovery in partially observable environments. a 7.1×--9.4× speedup on resource-limited UAV platforms. The main contributions are summarized as follows: [1)] We propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical onboard VLN framework that enable closed-loop semantic aerial navigation in complex 3D environments. [2)] We present a cognitive navigation agent with dynamic memory fusion and heuristic task decomposition to enhance long-horizon reasoning, resolve ambiguous instructions, and improve resilience under partial observability in unknown environments. [3)] We develop systematic onboard optimization techniques, including instruction-guided visual token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving a 7.1×–9.4× inference speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. [4)] We conduct comprehensive evaluations in both simulation and real-world environments, demonstrating that the proposed VLN-AR achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of success rate, accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. State estimation and environmental perception are typically implemented via LiDAR-based or visual perception modules 8421746, 9372856 , while semantic scene understanding is achieved through object detectors such as YOLO wang2024yolov10 , Faster R-CNN ren2015faster , and 3D scene graphs chen2025irsinstancelevel3dscene . High-level mission logic is subsequently resolved by rule-based or decision-tree modules, followed by motion planning algorithms such as A* hart1968formal , RRT karaman2011sampling , Fast-Planner 8758904 , and Ego-Planner 9309347 to generate feasible reference trajectories. Such conventional approaches offer clear interpretability, robust stability, and low computational overhead. However, they are often customized for specific application scenarios, such as target tracking 9561948 , gap traversal wu2026precise , and autonomous landing 10328688 , and lack the ability to understand open-vocabulary language instructions or exploit rich semantic information from visual observations. Furthermore, the sequential multi-module structure is prone to error propagation and accumulation, leading to significant performance degradation in cluttered, dynamic, and unstructured environments. title: Facet-SLAM: Real-Time Triangle Splatting SLAM
summary: Dense SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian splatting build maps that render photorealistically, but their surface geometry is poor, and obtaining a mesh requires extraction or fusion stages. Triangle splatting avoids this with surface primitives whose vertices can be triangulated directly into a connected mesh, yet SLAM with this representation has so far relied on photometric tracking, which is too slow for localization at sensor rate. We present Facet-SLAM, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM system for RGB-D cameras. Fast geometric registration is the natural alternative, but it is not sufficient alone, since the mapper's optimization displaces triangles from the observed surface and makes them unreliable registration targets. We therefore separate the two roles: the tracker sets each triangle's centroid from fused depth and registers frames to these centroids by GICP, while the mapper is restricted to non-translating updates via a change of variables. Our system achieves competitive tracking accuracy at around 100 FPS on a desktop GPU and runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin. Compared with the photometric approach, it is over 20 times faster, matches rendering quality, and improves surface accuracy, reducing the chamfer distance of the Delaunay mesh on Replica from 1.55 to 0.86 cm. We will release the implementation at https://github.com/edward62740/Facet-SLAM.

SLAM, Mapping, RGB-D Perception Introduction Recent SLAM systems use differentiable representations such as 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) kerbl3DGaussianSplatting2023 to build maps that render photorealistically. This is useful for applications such as visual navigation and embodied AI training, but many of these also need geometrically accurate maps. 3DGS maps often have poor surface geometry, and obtaining a good mesh requires post-hoc extraction guedonSuGaRSurfaceAlignedGaussian2023 , an intermediate representation guedonMILoMeshIntheLoopGaussian2025,yuGaussianOpacityFields2024 , or 2DGS huang2DGaussianSplatting2024 primitives requiring fusion. In contrast, the primitives of a differentiable triangle soup Held2025Triangle are themselves surface elements, so a connected mesh can be obtained by triangulating their existing vertices, without an intermediate representation or a separate fusion stage. More recently, Triangle Splatting SLAM fry2026triangle (TS-SLAM) introduced the first dense SLAM method based on triangle primitives, demonstrating the above-mentioned geometric properties, in addition to the ability to generate a photorealistic map. However, TS-SLAM lacks real-time performance, limiting deployment flexibility and its use for on-device localization while constructing the map. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM method. It runs in real-time on both desktop GPU and Jetson AGX Orin, with pose accuracy competitive with photometric methods, rendering quality on par with TS-SLAM, and more accurate map geometry than prior triangle splatting and 3DGS SLAM methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce a real-time triangle splatting SLAM system that runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin, and from which a connected mesh can be extracted directly. We propose a tracking-and-mapping strategy that makes triangles reliable GICP registration targets, by fixing their centroids to fused depth and restricting the mapper to non-translating updates. We improve surface accuracy over both prior triangle splatting and 3DGS SLAM methods while maintaining visual quality relative to triangle splatting methods. Related Work Photorealistic SLAM methods, such as 3DGS SLAM, initially estimated pose by minimizing dense photometric error matsukiGaussianSplattingSLAM2024, yugayGaussianSLAMPhotorealisticDense2024, keethaSplaTAMSplatTrack2024 , which is accurate but too slow for real-time localization. Later works reach real-time operation with faster trackers, such as Photo-SLAM huangPhotoSLAMRealtimeSimultaneous2024 which builds on ORB-SLAM3 camposORBSLAM3AccurateOpenSource2021a , and GS-ICP SLAM haRGBDGSICPSLAM2025 which uses GICP segalGeneralizedICP2009 . Surface geometry remains a limitation of 3DGS maps. Obtaining a good mesh from 3DGS requires post-hoc extraction guedonSuGaRSurfaceAlignedGaussian2023 , an intermediate representation guedonMILoMeshIntheLoopGaussian2025,yuGaussianOpacityFields2024 , or surface-aligned primitives followed by volumetric fusion huang2DGaussianSplatting2024 ; the latter have been adopted into SLAM system pakG2SICPSLAMGeometryaware2025 . In contrast, the primitives of a differentiable triangle soup Held2025Triangle are themselves surface elements, so a connected mesh can be obtained by triangulating their existing vertices, without an intermediate representation or a separate fusion stage. Triangle splatting Held2025Triangle was recently proposed as an alternative to 3DGS, and TS-SLAM fry2026triangle is the first dense SLAM method to use triangles as map primitives, motivated by the need for accurate surfaces in embodied AI applications. Like the early 3DGS SLAM methods, TS-SLAM estimates pose photometrically, which is accurate but runs at only a few frames per second, too slow for on-device localization. Point cloud registration against the map has been used in 3DGS SLAM by reusing the Gaussian properties such as the covariances haRGBDGSICPSLAM2025 , or means tanDualCovarianceGaussian2026 . A triangle appears to be a better registration target still, being a plane with an explicit normal. However, we show that point-to-plane registration on the triangles' own normals is unreliable on real depth, which we attribute to the mapper setting each triangle's orientation to minimize a composite mapper cost. We therefore take the GICP covariance from the scatter of neighboring triangle centroids, and fix those centroids to fused depth by restricting the map optimization to be non-translating. title: 3DTouch: A Tactile-aware VLA Model with 3D Geometric Relations for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in general robotic manipulation through large-scale pretraining on robot manipulation data ~ kim2025openvla,black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . However, contact-rich dexterous manipulation remains challenging, as small deviations in object alignment or contact conditions can lead to task failure. Similar visual observations may correspond to different physical interaction states, requiring the model to refine actions according to additional contact information. Moreover, visual observations alone usually lack critical local manipulation geometry, especially under occlusion which commonly occurs in dexterous manipulation. These limitations show the necessity for fusing complementary geometric and tactile information into VLA models to support precise action control. Recent studies have explored incorporating 3D spatial information and tactile feedback into robot policies. 3D-aware VLA methods mainly adopt two schemes to integrate spatial information, using 3D positional encoding to fuse depth with visual features ~ qu2025spatialvla , or conditioning the action expert with separately encoded geometric features extracted from 3D reconstruction ~ zhang2025spatial or observed point clouds ~ chen2026pointact . Additionally, tactile-aware VLA methods incorporate tactile feedback into action generation by encoding tactile data as additional input tokens alongside visual-language tokens~ huang2025tactilevla,zhang2025vtla . 3D visuo-tactile methods further represent visual observations and gripper tactile measurements as 3D points for visuo-tactile fusion, preserving their spatial relationships~ huang2025vitac . Despite these advances, two key limitations remain for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. First, although 3D visuo-tactile methods have explored unified visual-tactile 3D representations for policy learning, how to effectively encode spatially grounded multi-finger tactile feedback for pretrained VLA models remains underexplored. In particular, without explicitly associating multi-finger taxel force measurements with their corresponding 3D locations in scenes, the model may struggle to relate local contact conditions of the hand to surrounding objects. Second, downsampled scene point clouds are often too coarse and heavily occluded during five-finger grasping to capture small interaction clearances. Even when complete object surfaces are tracked, implicitly inferring fine-grained hand--object and object--object alignment without explicit relational descriptors remains challenging. These limitations motivate jointly modeling spatially grounded tactile feedback and explicit interaction relations to support precise dexterous manipulation. To address these challenges, we propose 3DTouch, a 3D conditioning approach to enhance pretrained VLAs with spatially encoded tactile representations and explicit interaction relations for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , 3DTouch consists of two complementary modules. 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG) represents RGB-D scene point clouds and dense five-finger tactile measurements in a shared robot-base coordinate system. By encoding each taxel's 3D position alongside force vectors, 3DTG provides tactile tokens spatially aligned with scene tokens. Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) further leverages kinematic hand landmarks and tracked 3D object surface points in the robot base frame to construct hand--object and object--object relation tokens, explicitly encoding relative displacements and distances between interacting entities. Together, spatially grounded tactile feedback supports contact-aware motion refinement under visual ambiguity, while explicit interaction geometry facilitates more precise hand--object positioning and object--object alignment. The resulting scene, tactile, and relation tokens jointly enhance VLA models for dexterous action generation. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and 20 percentage points over the strongest tactile-aware VLA. Ablation studies demonstrate the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with shared spatial grounding improving the average success rate by 11 percentage points over hand-local tactile encoding. Explicit interaction geometry further improves the average success rate by 12 percentage points, showing improvements in target localization and grasp stability during dexterous manipulation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG), which encodes dense five-finger tactile measurements and RGB-D scene geometry in a shared 3D coordinate system, providing spatially localized tactile feedback. We introduce Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM), which constructs structured hand--object and object--object representations from hand landmarks and 3D object geometry, explicitly encoding task-relevant relative displacements and distances for dexterous action control. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of 3DTouch on real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, with ablations validating the benefits of multimodal spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations, particularly with stronger target localization and grasp stability. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models adapt pretrained vision-language representations for robotic control. RT-2 discretizes actions into tokens~ rt2 , and OpenVLA learns from Open X-Embodiment demonstrations~ kim2025openvla . Moving beyond discrete action tokens, diffusion Transformers originally explored in image synthesis~ peebles2023dit,shen2026hidit have been adapted to robotic control~ liu2025rdt . \( _0\) introduces a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation~ black2025pi0 , while \( _ 0.5 \) uses heterogeneous co-training for open-world generalization~ black2025pi05 . To accelerate action generation, recent drifting-based policies enable native one-step inference~ gao2026dbpo,gao2026driftingvla . However, conventional VLA models primarily use vision and language, sometimes supplemented by proprioception, and lack direct measurements of local contact forces; contact states can remain ambiguous under visual occlusion. We extend \( _0\) with tactile and geometric conditioning while retaining its vision-language input pathway and flow-matching objective. 3D-Aware Manipulation Policies. RVT processes rendered scene views~ goyal2023rvt , while 3D Diffuser Actor and DP3 condition action diffusion on 3D representations~ ke2025diffactor,ze2024dp3 . Transferring pretrained 2D knowledge to point clouds, as explored in open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding~ peng2023openscene,zhang2025pgov3d , has also been applied to robotic manipulation, with Lift3D employing positional mapping~ jia2025lift3d . Within VLAs, SpatialVLA introduces spatial position encoding and adaptive action discretization~ qu2025spatialvla , PointACT employs multi-scale point--action attention~ chen2026pointact , while FALCON and GEAR-VLA leverage spatial foundation models to enhance action generation~ zhang2025spatial,zhang2026gearvla . We complement these approaches with tactile feedback and explicit surface relations computed using object shape priors aligned by estimated poses. -Aware Policies. Early work uses vision and touch for grasp adjustment~ calandra2018more . Robot Synesthesia represents binary contact signals as 3D points~ yuan2024robotsynesthesia , while TARS learns visuo-tactile affordances through a unified point-cloud representation~ wu2025tars . 3D-ViTac associates scalar tactile readings with their 3D locations and jointly encodes visual and tactile points~ huang2025vitac . ForceVLA incorporates six-axis force feedback through a force-aware mixture-of-experts~ yu2025forcevla , while Tactile-VLA combines tactile feedback with hybrid position--force control and tactile-informed reasoning~ huang2025tactilevla . FAVLA and ReTouch further exploit high-frequency contact feedback for reactive action generation~ li2026favla,zhang2026retouch . OmniVTLA aligns tactile representations with visual and linguistic semantics through dual-path tactile encoding~ cheng2025omnivtla . MLA and DreamTacVLA establish spatial correspondences by projecting tactile sensor locations into image space for contrastive feature alignment, combined with future sensory prediction~ liu2025mla,ye2025dreamtacvla . In contrast, our 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG) explicitly represents both the 3D location and force vector of each taxel across multiple fingers in a shared metric frame with scene geometry. Unlike 3D-ViTac's joint point-cloud encoding, 3DTG separately encodes scene geometry and finger-wise force distributions to accommodate their distinct spatial structures. Geometry for Manipulation. ReKep formulates manipulation tasks as relational keypoint constraints for trajectory optimization~ huang2024rekep , while OmniManip leverages reconstructed object meshes and estimated poses to define spatial constraints between object-centric interaction primitives~ pan2025omnimanip . TriRelVLA models entity-level interactions through a task-conditioned graph that combines learned object and hand representations with relative positions, poses, and distances~ zhou2026trirelvla . Rather than prescribing desired geometric constraints or modeling relations at the entity level, our Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) explicitly characterizes current interaction geometry at the surface level, computing relative displacements and distances between kinematic hand landmarks and nearby object surfaces, and between representative regions of interacting objects. These fine-grained geometric relations complement spatially grounded multi-finger tactile feedback for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. title: CoRA-VTLA: Contact-Guided Attention and Queryable Response Memory for Tactile Post-Training
summary: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models reuse visual and linguistic knowledge across manipulation tasks~ rt2,openvla,pi05 . Yet precision manipulation requires corrections after contact: small alignment errors can jam assemblies, while excessive force can deform parts or fixtures~ lift,univtac . Visual observations guide approach and alignment but cannot reliably distinguish free motion from hidden resistance once parts touch. This makes post-contact adjustment crucial in assembly and delicate handling. In peg insertion, combining visual feedback with wrist force/torque measurements improves policy learning~ makingSense . In Fig.~ fig:teaser (a), a part appears aligned but stops advancing against a fixture. Tactile sensing reveals such interactions and supports corrective action. Tactile data are scarce in VLA pretraining. Task demonstrations with tactile observations offer a practical route to post-training for contact-rich manipulation~ simpletouch . Force-aware control uses measured loads to guide motion~ forcevla2 . Tactile prediction provides supervision for learning contact dynamics~ simpletouch,tacwam . Force histories have also been used to track task progress through repeated contact events~ fmvla . The challenge during recovery is to determine which recent responses matter for the next correction. For example, initial engagement and a sustained jam can produce similar instantaneous loads, yet call for continued insertion or withdrawal and realignment (Fig.~ fig:plug-recovery ). Prior work uses executed motion to interpret sensor measurements~ interactiveperception and predict tactile signals during slip~ actiontactileprediction . For recovery, we consider how past contact responded to motion and which responses matter in the current state. How can a pretrained policy retrieve the contact responses most relevant to its next action? Tactile post-training also challenges visual grounding. Prior work uses the location of touch to relate local readings to the full visual scene~ crossmodalprediction and uses tactile geometry to localize grasped parts for insertion~ gelsightinsertion . Direct tactile injection can disrupt visual dynamics modeling in world action models~ tactilewam . In VLAs, direct tactile fusion can draw action-expert attention away from the target, motivating adaptive tactile injection~ atvla . On matched MuJoCo observations, direct tactile fusion likewise produces more dispersed main-camera attention for the first action token at layer 17 (Sec.~ sec:qualitative ). Regulating tactile injection leaves a spatial question open: which image regions correspond to the sensed contact? Reliable correction therefore requires both identifying where contact occurs and retrieving how it has evolved in response to motion. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA is proposed as a tactile post-training framework combining response-aware action generation with spatially grounded tactile perception. At the action level, a queryable action--response memory encodes measured contact changes and retrieves responses conditioned on current contact and robot state. At the perception level, contact-guided gaze supervision directs a tactile semantic token's visual attention toward projected fingertip contact regions. The two mechanisms support different aspects of contact-aware correction within one pretrained VLA. The action expert combines retrieved responses, current feedback, and VLM task context to generate the next action chunk. The main contributions are summarized as follows: Queryable action--response memory. CoRA-VTLA introduces state-conditioned retrieval of measured contact responses for corrective action generation, with next-step response prediction on task demonstrations to initialize action-side tactile encoders. Contact-guided gaze supervision. Projected fingertip contacts provide spatial supervision for grounding tactile semantic representations in visual contact regions during VLA post-training. Simulation and real-robot evaluation. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33 mean success across three custom MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50 for direct tactile fusion with matched inputs. The memory design reaches 67 on a public UniVTAC optical-tactile task~ univtac . The full framework averages 66.7 across three real-robot tasks. Related Work sec:related-work Pretrained Robot Policies Large-scale demonstrations and cross-embodiment datasets support reusable robot policies~ rt1,oxe,octo . Embodied language models incorporate continuous sensor inputs~ palme . Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer visual and linguistic priors to action prediction~ rt2,openvla . Action chunking, diffusion, and flow matching provide different ways to model continuous robot actions~ act,diffusionpolicy,pi0,pi05 . Optimized fine-tuning improves adaptation to downstream tasks~ openvlaoft . For policies pretrained primarily on visual, linguistic, and proprioceptive inputs, using measured contact responses to correct actions in closed loop remains a challenge during task-specific adaptation. Tactile Representations and Policies Robotic tactile sensing uses interfaces ranging from optical deformation sensors to magnetic soft skins~ gelsight,digit,reskin . Paired visual and tactile data support cross-modal prediction and multimodal representation learning~ crossmodalprediction,touchgo,makingSense . Self-supervised approaches learn tactile representations from robot interaction~ tdex,sparsh,sparshskin . Work on tactile representation learning studies transfer across sensors~ t3,anytouch and alignment of touch with vision and language~ unitouch,tvl . Force supervision provides additional cues about physical interaction~ tafvla . At the policy level, tactile feedback supports grasp adjustment, and visual rewards can guide the learning of tactile skills~ calandra,tavi . Tactile VLAs incorporate contact information through token fusion, contact gating, force-aware action experts, and adaptive feedback~ forcevla,tacvla,tactilevla,atvla,vlatouch,lift . Training approaches range from large-scale tactile policy pretraining to predictive supervision on task demonstrations~ ftp1,n0vtla,simpletouch . These approaches give policies access to contact information. During recovery, a remaining challenge is to determine whether the sensed contact warrants a correction and what that correction should be. Temporal Prediction and Spatial Grounding Tactile dynamics models support predictive control and slip prediction~ tactilempc,actiontactileprediction . ViTacFormer combines cross-modal fusion with autoregressive tactile prediction~ vitacformer . Visuotactile diffusion policies use temporal observations and auxiliary prediction of tactile changes~ auxiliarytactiledp . Recent world--action models use tactile histories and future supervision~ tacwam . Other approaches learn predictive contact states~ tacmind . Some combine prediction with reactive feedback~ touchworld,tacpac . Selecting which recent measured contact responses should inform the next action remains a challenge for closed-loop control. Spatial grounding links tactile feedback to visual information. Visuo-Tactile Transformers use tactile inputs to emphasize task-relevant visual features~ vtt . ReconVLA encourages visual grounding by reconstructing regions around manipulated objects~ reconvla . In precision manipulation, a further challenge is to associate a specific fingertip measurement with the image region where that contact occurs. Method sec:method As shown in Fig.~ fig:method , CoRA-VTLA conditions the action expert on current contact and responses retrieved from the action--response memory, while contact-guided gaze supervision aligns a tactile semantic token with the corresponding image regions. Training first uses response prediction to initialize the contact and memory encoders, then jointly optimizes the policy with action, semantic, and gaze supervision. Overview CoRA-VTLA adapts a pretrained VLA policy to contact-rich manipulation using synchronized task demonstrations. At step , the policy receives RGB images, a language instruction, robot state , recent robot history, fingertip pressure , and wrist force/torque . A pressure map captures how the fingers are loaded, while the wrist wrench measures the net loading on the gripper. Similar instantaneous readings can arise as the tool presses against an obstruction or as contact settles. Recent responses distinguish these interaction histories. As shown in Fig.~ fig:method (a), the action expert receives two tokens that encode the current load and retrieve recent responses. A third token supplies tactile semantics to the VLM. The policy predicts an action chunk, executes its first command, and replans. Contact Interaction Memory Current contact. The encoder combines fingertip pressure and wrist wrench into a contact feature . The projection maps this feature to the action expert's token space. The contact encoder receives the fingertip map and wrist wrench together. The map retains the distribution across both fingers, so a load concentrated on one side and a balanced load can yield different contact features even when their total pressure is similar. Action--response memory. The memory records the load response measured after each executed action. Each event combines the changes in pressure and wrist wrench between consecutive observations with the wrist wrench relative to its initial reading . The differences capture the load change after each executed command. The episode-relative wrench retains sustained loading even when the stepwise difference becomes small. At step , the window ends with the response already observed at . In MuJoCo, the most recent events span 0.8 s. A temporal Transformer encodes the ordered events as ~ transformer . The query combines the current contact feature and robot state. The query reads as keys and values. The resulting memory token is During insertion, a tool still pressing against a rim and one re-establishing contact after backing off can produce similar instantaneous loads. Their recent responses differ: a drop in load during withdrawal can indicate that the tool has cleared the obstruction, and a subsequent rise can signal renewed contact. Conditioning the query on the current pose and load lets the action expert use the part of that history relevant to its next move. Semantic Grounding and Policy Integration Action-side integration. The contact and memory tokens precede the noisy action tokens in the action-expert suffix. The expert denoises the action chunk using both tactile tokens and the context from the VLM prefix. The two tokens let the expert read the instantaneous load and its recent evolution separately while predicting the same chunk. Tactile semantics. A parallel temporal encoder pools recent absolute pressure and wrist readings into . Three heads predict contact, stability, and load change. For each of the properties, the probabilities weight the two word embeddings in . The semantic token for the VLM prefix is the mean of these weighted embeddings plus a residual projection. Training labels for the three heads are derived directly from tactile measurements. Total fingertip load determines whether contact is present. During sustained contact, the magnitude of recent pressure and wrist-wrench changes determines stability. A load change is flagged when fingertip pressure rises or the wrist wrench varies beyond a threshold. The word anchors express these properties in the VLM embedding space, and the residual carries information beyond the three predictions. Contact-region grounding.
