title: LaST1.0: A Unified Latent World-Action Model with Control-Centric SpatioTemporal Reasoning
summary: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST1.0, a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST1.0 predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot-object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST1.0 revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation.
full_text: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST , a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot--object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---demonstrate that LaST achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a strong foundation for generalist robot manipulation by directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,liu2025hybridvla,kim2025fine,liu2026last . Despite their strong visual and semantic capabilities, the imbalance between dense visual inputs and sparse action supervision can lead to shortcut mappings rather than learning underlying physical dynamics ye2026gigaworld,luo2026being . Consequently, these models can struggle with robust control in complex scenarios that require anticipation of future interactions. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by coupling action learning with future-state prediction, using future prediction as an auxiliary objective that encourages the shared representation to capture task-relevant changes in the environment ye2026world,cheang2024gr,kim2026cosmos,team2026gigaworld . A central question, however, is what a policy model should predict about the future. Many existing WAMs instantiate future-state modeling through video generation ye2026gigaworld,ye2026world,yuan2026fast,kim2026cosmos . While visually expressive, this paradigm allocates substantial capacity to texture, illumination, background appearance, and other photometric details that have little bearing on the next physical interaction luo2026being . In contrast, fine-grained control depends more directly on localized object motion, relative geometry, contact configuration, and how the interaction region between robot-object evolves over time. We therefore propose that world modeling for manipulation should be control-centric rather than observation-complete. For manipulation, the future latent representation should satisfy three properties: (1) preserve the geometric evidence needed for precise action, (2) focus modeling capacity on the region where interaction occurs, and (3) provide predictive supervision during training without becoming mandatory computation at deployment. This perspective changes the role of future prediction: the goal is not to reproduce the world in all observable detail, but to predict the subset of future dynamics that is useful for control. Guided by this principle, we introduce LaST , a unified latent WAM that jointly optimizes action generation and control-centric future dynamics prediction. Rather than predicting appearance-oriented video latents or visual-semantic image latents, LaST utilizes a geometry-aware encoder wang2026vggt to construct compact targets exclusively from future wrist-camera observations, as described in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a). This concentrates the latent supervision on the interaction region, forcing the policy to capture fine-grained relative motions and robot--object geometric relationships. Crucially, our experiments reveal that formulating latent world modeling as a training-time regularizer not only yields improved performance but also enhances closed-loop control efficiency. To operationalize this control-centric paradigm, we further redesign the visual interface and attention mechanism for LaST , as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (b) and (c). Semantic vision encoders and reconstruction-oriented VAEs can bias visual representations toward high-level semantics or appearance reconstruction, potentially attenuating the localized visual details vital for manipulation luo2026look,wang2026repwam,liu2026tuna,diao2026pixels,wei2026pixelumm . LaST therefore adopts a vision-encoder-free interface, using a lightweight patch embedder to project raw image patches directly into the unified Transformer backbone, thereby preserving fine-grained visual cues. Within this backbone, rather than relying on conventional attention mechanisms, we introduce LaST-Attention to facilitate the spatiotemporal fusion of multimodal information across 4D subspaces (token sequence, image height, image width, and relative time), effectively supporting our latent world-action modeling paradigm. For evaluation, we deploy LaST across two distinct embodiments, utilizing both parallel grippers and dexterous hands across five challenging manipulation tasks. These tasks evaluate the model's ability to perform fine-grained control, spatial reasoning, and long-horizon manipulation. Empirical results demonstrate that LaST achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) success rates, exhibiting remarkable generalization to novel object, background, and position settings. Moreover, evaluations on three benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---confirm that LaST outperforms prior SOTA baselines, further validating the efficacy of our latent world-action modeling paradigm, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (d). The main contributions of this work are as follows: [nosep, leftmargin=*] We reformulate world modeling as the prediction of geometry-aware, control-centric future dynamics in latent space, using latent targets derived from future wrist views to capture evolving robot--object interactions. We introduce LaST , a latent World-Action Model that natively unifies vision-language understanding, latent world modeling, and action generation. Within this model, we design a vision-encoder-free interface and LaST-Attention to preserve fine-grained spatial cues and facilitate structured spatiotemporal fusion across modalities. Experiments demonstrate that LaST achieves state-of-the-art performance across two embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks, together with robust generalization to novel scenarios. Related Work Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models Generalist robot policies have primarily evolved along two complementary paradigms. Vision-language-action (VLA) models directly map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,liu2025hybridvla,kim2025fine,chen2025fast,black2024pi_0,kim2024openvla,ye2026starvla,gu2025manualvla,liu2026last,wu2026pragmatic,nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation,liurdt,team2026xiaomi,li2026sla,fang2026molmoact2,li2026spatial,qu2025spatialvla,cen2025worldvla . World-action models (WAMs) additionally model future visual dynamics, either jointly with action prediction or through an imagine-then-act formulation, to provide predictive priors for control cheang2024gr,li2025unified,bi2026motus,yuan2026fast,nvidia2026gr00t2,li2026causal,ye2026world,huang2026long,guo2026video,kim2026cosmos . To focus on more informative representations and improve inference efficiency, recent works have explored world modeling in latent spaces luo2026being,sun2026vla,chen2026last,lyu2026lda,wang2026st . However, these approaches often emphasize scene-level representations rather than information directly relevant to robot-object interaction and manipulation control. LaST instead focuses latent world modeling on control-centric information by constructing geometry-aware latent targets that capture the evolving robot-object interaction, providing more relevant predictive supervision for action generation. To better support this control-centric latent reasoning, we further co-design the visual interface and the unified backbone. An encoder-free patch interface preserves fine-grained interaction cues, while LaST-Attention with 4D-RoPE enables multimodal fusion that respects spatial and temporal structure. Task-routed experts specialize in context understanding, latent dynamics modeling, and action generation, providing complementary capacity for learning control-relevant predictive representations. Geometric Representation for Robotic Manipulation Geometric information is essential for precise manipulation, where actions depend on spatial relations and robot--object configurations. Existing approaches incorporate geometry through explicit inputs, feature fusion, or representation supervision. DepthVLA yuan2025depthvla enriches policies with depth information, while point-cloud-based VLAs, including PointVLA li2026pointvla and GeoVLA sun2025geovla , integrate 3D features into action prediction liu2025mla,li20253ds . BridgeVLA li2025bridgevla instead projects 3D observations into multiple 2D views, aligning visual inputs and action heatmaps within a shared image space. FALCON zhang2025falcon supplies an action head with spatial tokens from geometric foundation models, while Evo-0 lin2025evo incorporates geometry-aware features extracted from RGB observations. SpatialVLA qu2025spatialvla further introduces egocentric 3D position encodings during policy pretraining. These designs retain depth estimation, point-cloud processing, or geometric feature extraction in the inference pipeline. A complementary direction internalizes spatial structure through training-time supervision. Spatial Forcing li2026spatial aligns intermediate policy features with geometric representations, and ROCKET sun2026rocket extends alignment across multiple backbone layers through a shared projector. VEGA wang2026vega directly supervises visual encoder outputs, while Mind-VLA ding2026mindvla uses instruction-aware target-object representations to focus geometric supervision on the manipulated object. These approaches strengthen spatial perception without requiring the auxiliary geometric modules at deployment. Beyond spatial representation alignment, 4D-WAM yang20264d transfers spatiotemporal knowledge from 3D trajectory fields through motion and destination alignment. LaST liu2026last also uses future point-cloud features as predictive supervision. LaST advances this direction by predicting compact geometry-aware latents extracted from future wrist-camera observations, concentrating supervision on evolving local robot--object interactions without requiring explicit point-cloud data. Its branch-decoupled training makes future geometry a predictive regularizer, allowing both the geometric teacher and the latent prediction branch to be omitted at inference. Method sec:method We first formulate the problem in Sec.~ sec:problem_formulation , then introduce the architecture of LaST and LaST-Attention in Secs.~ sec:last_architecture and sec:last_attention , respectively. We describe control-centric latent world modeling in Sec.~ sec:latent_world_modeling and the training and inference procedures in Sec.~ sec:training_inference . title: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
summary: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

Code Website . Introduction sec:intro Quadrupeds reach terrain that wheeled and fixed-base robots cannot, and language is a natural way to instruct them. To manipulate, most quadrupeds carry an arm or a gripper~ liu2024vbc,ha2024umilegs,wu2024doggybot , but an arm-free quadruped can also walk on three legs and use a front leg as the end-effector~ cheng2023legsmanip,arm2024pedipulate,cheng2025rambo . Manipulating with a leg spares the robot the weight and mechanical complexity of an added arm~ arm2024pedipulate . Existing visual planners for such leg manipulation learn from point clouds and cannot map language instructions to actions end to end~ he2024visualmaniplegs,he2024legmanip , and, to our knowledge, no demonstrations with language instructions exist for this setting. Meanwhile, world action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future observations and actions, have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies~ wu2023gr1,cheang2024gr2,guo2024pad,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva . This paper brings a WAM to arm-free quadrupedal loco-manipulation ( ). This raises two challenges. First, pretrained WAMs are arm-centric, and their multi-step sampling is slow. Our base WAM, LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva , sees head and wrist cameras and emits a 30-dimensional dual-arm command, whereas the cameras of a quadruped move with its body and its manipulating leg also supports it. Its video and action streams are each sampled over many steps at one network function evaluation (NFE) per step, so our transferred policy needs 2.226\,s for a chunk that covers 0.32\,s of robot time, and sampling with one video and two action steps lowers its success. On the real robot, the body drifts while the whole-body controller~ cheng2025rambo balances it during sampling, so actions computed from the state before sampling no longer fit the state after it. Second, the distilled policy remains bounded by imitation. A distilled student is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations and still fails on some hard tasks. Reinforcement learning with task-specific rewards can go beyond the demonstrations, but it tunes the slow high-NFE policy one task at a time, so it yields several slow specialists that must be merged into one policy and accelerated again. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages, one for each challenge: Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration (Stage~1) and Task-Specific Improvement and Merging (Stage~2). Both stages end by distilling a high-NFE teacher, the policy itself in Stage~1 and the task-routed teachers in Stage~2, on-policy into a 1/2-NFE student (one video and two action steps), so the final policy is stronger than the transferred one at a fraction of its inference cost. Our contributions are: Cross-morphology adaptation and acceleration. Stage~1 replaces only the visual and action interfaces of a WAM, fine-tunes it on quadruped demonstrations, and accelerates it by a few-step form of on-policy self-distillation (OPSD)~ zhao2026opsd , in which the same network with more sampling steps labels the student's own samples. The transferred policy reaches 77.0 , and the OPSD student keeps 76.7 (69.3 without distillation) while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific improvement and merging. Stage~2 tunes specialist teachers by per-task reinforcement learning and merges them by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD)~ ni2026multiteacher , which routes each context to the teacher of its task. On pushing a box and opening a door, the specialists succeed in every episode, against 47 and 53 for the OPSD teacher, and the M-OPD student reaches 90 and 87 , raising the ten-task success from 76.7 to 85.0 , above the OPSD teacher (77.0 ). QLM-Bench, ten simulated loco-manipulation tasks with 1,000 language-annotated demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, and evaluation in simulation and on a real Unitree Go2 Air, where the OPSD student runs without real-robot data. Related Work sec:related Quadrupedal loco-manipulation. Quadrupeds that follow language mostly pair a VLA/VLM with a controller for velocity, gait, or navigation~ ding2024quarvla,tong2025quartonline,zhao2025more,cheng2025navila , while manipulation systems attach an arm or gripper~ liu2024vbc,ha2024umilegs,wu2024doggybot,minelli2026tabletop , sequence skills via an LLM~ ouyang2024longhorizonllm , or track foot targets with leg controllers~ cheng2023legsmanip,arm2024pedipulate,cheng2025rambo . Visual leg-manipulation planners learn from point clouds by reinforcement learning~ he2024visualmaniplegs or imitation (Leg-Manip~ he2024legmanip ) without language; WAM-Policy is a single language-conditioned RGB policy. World action models. World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future scenes and actions using video-pretrained priors~ wu2023gr1,cheang2024gr2,guo2024pad,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero , including our base model LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva . Prior WAMs target fixed-base arms, humanoids~ zheng2026motionwam,li2026omega0,li2026wholebodywamwbc,zhang2026wholebodywam,qin2026wbwam , or an armed wheeled-legged quadruped~ ma2026decowam , and quadruped world models address locomotion or navigation~ wu2022daydreamer,lai2024wmp,bar2025nwm ; none manipulates with a load-bearing leg. Rather than training a cross-embodiment policy~ oxe2024openx,doshi2024crossformer,wang2024hpt , we adapt one arm-centric WAM---to our knowledge the first WAM for arm-free quadrupedal loco-manipulation. Few-step WAMs and on-policy distillation. Multi-step joint denoising makes WAMs strong but slow~ li2026lingbotva,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero ; unlike methods that skip full future prediction~ yuan2026fastwam,zheng2026motionwam,ma2026dit4dit,li2025uva,lv2026realtimewam,su2026onestepwam,zhang2026oswam , we accelerate the latent plan so that the teacher can supervise it. Few-step distillation~ salimans2022progressive,song2023consistency,luo2023lcm,yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2,liu2023rectifiedflow,prasad2024consistencypolicy,wang2025onedp has been applied offline to WAMs by Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flashwam and concurrent DirectWAM~ zheng2026directwam and AnyStep-WAM~ wang2026anystepwam , whereas on-policy training supervises a student on its own samples~ ross2011dagger,bengio2015scheduled,agarwal2024gkd,huang2025selfforcing . Existing on-policy WAM/VLA distillation either labels a single rollout batch~ yang2026wamopd , preserves the step count~ liu2026wamopd,ni2026multiteacher , or runs on-policy only along the denoising chain~ oh2026fastopd . Whereas prior on-policy self-distillation grants the teacher privileged context~ zhao2026opsd,liu2026opsdv , our OPSD teacher uses the same closed-loop context with more sampling steps, distilling the student to one video and two action steps along its own denoising chain. Reinforcement learning and policy merging. Reinforcement learning fine-tunes diffusion and flow models~ liu2025flowgrpo,zheng2026diffusionnft and policies~ ren2024dppo,zhang2025reinflow , including VLAs~ chen2025pirl,li2025simplevlarl , and lets a policy go beyond its demonstrations; it is best used to adjust an already competent policy~ huang2026rlposition . Tuning one task at a time, however, yields several specialists; Multi-Teacher OPD~ ni2026multiteacher distills several teachers into one student but keeps their step count, whereas merges the specialists into one few-step student. title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on The Action Gap (TAG 2026). OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=b7wZqqQzON
summary: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail when an instruction is reworded without changing the task liberopara , the released among them industrialvla . Yet for some policies, OpenVLA-OFT above all, success barely changes when the instruction is rewritten or removed, which LIBERO-Plus reads as the instruction being ignored liberoplus . Success rates cannot tell a wrong choice of object from a failure to finish after the right one. Prior work finds an instruction's meaning kept inside the policy gsr,encodednotcontrol and the intended object kept while success falls intact ; what it leaves open is where inside the policy a single word's effect can be changed ( sec:related ). On one released policy and two tasks that differ only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to pick up, we ask where along the path from language to action a single word's action gap can be changed. By that gap we mean the difference between how the policy acts on a wording and how the parent VLM resolves it ( sec:reach ). The parent VLM is the pretrained vision-language model (VLM) the policy's own VLM was cut from. Our answer is the connector between the VLM and the action-generating diffusion transformer: the landmark word's tokens act differently before and after it, and its weights alone can carry a repair, which other weights also partly carry (claims~2--3). This locates where interventions and repairs act; where the failure originates we leave open ( sec:entry , sec:position ). Operationally, we study the mirror pair of LIBERO-Spatial liu2023libero , two tasks in one scene (Appendix~ app:cells , Fig.~ fig:scene ): t7 (the bowl on the stove) and t9 (the bowl on the wooden cabinet). We vary the landmark noun, not the verb, which the training instructions share and whose rewriting costs little ( sec:calib ); object nouns also drive most of LIBERO-Para's drop liberopara . By a synonym we mean a word we judged to name the same landmark in this scene (five per landmark, Table~ tab:subst_cells ). An unpresented synonym is one absent from the training instructions, whether or not pretraining saw it. We say the meaning of a landmark word reaches the choice of bowl---the bowl the policy comes within 10~cm of ( sec:stats )---if, for an unpresented synonym, (a) the policy approaches the bowl the synonym names, (b) a nonce (made-up) word in the same slot rarely approaches that bowl, and (c) an unpresented synonym of the other landmark sends the policy to the other bowl. We say it does not reach completion if (d) its completion is separated ( ; sec:stats ) below the training word's; otherwise the comparison is unresolved. The policy's VLM passes one vector per token (the image tokens of two views, the instruction's other tokens and one to four tokens of the landmark word; sec:path ) to the action head, the model's term for everything after the VLM: a connector of 66 tensors that mixes all positions, then a diffusion transformer that outputs actions. A position is an index in this sequence, not a place in the scene; the landmark position is the landmark word's token span. To paste is to replace the vectors at chosen positions with those computed for the same frame under another instruction ( sec:interventions ); to mask is to drop positions from the instruction cross-attention of the action head; a transplant copies tensors from one finetuned policy into another without training. We contribute four claims about this one checkpoint and task pair, each resting on single-change comparisons on the same frozen VLM. (1)~Meaning reaches the choice, not completion: (a)--(c) hold, and (d) holds on t9's five synonyms pooled and on one word of t7; elsewhere on t7 completion is unresolved ( sec:reach ). (2)~Before the connector the landmark position alone suffices to set the choice; after it the choice is distributed, yet the landmark position still matters ( sec:preneck -- sec:postneck , sec:residual ): the other landmark's vectors pasted there move nearly every episode to the other bowl before the connector and almost none after it, where any two of the three groups (landmark, rest of the instruction, image) move most episodes. Masking that position after the connector still costs approach and completion for the synonyms that fall short ( sec:stats ). (3)~Finetuning on a few landmark-diversified instructions repairs t9's completion for synonyms absent from that finetuning, and the connector's 66 tensors suffice for the repair ( sec:var -- sec:transplant ): in three training seeds, training only those tensors on those instructions suffices, as does copying them from the landmark-diversified policy into one finetuned on the original instructions; copying the other action-head tensors instead carries part of the repair. After the repair, masking the landmark position costs less completion than on the undiversified policies (separated in two of three seeds), but not zero ( sec:after ). (4)~Two measures misread this path, each on one task ( sec:position ): masking every instruction word after the connector leaves t7 nearly intact, which, read alone, suggests the instruction's words go unused; a single-frame open-loop score misses t9's closed-loop gain from transplanting all but the connector. Hence we recommend judging robustness to rewording not by success rates alone but along the path from language to action ( sec:position ). Related work sec:related Paraphrase robustness and grounding gaps. Robustness of VLA policies to rewording has been measured suite-wide liberopara,industrialvla,liberoplus and across languages beyondenglish , and vision-only ablations show how much of a suite needs no language liberocf . Suite-wide scores hide a failure's shape: retrieve report the released Spatial within five points of its original score under LIBERO-PRO's paraphrases liberopro , and LIBERO-Para reads most failures as misidentifying the task. Yet with its policy's VLM frozen, some episodes fail near a successful trajectory, which LIBERO-Para suggests may be the VLM identifying the task while the action-generating part fails to execute it liberopara . Language is not simply ignored: retrieve explain failures on as instructions retrieving stored trajectories, gsr find a paraphrase's meaning kept inside the model, and encodednotcontrol find another named object linearly decodable inside while it does not control which object the policy approaches, with a checkpoint trained on all of LIBERO by their account (Appendix~ app:otherckpt ). The choice of object has been scored apart from success pi05,liberocf,robofollow,encodednotcontrol,retrieve ; under commonsense paraphrase, intact find the intended object still chosen while success falls, the shape of our claim~1. We add controls that tie the kept choice to the word's meaning (a nonce word in the same slot, a synonym of the other landmark) and interventions inside the policy: intact vary only the inputs, and encodednotcontrol vary the instruction and read internal states without changing them. Intervention inside VLAs. Interventions on these models replace the feature sequence the action head reads with another task's, in retrieve , or a paraphrase's features with the original's, layer by layer gsr , knock out attention vlatrace , steer sparse features or inject activations notallfeatures , and attribute in closed loop impactvla . Concurrently, wulff patch the diffusion transformer of a LIBERO-10 layer by layer in open loop, find synonym replacement among the weakest perturbations, and call for closed-loop tests of it. We use such established operations; what is new is their combination: a single word's token span, both sides of one module, closed-loop scoring of choice and completion, and the same interventions after a repair. Repair. Instruction diversification and augmentation stablelanguage , counterfactual training that makes language covary with the action cast , inference-time guidance against a vision-only prior liberocf,stablelanguage , and re-binding the instruction through a new pathway with a re-initialized action module gsr repair fragility. Where a change lies has been located by merging parameter groups, which places a VLA's robustness to scene changes in its language backbone retain ; by module swaps for a reinforcement-learning update lowrankrl ; and by finetuning one region at a time, which places adaptation to instruction shifts in the language backbone across five architectures notalllayers . With the VLM frozen, we instead test which action-head tensors suffice to carry one repair, by transplant and by connector-only finetuning, and re-apply the mask (and, in Appendix~ app:flipft , the paste) after the repair. Setup and calibration sec:setup The readout path sec:path gr00tn1,gr00tn17card runs a VLM cut from Cosmos-Reason2-2B cosmosreason2card (the parent VLM): its first 16 of 28 layers, further trained before the LIBERO finetuning (Appendix~ app:ckpt ). The policy reads the output of layer 16 before the final normalization and passes it through the connector ( sec:intro ) into a 32-block diffusion transformer, one vector per token: 128 image tokens (two views), 22 tokens of the instruction's other words, template and separators (23 on t1, sec:calib ) and one to four landmark tokens, 151--155 positions. The transformer denoises an action chunk (8 of its action steps are executed before the next prediction) and cross-attends in alternate blocks to the instruction positions and to the image positions. The action head ( sec:intro ) holds 537 tensors: 66 in the connector (a layer norm of 2 tensors and four self-attention blocks of 16 each) and 471 outside it (Appendix~ app:subsets ). The VLM is causal and the images precede the instruction, so before the connector only the landmark position and those after it (eight on the mirror pair) can differ between two instructions that differ only in the landmark word; after the connector every position can. The released LIBERO-Spatial checkpoint was finetuned with the VLM frozen, as is every policy we train ( sec:repair ). title: Ego2X: Contact-aware Transfer from Egocentric Human Data to Any Robot
summary: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action policies and robot world models depend on physical interaction data. Teleoperated demonstrations are slow to collect and tied to specific hardware~ aloha,droiddataset , whereas egocentric human videos capture diverse manipulation skills at scale~ egodex,hot3d,ego4d . Converting human video into robot observations and actions provides a direct route to scalable embodied learning. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines perform this conversion by retargeting 3D human hand kinematics to robot joints~ huro,ego2robot,phantom,egomimic . Phantom~ phantom composites rendered arms over inpainted hands, EgoMimic~ egomimic aligns human and robot action spaces, and HuRo~ huro and Ego2Robot~ ego2robot map reconstructed 3D hand trajectories via inverse kinematics. Their transferred unit is hand motion. The monocular hand estimates drift by centimeters along the camera ray, whereas stable manipulation demands millimeter precision on the object surface. Consequently, retargeted fingers hover beside objects, and parallel grippers close on empty space. Recovering and transferring object-frame contact from monocular RGB video poses three coupled challenges. First, monocular hand and object estimators exhibit depth and scale drift along the viewing ray. Therefore, using the hand to fix the object scale and that object to correct the hand depth couples their errors in a circular loop. Second, contacts occur on occluded surfaces and span timing, surface geometry, and force distribution that raw images do not directly expose. Third, the recovered contacts must drive robots with distinct kinematics and contact surfaces while replacing the human arm in video without erasing the held object. We present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers ( ). Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact in the object frame by its surface anchor, outward normal, push direction, relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state ( ). Recovered from tactile timing and camera-ray surface intersection, CORE unifies every stage of the conversion pipeline. To resolve ray-depth drift without circular scale coupling, Ego2X diagnoses object pose reliability and decouples depth estimation. Furthermore, it fuses hand scale with multi-view ray triangulation on the object path while shifting the hand along the camera ray against hand-ruler-free multi-view object geometry. To bridge morphologies, a URDF compiler maps robot collision geometry into mode-compatible contact pads, and contact-driven inverse kinematics pulls dexterous pads onto CORE anchors or synthesizes antipodal object-frame grasps for parallel grippers. Finally, CORE interaction states guide object-protected arm erasure and contact-edge de-skinning during video compositing, while closed-loop simulation replay verifies physical task completion. Across HOT3D~ hot3d , EgoDex~ egodex , and RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin2 , Ego2X substantially improves geometric accuracy, physical contact realization, and downstream policy performance. title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
summary: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.

Cellular-connected UAV, latent imagination, LiDAR, multimodal sensing, ray tracing, world models. Introduction Rapid growth of the low-altitude economy has accelerated urban deployments of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, and emergency rescue~ ping2026wcm,ping2026nsaai . Safe execution of such missions requires reliable command, control, and payload links between the UAV and ground cellular base stations (BSs)~ zeng2019accessing . Unlike flights at high altitude with dominant line-of-sight (LoS) propagation, urban airspace below rooftop height experiences coupled collision risks and abrupt coverage degradation: dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, cast deep non-LoS (NLoS) shadow fading on serving BSs, and expose UAVs at street intersections to strong LoS co-channel interference from neighboring sectors, causing severe signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) outages~ ping2025gcs,ping2026stl_urllc . Safe and connectivity-aware trajectory planning in unfamiliar urban canyons is therefore essential. Early trajectory planning relied on mathematical optimization under statistical path loss or probabilistic LoS models~ zhang2019cellular,ping2025gcs , which average out local building geometry and miss sharp shadowing transitions. Subsequent studies adopted channel knowledge maps (CKMs)~ zeng2021ckm and ray tracing simulators such as Sionna RT~ hoydis2023sionna_rt for site specific channel modeling, yet both offline trajectory optimization~ ping2026llm_stl and CKM aided planning depend on prior information unavailable onboard during flight, including global 3D city meshes, full area radio maps, and exact BS antenna patterns. Although deep reinforcement learning (DRL) relaxes explicit channel priors in communication-aware trajectory planning~ challita2018interference,zeng2021simultaneous , existing DRL planners still suffer from poor generalization across cities and low sample efficiency: policies conditioned on global coordinates over a fixed BS layout memorize a city specific SINR lookup map that fails in unseen cities~ challita2018interference , whereas model-free value and actor-critic planners~ zeng2021simultaneous map instantaneous observations directly to actions without a predictive model of blockage and interference evolution, requiring extensive interactions and failing to foresee abrupt corner outages~ hao2026look . To address these challenges, we propose CommDreamer, a radio-geometric world model for mapless cellular-connected UAV trajectory planning in unfamiliar urban canyons. Our core physical insight is that the omnidirectional 3D building facades captured by raw onboard LiDAR point clouds are the exact scatterers governing directional LoS blockage and intercell interference shielding, inherently coupling visible street geometry with multicell radio propagation. Inspired by DreamerV3~ hafner2023dreamerv3 , which decouples dynamics modeling from policy learning via imagined rollouts, CommDreamer compresses local LiDAR and cellular measurement histories into a compact latent belief invariant to global coordinates, eliminating explicit 3D maps and global CKMs. Predicting future trajectories in latent space enables the UAV to foresee upcoming shadow zones and interference surges, bypassing obstacle traps and coverage holes with a lightweight online policy. Our main contributions are threefold: We formulate mapless cellular-connected UAV trajectory planning as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) invariant to coordinate shifts, driven solely by raw onboard 3D LiDAR point clouds, multicell RSRP and SINR reports, and relative BS and goal kinematics without prior 3D maps or BS antenna patterns. We develop a multimodal radio-geometric world model fusing spherical LiDAR projections with symlog encoded cellular and kinematic features inside a categorical recurrent state space model (RSSM), jointly inferring local obstacle clearance, directional LoS/NLoS shadowing, and multicell interference dynamics for multi-horizon latent trajectory optimization. We build an open-source 3D urban wireless simulator, AeroCity-RT , coupling procedural city generation and 3GPP multicell deployments with Sionna RT ray tracing~ hoydis2023sionna_rt . Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies show that CommDreamer converges within episodes where model-free DRL fails to complete flights, achieves mission success with zero collisions, boosts mean route SINR by to and median SINR by to , and cuts effective link outage by down to over radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines. title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 17 pages, 13 figures, 17 tables (including supplementary material). Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/
summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.

Vision-language-action models, few-shot imitation learning, robot manipulation, viewpoint robustness, camera-to-robot calibration, canonicalization, benchmark. ecent vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05 have made few-shot fine-tuning the standard route to a deployed manipulation policy: mount a camera, dock the robot at a table, teleoperate 50--100 episodes, fine-tune a pre-trained model and deploy. In distribution the recipe works remarkably well; the public LIBERO release of succeeds in of episodes~ cadene2024lerobot,liu2023libero . However, the demonstrations are collected from a single camera pose and a single robot-base pose, and the policy silently bakes both into its weights. In practice the tripod gets bumped, the camera is re-mounted after maintenance, or the mobile base re-docks a few centimetres off; each of these is a rigid pose shift of a few centimetres and degrees, and each makes the policy reach for the wrong place ( ). A camera yaw moves the target by 21 pixels in a image; a 5\,cm base offset moves it by 5\,cm in the frame in which the policy commands its end effector, while the third-person image barely changes. LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus has quantified the camera half of this problem, with dropping from to under camera perturbations, but the base half has neither a benchmark nor a method for RGB VLAs. This raises two questions: (1) Can a policy trained at a single camera and base pose be made robust to pose shifts without data from other poses? (2) Can the shifts be recovered at deployment without a calibration object, ground-truth extrinsics or new data? Existing remedies answer the first question with data or with geometry. Data-side methods synthesise thousands of viewpoints~ chen2024roviaug,tian2024vista,yang2025robosplat,fei2026liberoplus or regularise the policy across simulator-rendered views~ huang2026crossview ; they need perturbed data at a scale that few-shot fine-tuning cannot afford, and they have no counterpart for a moved base, whose action labels change as well as its images. Geometry-side methods condition the policy on camera rays~ jiang2025camcond,wang2026rayvit,peng2026g3vla or re-synthesise the training view~ heo2026anycamvla , but they need the true extrinsics at test time, which a bumped camera no longer has; the one calibration-free VLA we know of~ li2026camvla regresses the hand-eye transform with an error of at a shift. None of them addresses a moved robot base. We answer both questions with world-anchored canonicalization: instead of asking the policy to learn to generalise across poses from data, we recover the shifts from what the robot already knows and map the observation back to the pose it was trained at. Three observations make this possible. First, both shifts are one quantity: each changes the camera-to-base extrinsic , and a base shift also moves the objects in the base frame. Second, the arm is its own calibration target: forward kinematics at the measured joint angles places every link in the base frame, so the visible arm pins down from a single RGB-D frame, without a checkerboard and without training~ lee2020dream,lu2024ctrnetx . Third, the arm alone is not enough: every camera and base shift with the same renders the arm identically yet demands different actions, the classical ambiguity~ zhuang1994axyb , and the static scene provides the missing world anchor for free. ( ) turns these observations into a training-free estimator with a ground-truth-free consistency gate, a canonicaliser that warps the image with the camera shift only and re-expresses state, action and start pose with the base shift only, and an error-aware fine-tuning that trains the policy on the canonicaliser's own artefacts. The policy architecture is untouched, and a base shift is reduced to ``the object is elsewhere on the table'', a variation the demonstrations already cover. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] We formulate camera and base shifts of a VLA as one extrinsic change, expose the gauge ambiguity of arm-based self-calibration, and show that LIBERO's world-frame convention silently absorbs base shifts. We propose , a calibration-free two-anchor estimator, a channel-separated canonicaliser and an estimator-matched augmentation that make an unmodified robust to camera, base and compound shifts. We introduce , the first RGB-VLA benchmark with graded base and compound shifts and a base-frame protocol that is isomorphic to a real robot. On , the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, recovers most of the gap to a ground-truth oracle, and gains the most where demonstrations are scarcest. Related Work sec:related Pose-Shift Vulnerability of VLAs. LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus finds camera and robot initial-state perturbations to be the two most damaging of seven factors for , OpenVLA-OFT and UniVLA~ black2024pi0,kim2025oft,bu2025univla ; LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025liberopro , COLOSSEUM~ pumacay2024colosseum , AGNOSTOS~ zhou2025agnostos and REALM~ sedlacek2025realm reach similar conclusions, and Mobi- ~ yang2025mobipi shows that a base offset of about 3\,cm halves the success of a fixed-base policy. None of them perturbs the base of an RGB policy or combines camera and base shifts. A wrist camera improves viewpoint robustness~ hsu2022hands , which we confirm and rely on. The dominant remedy is to show the policy more viewpoints: simulator re-rendering~ fei2026liberoplus , novel-view synthesis~ chen2024roviaug,tian2024vista,zhu2024nerfaug,yang2025robosplat,wang2026gensplat,cai2026robonvs,xu2025egodemogen,pan2026actionview , sim-to-real translation~ coholich2026mango or large augmented corpora~ ji2025oxeauge ; Cross-View Action Consistency~ huang2026crossview regularises across simulator-rendered view pairs of the same state. These approaches need thousands of extra trajectories or a simulator that re-renders arbitrary states, and they only change the image; when the base moves, the action labels must move with it ( ). title: Homeward: No Place Like the Training View
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies implicitly assume that third-person cameras remain fixed at their data-collection poses; once a camera is bumped, remounted, or swapped at deployment, task success degrades precipitously even though the underlying task and robot remain unchanged. We present Homeward, a training-free, plug-and-play observation adapter that canonicalizes observations from an uncalibrated deployment camera back into the training view for frozen VLA policies. Our design stems from a closed-loop diagnostic paradox in simulation: while re-rendering perturbed views into the training camera with oracle geometry recovers much of the lost performance, substituting an off-the-shelf feed-forward 3D foundation model can leave the policy worse off than applying no correction at all. This degradation concentrates on the thin, articulated robot arm, which feed-forward depth prediction tears and scatters - yet the arm's exact 3D state is already known from robot kinematics. Homeward exploits this asymmetry: it estimates what is unknown - camera parameters and static scene depth - from the live RGB frame and a single training-view reference, and renders what is known - the moving robot links - directly from the kinematic model. Evaluated across $\sim$300,000 closed-loop episodes spanning four frozen VLAs, Homeward boosts success across all 1,599 camera variants of LIBERO-Plus from 62.5%, 76.5%, 68.0%, and 3.6% to 77.6%, 95.1%, 91.2%, and 26.4% for OpenVLA-OFT, $π_{0.5}$, $π_0$, and OpenVLA, respectively. Without any scene fine-tuning or deployment camera calibration, Homeward extends to 6-DoF random placements, focal-length changes, and, with per-step pose estimation, continuous intra-episode camera drift, while matching or surpassing a calibrated, scene-trained view-synthesis baseline on three of four policies on LIBERO-Plus.

title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
summary: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.
full_text: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception--action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95 of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0 without defense to 70.0 . Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models use visual observations and language instructions to predict robot actions~ rt2,openvla . Their visual representations determine the scene information available for action prediction, so corrupted perception can change how the robot interacts with its surroundings. The security of embodied deployment therefore depends on the integrity of visual perception. Adversarial patches introduce localized patterns to redirect visual predictions~ brown2017patch . In VLA control, they exploit this dependence by altering the camera observation: the altered pixels change the encoded visual features and can redirect action predictions without changing policy parameters~ uada,edpa . The resulting interference can propagate through the perception--action loop. An erroneous movement changes the robot and object state, altering the next observation and potentially compounding the initial disturbance. Protecting VLA deployment thus requires recovering instruction-following control as interaction continues. Existing defenses address this vulnerability through auxiliary perception or adversarial training, introducing additional deployment requirements~ pad,edpa . PAD refines patch localization with pretrained segmentation~ pad , adding model inference to input processing. Xu et al. fine-tune the visual encoder to align clean and adversarial representations~ edpa , requiring perturbed training samples and parameter updates before deployment. Run-time intervention avoids updating the controlled policy but can retain external dependencies: BYOVLA identifies task-irrelevant regions through external scene interpretation and probes policy sensitivity before editing them~ byovla . Its scene interpretation adds auxiliary inference to the intervention process. These requirements increase online computation or offline adaptation work, complicating deployment when resources or opportunities for retraining are limited. Reducing these dependencies calls for a defense that guides localization and treatment selection using the VLA's available responses. This requirement raises a spatial challenge of distinguishing suspicious attention from legitimate manipulation responses, and a temporal challenge of maintaining suitable interventions as the scene changes. Analyses of VLA visual attention show that patches can attract responses away from the arm and relevant objects~ edpa . Yet the gripper and manipulated object also attract attention, making response strength alone ambiguous. To interpret the robot-related part of this response, known robot geometry can account for attention associated with the arm and gripper, leaving residual concentrations for inspection. For each proposed region, the defense must then determine the most suitable treatment while retaining visual evidence needed for manipulation. As motion changes the robot--object relationship, earlier choices require renewed assessment so that useful treatments remain available and unsuitable ones can be replaced. Sustained recovery therefore depends on spatial interpretation, treatment selection, and temporal updating. Our key insight is that the defended VLA can assess local interventions through changes in its own attention and action predictions. Comparing alternative views of the same observation with the same frozen policy makes these responses comparable in the current task context, even when a corresponding clean observation is unavailable. Repeating this assessment as interaction progresses connects purification to the policy's changing perception and action. Figure~ fig:at_a_glance introduces RECLAIM, which couples three components for inference-time protection of the perception--action loop. Geometry-Guided Attention Localization (GAL) combines persistent attention with projected arm and gripper geometry to expose suspicious residual concentrations. Attention-Response-Guided Purification (ARP) compares local treatments through attention redistribution and action uncertainty. Memory-Assisted Temporal Revalidation (MTR) retains earlier treatments for comparison with fresh proposals and reassesses their suitability as the scene changes. The selected treatment modifies the observation supplied to the same frozen VLA for action generation. We evaluate RECLAIM on frozen OpenVLA across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites~ libero and four patch attacks~ uada,edpa,rfas . Under matched UADA conditions, RECLAIM raises rollout success from 0.0 without defense to 52.92 , versus accelerated PAD's 40.83 . It also improves mask alignment and uses 77.31 less mean decision time than accelerated PAD. With unchanged defense settings, success ranges from 38.33 to 54.58 across the four attacks. Ablations support the contributions of response-guided treatment selection and temporal revalidation. Our contributions are as follows. We formulate input-side defense for a frozen VLA as stateful local visual intervention, using the policy's attention and action responses to guide recovery of instruction-following control. We develop , coupling geometry-guided localization, response-guided purification, and memory-assisted temporal revalidation to counter patch interference and sustain instruction-following control as embodied interaction changes the scene. We demonstrate task recovery across four patch attacks, quantify intervention alignment and decision cost, and examine component contributions through ablations. Related Work sec:related_work Adversarial patches in VLA control. Wang et al.~ uada expose the vulnerability of VLA-controlled manipulation to localized visual patches. Their Untargeted Action Discrepancy Attack (UADA) maximizes action deviations, while UPA disrupts movement directions and TMA induces targeted manipulation errors. UADA reaches a maximum average task failure rate of \(100 \) in their simulation experiments and an attack success rate exceeding \(43 \) in real-world trials. The resulting erratic movements show how image corruption can propagate into physical execution, threatening both task completion and safe interaction. These risks underscore the importance of defending the perception--action loop for reliable embodied deployment. This attack framework underlies our primary evaluation. Complementing these attacks on action outputs, Xu et al. introduce the Embedding Disruption Patch Attack (EDPA), which generates patches by disrupting visual--textual alignment and separating perturbed visual representations from clean ones~ edpa . They counter this representation-level interference by adversarially fine-tuning the visual encoder, requiring clean--perturbed training pairs and parameter updates. Lu et al. develop UPA-RFAS, combining feature disruption, attention dominance, and image--text misalignment to improve universal patch transfer~ rfas . We denote this attack as RFAS to distinguish it from Wang et al.'s UPA~ uada . Input-side adversarial patch purification. Patch purification methods locate and remove corrupted image content before prediction. PAD uses semantic independence and spatial heterogeneity for localization, followed by pretrained segmentation to refine removal masks~ pad . DIFFender couples localization and restoration through text-guided diffusion with few-shot prompt tuning~ diffender , while APEX combines region extraction, blur and boundary cues, and structure-guided inpainting~ apex . These methods evaluate purification through visual recognition performance and patch-localization quality. Such criteria do not determine whether a treatment preserves the visual cues needed for a robot's next action or remains appropriate as manipulation changes the scene. Their auxiliary processing also introduces deployment dependencies: PAD invokes a segmentation model, while DIFFender requires diffusion inference and prompt adaptation. Building on local patch purification, addresses these control and deployment requirements by using the defended VLA itself to assess treatments in the current task context, without auxiliary perception or a separately trained defense model. Policy feedback for run-time intervention. BYOVLA uses action sensitivity to guide observation editing without policy fine-tuning~ byovla . External VLM and segmentation models identify task-irrelevant regions; regional perturbations measure their influence on predicted actions and guide inpainting or background recoloring. adopts the principle of consulting the controlled policy, but extends the feedback beyond action sensitivity. Sensitivity to a region does not alone establish which purification to prefer. compares treatments through regional attention reduction and action uncertainty, requiring cross-operator attention agreement outside the edited region. It therefore assesses both suppression within the candidate region and consistency over the remaining scene, enabling purification selection without first assigning the suspected patch an external task-irrelevance label. Spatial information in attention. Attention studies provide evidence that frozen vision-language models retain spatial information useful beyond image-level prediction. Kang et al.~ localizationheads identify a small set of heads whose responses localize text-referred objects. ResCLIP finds that intermediate-layer query--key attention captures spatial correspondences between image regions; incorporating these responses into the final layer improves localization for dense visual prediction~ resclip . Together, these findings support using native attention as a source of spatial cues for localization. In manipulation, strong responses can also arise from the arm, gripper, and task objects. Wang et al.~ uada suggest robot-joint relationships as a potential defense cue. Robot geometry can therefore help interpret attended regions, while comparing attention before and after local edits provides feedback about their effect on the policy's visual processing. These complementary insights motivate grounding patch purification in embodied policy feedback, connecting spatial localization and treatment selection to continued task execution.
