title: SHAPE: Discrete Supervision and Parallel Continuous Streams for Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Human Data
summary: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn general manipulation skills by pretraining on large collections of robot demonstrations~ rt2,openvla,pi0,gr00tn1,gr00tn17 . For dexterous bimanual manipulation such demonstrations are expensive: each one requires an operator to teleoperate two arms and two multi-fingered hands. Egocentric human recordings with tracked hand poses are much cheaper to collect at scale~ hoi4d,holoassist,taco,hot3d,egodex,egoverse and cover the same everyday activities. Such recordings hold two promises for dexterous manipulation: improving pretraining when downstream robot demonstrations are available, and enabling a policy to learn new tasks directly from human demonstrations alone, with zero task-specific robot data. Fulfilling both promises on dexterous hands is challenging because humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics. Human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies: tracked hands can be retargeted to a shared end-effector (EEF) space, whereas mapping them to robot joints via inverse kinematics (IK) relies on embodiment-specific correspondences and yields out-of-distribution arm postures. This action gap creates two dilemmas. First, how should human data supervise the policy? Many methods supervise shared EEF actions via a continuous action decoder~ egomimic,egovla,hat,egozero,duet , sending gradients to the backbone only through that decoder; recent VLAs also train the backbone on discrete action tokens~ beingh0,pi05,ki , including on human data~ pi05ego . Yet because they differ in data and architecture at once, or combine both losses without separating them~ pi05ego , whether and how discrete supervision helps learn from human data remains unclear. Second, how should a dexterous robot read out actions at deployment? Unlike 1-DoF grippers, multi-fingered hands introduce high redundancy between fingertip poses and finger joints. Prior policies add a robot-only joint output beside a shared EEF output but execute only the joint output~ egomimic,duet,nexusvla . Yet the two outputs excel in different settings: direct joint readout is more accurate when fine-tuned with robot demonstrations, while EEF readout via IK transfers better from human demonstrations. In this work, we find that auxiliary discrete action supervision helps the backbone learn from egocentric human data, and we pair it with a dual-stream action expert that keeps both EEF and joint streams executable: the joint stream for precise control with robot demonstrations, and the EEF stream for human-to-robot transfer. As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), the backbone predicts discrete FAST tokens~ fast of each EEF chunk in one vocabulary for human and robot samples, supervising the backbone directly. In parallel, a shared flow-matching action expert independently outputs an EEF stream, supervised by both human and robot data, and a joint stream, supervised only by robot data in pretraining. Because both streams share the backbone and expert, human pretraining improves the joint stream without human joint labels, while either stream can drive the robot at test time. To evaluate both choices under controlled conditions, we pretrain four models in a matched 2 2 design that toggles human data and shared while fixing the architecture, robot data, and training budget. The human data comprise 2.8k hours of egocentric recordings, and the robot data 228 hours of teleoperation of two 7-DoF arms with 22-DoF hands. We evaluate the four models (reading out both streams) and two baselines in 1,680 real-robot trials, offline on held-out tasks, and via their representations and gradients. In simulation, we also evaluate all four models alongside both baselines on a second robot absent from pretraining, across both real-to-sim and cross-embodiment gaps. Our contributions are: We find that discrete action supervision helps a VLA learn dexterous manipulation from egocentric human data, driving backbone gradients and task-aligned action representations across domains. We propose a dual-stream action expert with executable EEF and joint streams, transferring human pretraining to joint control without human joint labels while supporting flexible stream selection at deployment. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE excels in both downstream regimes: fine-tuned on human demos alone, it learns new tasks without task-specific robot data; fine-tuned on robot demos, it scores 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for . Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action models. Recent VLAs couple a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with an action decoder, either by emitting discretized action tokens~ rt2,openvla,fast or by attaching a continuous diffusion or flow-matching expert~ pi0,pi05,gr00tn1,cogact,ctvam , with extensions for tactile feedback or sensory prediction~ tacforcing,star and cross-embodiment pretraining~ octo,rdt,hpt,beingh05 . with knowledge insulation~ ki also trains the VLM on FAST tokens while an expert produces continuous actions, but stops expert gradients from reaching the VLM and learns actions from robot data only. We keep both paths trainable and ask a different question: what discrete supervision does for learning from human data. Learning manipulation from human videos. Human videos have been used to pretrain visual representations~ ego4d,r3m,mvp,vc1 or action priors~ videodex , predict affordances, flow, point tracks, or keypoints~ vrb,atm,track2act,kai,skelwam , learn latent actions or visual foresight~ lapa,gr00tn1,mantis,internvlaa1 , and, with tracked hands or motion-capture gloves, supervise actions in a shared EEF space~ dexcap,egomimic,egovla,beingh0,beingh05,hrdt,phantom,dexwild,egozero,hat,pi05ego,psi0,emma,duet,motiontrans,egopi,egoscale,egoverse,exe,nexusvla . Co-training does not always help: gains require diverse pretraining~ pi05ego or embodiment-specific networks~ whatmatters . While Phantom~ phantom renders a robot over the human arm and others align human and robot features~ egobridge,innon , +ego~ pi05ego uses both FAST tokens and flow matching on human data for grippers without separating the two, and EgoLAP~ egolap supervises the VLM with structured language actions and motion rationales on bimanual grippers while stopping flow-expert gradients at the backbone~ ki . Using neither rendering, explicit feature alignment, nor gradient insulation, our matched 2 2 pretraining study and continuous-head controls on a dexterous bimanual robot isolate what direct backbone supervision adds to learning from human data, when fine-tuning downstream tasks both with and without robot demonstrations. Action representations for dexterous control. Action chunks can be tokenized~ rt1,vqbet,fast or modeled continuously with diffusion~ diffusionpolicy or flow matching~ pi0 . For dexterous hands, policies act either in EEF and fingertip space, which transfers across embodiments via IK~ dexcap , or in joint space, which is precise but embodiment-specific~ videodex,dexmv,anyteleop,dexpilot ; a large study on arms with grippers finds joint space more stable and task space better at generalizing~ demystifying . EgoMimic~ egomimic,act , DUET~ duet , and the concurrent Nexus-VLA~ nexusvla add a robot-only joint output beside a shared EEF output, but execute only the joint output. We keep both streams executable and, from the same checkpoints, find direct joint readout more accurate when fine-tuned with robot demonstrations, while wrist-frame EEF readout via IK transfers better from retargeted human demonstrations. Method sec:method Problem setup sec:setup We learn a policy that maps an observation and an instruction to an action chunk with , from two data sources. Robot teleoperation provides head and wrist camera images, proprioception, and actions in both EEF and joint space. Egocentric human recordings provide head-camera images and tracked 3D hand poses, but lack executable joint states and actuator commands; we retarget the tracked hands to derive EEF actions. Action parameterization. Both action spaces are relative to the current state. For each hand, let be the wrist pose at time and the positions of the five fingertips in the wrist frame, and let be the joint positions. For , the EEF action contains the wrist pose expressed in the current wrist frame, , and the fingertip offsets ; the joint action is the offset . In pretraining, each data source is normalized with its own statistics. For human recordings, the hand is first estimated with the MANO hand model~ mano and then retargeted to the robot hand, and the fingertip positions are those of the retargeted hand. Expressing EEF actions in the current wrist frame cancels camera extrinsics and decouples the action target from the underlying arm joint configuration. Backbone and dual-stream action expert sec:arch As shown in Fig.~ fig:method , a single backbone and a single action expert serve both embodiments; only the output streams differ. The backbone is Qwen3-VL-4B~ qwen3vl . Its input contains image tokens, instruction tokens, and a state prefix of two tokens that embed the current EEF state and, for robot samples, the joint state. During training each state token is dropped independently with probability 0.5, so that the policy can run with or without it. Following recent VLAs, the backbone also predicts the current sub-task as text ( ; ) and processes 64 learnable future queries that condition a Wan video diffusion head~ wan to predict frames about 1\,s ahead ( ; ). The action expert is a 0.6B transformer that attends to the backbone keys and values at every layer~ pi0 . Appendix~ supp:impl gives architectural details. The action expert is shared by two parallel output streams. The 55-d EEF stream represents each side by its 3D wrist position, a 6-d wrist rotation, and five 3D fingertip positions, and adds 7 torso and neck joints. The 65-d joint stream covers two 7-DoF arms, two 22-DoF hands, and the same 7 torso and neck joints. Each stream has its own input and output projections and is trained with a flow-matching loss~ flowmatching , or . In the attention mask (Fig.~ fig:method , bottom right), each stream reads the image, sub-task, and query tokens and its own state token, but neither the instruction nor the other stream, so the two streams can be executed independently at deployment. title: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) have demonstrated promising generalization and data efficiency for robot manipulation by coupling action generation with future visual prediction~ hu2025vpp,zhu2025uwm,li2026lingbotva . Recent models generate continuous action chunks through flow matching, providing an expressive interface between visual predictions and robot motion~ li2026lingbotva,akbari2026flashwam . Despite this progress, reliable execution on downstream tasks~ li2026vision,li2026badwam still requires adaptation to task-specific demands and to the deviations that arise during closed-loop interaction. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) offers a straightforward adaptation strategy by providing dense action targets from expert demonstrations. However, SFT supervises the model only on demonstration data. During training, the action expert sees only noised versions of the ground-truth actions and never the intermediate states produced by its own sampler, a form of exposure bias~ ning2023exposure and the sampler-level counterpart of the compounding errors at deployment~ ross2011dagger , whose environment-level gap requires closed-loop interaction. Moreover, given only the current observation, a demonstrated action chunk is one of several plausible continuations, and the SFT target does not reveal which one the demonstrator followed. Finally, adapting a pretrained model to a narrow task distribution can degrade previously acquired capabilities~ shenfeld2025rlrazor . On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) addresses the state-distribution mismatch by optimizing the policy on its own rollouts, motivating its use in VLA and WAM post-training~ li2025simplevlarl,lu2025vlarl,qian2026wamrl . However, many manipulation tasks offer only sparse success rewards, making exploration and credit assignment costly when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. Even with denser, reconstruction-based rewards~ qian2026wamrl , reward-based optimization only evaluates sampled behavior through scalar feedback, leaving the policy to infer how its actions should change. This motivates supplying structured action supervision directly on the states produced by the policy's own action sampler. Our key insight is that the future frames of a demonstration, which we call hindsight, carry privileged information about the intended task progression, connecting learning with privileged information~ vapnik2009lupi,chen2019lbc to on-policy distillation~ agarwal2024gkd . We build on this insight in HINT-WAM: the same model serves as a teacher that additionally reads the hindsight, whereas the student observes only the inputs available at deployment and is supervised on the states produced by its own action sampler. Throughout this paper, on-policy refers to the generation of actions: as in on-policy distillation for language models~ agarwal2024gkd , where prompts are drawn from a dataset and the student generates the response, observations are drawn from demonstrations and the student generates the denoising trajectory of its action chunk. We do not collect new environment states. Transferring this supervision to a flow-matching action expert introduces a further challenge. Such experts generate continuous actions by integrating a velocity field, so the token-level probability matching used in autoregressive distillation does not apply directly. Regressing the teacher's velocity field would drive the student toward the teacher's conditional mean, which averages over modes that the student cannot distinguish without hindsight. We therefore distill the teacher with the energy score~ gneiting2007scoring , a strictly proper scoring rule that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples and one teacher sample. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce HINT-WAM, a self-distillation framework for world action models in which the policy acts as its own teacher given hindsight, requiring neither a separately trained teacher nor environmental rewards or simulator interaction. We propose a distribution-level distillation objective for flow-matching action experts based on the energy score, which avoids the mode averaging of velocity regression and requires no action-likelihood evaluation. The framework adapts the action expert while keeping the world-modeling backbone frozen. Comprehensive experiments on LIBERO-90 and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate that HINT-WAM consistently improves post-training performance over SFT and matched baselines, while mitigating the catastrophic forgetting of pretrained skills. Related Work sec:related World Action Models sec:related_wam Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine large-scale multimodal pretraining with diverse robot demonstrations to translate camera observations and language instructions into robot commands~ brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,oneill2024openx,kim2024openvla . Rather than discretizing actions into tokens, many recent policies generate continuous action chunks with diffusion~ chi2023diffusionpolicy or flow matching~ lipman2023flow,black2024pi0 . World action models (WAMs) additionally reason about how the scene will evolve~ shen2026worldactionmodelssurvey , and differ mainly in how tightly they tie prediction to control. Some extract predictive visual representations from a video model to condition a separate action head~ hu2025vpp , while others generate future frames and actions jointly through a shared denoising process or a unified video--action backbone~ guo2024pad,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm . Autoregressive designs such as LingBot-VA interleave video and action prediction for closed-loop control~ li2026lingbotva , and RoboDreamer exploits imagined dynamics for planning~ zhou2024robodreamer . Recent architectures pair a large world-modeling backbone with a lightweight flow-matching action expert~ akbari2026flashwam . While these works study WAM design and pretraining, HINT-WAM post-trains only the action expert on the states the policy visits. On-Policy Self-Distillation sec:related_opsd On-policy distillation builds on the observation, first formalized by DAgger~ ross2011dagger , that a policy learns most effectively from the states it reaches on its own rather than from those recorded by a demonstrator. GKD~ agarwal2024gkd and MiniLLM~ gu2024minillm adopt this principle for compressing large language models: the student generates its own sequences, which the teacher then scores token by token, and MiniLLM additionally argues for the mode-seeking reverse KL as the distillation objective. A more recent line of work removes the need for a separate, larger teacher by letting a single model play both roles, where the teacher is the model itself given privileged information that the student does not see. Self-Distilled Reasoner~ zhao2026opsd trains a reasoning model on its own on-policy samples under the supervision of a copy conditioned on reference solutions, dOPSD~ dat2026dopsd extends this self-distillation scheme to diffusion language models, and PRISM~ dat2026prism applies it to the design of communication topologies in multi-agent systems, guiding the designer with a privileged sibling. All of these methods operate on discrete tokens and rely on likelihood-based objectives. HINT-WAM brings on-policy self-distillation to embodied control, where the student is a flow-matching action expert that generates continuous actions without a tractable likelihood. Unlike prior flow-matching distillation methods, which regress the teacher's velocity field~ fang2026flowopd,li2026diffusionopd , we match action distributions with a proper scoring rule, the energy score~ gneiting2007scoring , which needs only one teacher sample per state. On-Policy Distillation for World Action Models sec:related_wamopd Recent works bring on-policy distillation to WAMs, supervising the student on its own rollouts with a separate, stronger task-specific teacher, either through joint video--action targets~ yang2026wamopd or by replaying a fixed pool of student and teacher trajectories~ liu2026wamopd . The former queries the teacher for paired video and action targets on student rollout histories, while the latter reweights each replayed decision with prefix-based importance weights to correct the shift between stored and current histories. These methods require an additional teacher model, making post-training computationally expensive. In contrast, HINT-WAM derives the teacher from the student itself by adding only a lightweight hindsight branch. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first self-distillation framework for world action models. Method sec:method This section presents HINT-WAM, which post-trains a pretrained WAM by letting the model act as its own teacher given hindsight. We first review the base model ( ) and outline the framework ( ), then describe the hindsight teacher ( ) and its distillation into the student ( ). Preliminaries sec:method_prelim Base world action model. We build on Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam , a world action model whose backbone is a Mixture-of-Transformers~ liang2024mot with two experts that share a single attention operation in every layer. The video expert is a large pretrained video diffusion transformer~ wan2025wan operating on video VAE latents, and the action expert is a lightweight diffusion transformer that generates an action chunk of control steps. The policy is conditioned on an observation consisting of the current camera frame , the language instruction , and the proprioceptive state . title: RoboMorpher: Scaling Robot Morphology Representations for Cross-Embodiment Action Prediction
summary: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.
full_text: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology--state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision--language--action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40 success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 23.27 on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning. Introduction sec:intro Generalist robot policies learn from demonstrations across platforms~ oxe,octo,rdt , but the kinematic meaning of joint-space actions depends on robot morphology. Identical joint values can produce different link poses as link lengths and joint arrangements vary; padding actions to a common dimension does not resolve this ambiguity. End-effector (EE) control provides Cartesian targets but requires robot-specific inverse kinematics and does not uniquely specify the full joint configuration. A shared joint-action representation should therefore preserve control coordinates while accounting for their morphology-dependent spatial effects. To learn this relationship without collecting manipulation demonstrations for every morphology, we use robot kinematics as supervision. We introduce MorphGen, a procedural generator informed by a survey of 33 URDF/MJCF descriptions. MorphGen normalizes serial-arm kinematics into a common local- convention, samples six- and seven-joint manipulators from empirical link-length priors, and selects feasible home poses through collision-aware inverse kinematics. Forward kinematics provides link-pose targets for 40 million morphology--state pairs. We present RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer pretrained on these data. Morphology conditions its encoder and decoder, while kinematic-chain attention biases encode relative joint positions along the chain. Joint-angle reconstruction preserves control coordinates, and link-pose reconstruction supervises their kinematic effects. The pretrained tokenizer is then frozen and integrated into a vision--language--action (VLA) policy. Following Discrete Forcing~ discreteforcing , a discrete branch predicts action codes, which are decoded into coarse trajectories and refined by a continuous flow-matching branch. Pretrained morphology features condition both branches. We evaluate on 15 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks across five embodiments~ chen2025robotwin and introduce EmbodiBench, comprising ten tabletop tasks with 30 generated URDFs each. Downstream URDFs are excluded from tokenizer pretraining; policies learn from task demonstrations. RoboMorpher achieves 56.40 and 23.27 success, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success to 5.33 , supporting its contribution to downstream performance. Our contributions are as follows. MorphGen, a survey-guided generator of robot morphologies and large-scale kinematic pretraining data. RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer trained through joint-angle and link-pose reconstruction, integrated into a VLA policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. EmbodiBench, a benchmark for manipulation across generated morphologies, with experiments on task performance, representation design, and reconstruction fidelity. Related Work sec:related Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning. Open X-Embodiment aggregates demonstrations across robot platforms~ oxe , supporting generalist policies such as Octo and RDT~ octo,rdt . HPT and CrossFormer learn shared representations from heterogeneous embodiments~ wang2024hpt,doshi2025crossformer . MetaMorph and Shared Modular Policies incorporate robot morphology through policy conditioning and inter-module communication~ metamorph,smp , while Body Transformer and BodyVLA exploit kinematic structure in policy architectures~ pmlr-v270-sferrazza25a,suzuki2026embedding . UniAct, X-VLA, and XL-VLA further explore universal actions, embodiment-specific prompts, and shared latent action spaces~ zheng2025uniact,zheng2025xvla,Jiang_2026_CVPR . Our focus is morphology-conditioned action encoding and decoding, learned from kinematic supervision before policy training. Robot Action Representations and Tokenization. Vector quantization learns discrete representations through reconstruction~ vqvae . FAST, VQ-VLA, and FASTer explore action tokenization for efficient sequence modeling~ fast,wang25vqvla,liu2025faster , while X-Tokenizer aligns discrete action codes with pretrained vision-language representations~ kang2026xtokenizer . Discrete Forcing combines discrete action prediction with continuous flow-matching refinement~ discreteforcing . RoboMorpher extends configuration-level tokenization with morphology conditioning and joint-angle/link-pose reconstruction, explicitly supervising the relationship between control values and spatial effects. Robot Data Generation and Benchmarks. RoboGen synthesizes robot tasks, scenes, and training supervision through simulation~ robogen . RoboTwin~2.0 and RoboDojo provide diverse manipulation tasks and evaluation across simulation and real-world settings~ chen2025robotwin,chen2026robodojo . MorphGen targets kinematic supervision by generating chains and configuration--pose pairs from survey-derived priors. EmbodiBench evaluates the resulting action representations across generated morphologies on ten tabletop tasks. Method sec:method-overview Our pipeline separates kinematic representation learning from task-specific action selection ( ). MorphGen generates morphology--configuration pairs with forward-kinematics (FK) supervision. RoboMorpher encodes configurations into joint-aligned codes and reconstructs angles and link poses conditioned on morphology. A VLA policy predicts these codes and refines decoded trajectories while keeping the tokenizer frozen. FK then supplies configuration--pose supervision without manipulation demonstrations. title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
summary: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

Which past experience a WAM reuses decides whether it succeeds. (a) Form turns a rollout into short multimodal records. (b) On the same knife-to-bowl task, the native WAM times out, whereas reusing the right records succeeds in 237 and then 139 steps. (c) Fusion feeds the images, text and actions of a selected record to the WAM as a prefix and an action prior. fig:opening-experience Introduction sec:intro Post-deployment self-improvement is essential for world-action models (WAMs) to operate autonomously over the long term in real-world environments~ guo2026loopwam . Every rollout shows a WAM the consequences of its own actions, and this experience could guide later attempts at the same task and inform decisions in other tasks under similar conditions~ chen2026zeva , but how a WAM should use it remains open. Existing methods supply such experience, or demonstrations from other sources, to the policy as context. Zero-WAM~ zhou2026zerowam specifies an unseen task with a human video, WATCH~ park2026watch predicts actions and frames from one demonstration of the same task, ~ jang2026ravla retrieves demonstrations by behavioral similarity, AED~ lyu2026aed feeds retrieved action embeddings to the policy, and Zeva~ chen2026zeva retrieves action effects by task phase. Each selects a record, a retrieved piece of experience, by its source or by its match to the task, behavior or phase, assuming that such a record will help. Our experiments, however, suggest otherwise. In paired closed-loop trials, giving Cosmos~3 Nano~ nvidia2026cosmos3 , the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the most similar record from its own past rollouts as text and frames breaks 21 episodes it would otherwise solve and rescues only~7, lowering its success from 55 to 41 (Fig.~ fig:results-summary c). We therefore ask what makes good experience for a world-action model. We show that experience is valuable only in use: a record is valuable at a state if supplying it raises the probability that the policy completes the task from there. This value follows neither from the record's source nor its similarity to the task. It depends on three choices: what is stored, since failures hold useful operations (Sec.~ sec:exp-form ); when it is used, since injecting by predicted gain, not similarity, breaks fewer successes (Sec.~ sec:exp-fit ); and where it enters the policy, since raw records hurt, whereas the same records help once they enter through trained readers (Sec.~ sec:exp-naive ). We therefore propose , built on three components that decide what to store (Form), when to use it (Fit), and where it enters the policy (Fusion). Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short operation records, each verified against the recorded frames and states, so that failures still contribute the operations that made progress. Fit teaches the policy to read records and injects one only when its predicted gain exceeds a margin, learning that gain from paired continuations with and without the record rather than from similarity alone. Fusion encodes the record's images, text and actions and feeds them to both streams of the WAM, as a prefix that tells the Reasoner which operation to perform and an action prior that tells the Generator how to move. On the knife task in Fig.~ fig:opening-experience b, the native WAM times out, whereas finishes in 139 steps by reusing fork, ladle and spatula records, none of which involves a knife. On MolmoSpaces and RoboLab, achieves state-of-the-art results (Fig.~ fig:results-summary ), although it is never trained on RoboLab: it raises the success of Cosmos~3 Nano from 55 to 67 and from 29.2 to 40.0 , reduces steps to success by 12.2 and 11.3 , and cuts regressions against direct input by 57 . contributions are threefold. We show that experience supplied directly as context can hurt a WAM, and propose to judge a record by its gain for the receiving policy at the current state rather than by its source. This view yields three requirements for reuse: what to store, when to use it, and where it enters the policy. We propose , which meets each requirement with one component. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts into verified operation records, with a verification bound that links local checks to the whole rollout; Fit learns when a record helps from paired continuations rather than from similarity; and Fusion injects its images, text and actions into both the reasoning and action streams. We demonstrate that , trained once on 200 examples and fixed at deployment, achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and on RoboLab, where it is never trained, and that ablations support each requirement. Related Work sec:related from experience. Agents have long improved from past attempts. Case-based reasoning retrieves, reuses and revises prior solutions~ aamodt1994case , language agents store verbal reflections, distilled lessons~ shinn2023reflexion,zhao2024expel or reusable skills scored by swapping them out~ huang2026skillrubricsrl , and ICAL~ sarch2024ical extends this to VLM agents. Robot policies instead update their weights, from expert labels on visited states~ ross2011dagger or from successful and failed deployment rollouts~ guo2026loopwam,intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience . keeps the policy fixed at deployment and stores experience in the robot's images, states and actions, which the policy learns to read. experience. title: DiWALI: Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play
summary: Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce DiWALI, a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a world model trained on human and robot play. DiWALI infers latent actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN benchmark, DiWALI policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.
full_text: : Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models \\ via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play Akshay L Chandra , Iman Nematollahi , Lingyue Zhao , Daria Kulikova , \\ Angela P. Schoellig , Fabien Despinoy , Abhinav Valada Department of Computer Science, University of Freiburg, Germany Toyota Motor Europe ZUSE School ELIZA Technical University of Munich, Germany Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce , a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a world model trained on human and robot play. infers latent actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN benchmark, policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de . Introduction Robot manipulation data is fundamentally constrained by robot time. Demonstrations are typically collected through teleoperation, with a single operator controlling a single robot in real time. As a result, every hour of recorded data requires roughly one hour of both human and robot time~ openx2024 , leaving even the largest robot datasets small by the standards of vision and language. World models~ hafner2020dreamer, hafner2025dreamerv3 learned from play can stretch this limited data budget. A single play dataset collected in a scene can support a simulator in which policies are trained and refined through imagined rollouts~ nematollahi2025lumos, chandra2025diwa . However, both the play data and the demonstrations must still include robot actions, since the learned dynamics are conditioned on those actions. Human demonstrations are not subject to the same robot-time bottleneck. A person can demonstrate a skill in seconds, yielding an order of magnitude more demonstrations per hour than teleoperation. This makes human interaction a far more scalable source of behavioral data, and policies pre-trained on tens of thousands of hours of human data have required only a few hours of robot data for adaptation~ zheng2026egoscale . However, these results rely on sensorized humans using tracked hands~ kareer2025egomimic , gloves~ zheng2026egoscale , or handheld and wearable grippers~ honerkamp2025whole to convert human motion into action labels. Plain video of a person acting in the robot's workspace provides no such action signal and, moreover, depicts a different embodiment. We seek a single model that learns from such video and subsequently serves as a simulator in which a robot policy can be improved. Two lines of work each address one half of this challenge. Latent action models~ ye2025latent, liang2025clam, bu2505learning infer transformations between consecutive frames of action-free video and use them to pre-train policies, but the learned dynamics serve only as a training signal rather than as a simulator. Action-conditioned world models provide such a simulator~ hafner2021dreamerv2, hafner2025training, jiang2025world4rl, xiao2025worldenv , but require action-labeled data. To our knowledge, no existing method combines both capabilities in a single learned model that is used to improve a robot policy. We close this gap with , which conditions the world model on a latent action inferred from two consecutive observations rather than on a robot command ( ). An inverse dynamics model infers this latent action, which the forward dynamics of a recurrent state-space model use to predict the next latent state. Both are trained end-to-end without action supervision, so the latent action captures whatever aspects of a transition are needed to predict the next observation, with the same representation used for human hands and robot grippers. A single model can therefore learn scene dynamics from both human and robot play. A small decoder, trained only on robot play and conditioned on the latent state, grounds latent actions in executable robot commands, while a diffusion policy is trained and fine-tuned entirely in the latent action space. The world model thus serves both as the bridge between embodiments and as the simulator in which the policy improves. As imitation takes place in the latent action space, demonstrations no longer require action labels. A skill shown by a human is encoded as latent actions, imitated by the diffusion policy and decoded into executable robot commands. On the CALVIN benchmark~ mees2022calvin , a policy trained solely from human demonstrations outperforms policies trained with a few robot demonstrations, whether based on a world model conditioned on ground-truth robot actions or a latent action model with a jointly trained decoder. Human play further broadens the world model's training distribution, enabling imagination-based fine-tuning to produce stronger policies than with the same amount of robot play alone. Finally, on a real robot, policies learned primarily from human demonstrations improve further through imagination, without additional real-world interaction. In summary, our contributions are: A latent-action world model for human and robot play: a recurrent state-space model driven by an inverse dynamics model and trained end-to-end without action supervision, together with an action decoder trained separately on robot play and conditioned on the latent state. The ablations show that both design choices are critical for making the latent actions decodable. Skill policies from action-free human demonstrations: diffusion policies over latent actions that, when trained solely from human demonstrations, outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Human play for policy improvement in imagination: action-free human play is incorporated into the latent-action world model that serves as the simulator, allowing human experience to shape the imagined rollouts used for policy improvement rather than only policy pre-training. Policies fine-tuned in this simulator outperform those fine-tuned with the same robot play alone. Real-world validation: the full pipeline, from play data to a fine-tuned skill policy, deployed on a physical robot. =-1 We make the code publicly available at . Related Work sec:related Robot Manipulation from Human Video: Learning manipulation from human video requires a representation that bridges the embodiment gap. Explicit approaches build it from geometric cues extracted by off-the-shelf perception: point tracks predicted from video and followed by the robot~ wen2023any, bharadhwaj2024track2act , object flow used as a cross-embodiment interface~ xu2024flow, heppert2026scaling , and human hand poses retargeted to a robot hand~ zheng2026egoscale, luo2026beingh07 . These representations are geometrically grounded, but inherit perception failures and impose a hand-designed interface between embodiments. Implicit approaches instead learn how human video should transfer to robot behavior. They include visual encoders and skill embeddings pre-trained on human video~ karamcheti2023language, kim2025uniskill , policies co-trained on human and robot data~ kareer2025egomimic, punamiya2026egoverse , video generators that predict how a task unfolds~ liang2025videopolicy , and latent actions inferred between frames. Latent actions can be learned from arbitrary video, but must later be grounded in executable robot commands. belongs to this family, with one key distinction: the latent actions learned from human video are also the world model's action space, so the model bridging the embodiments also serves as the simulator. =2pt Action Models: sec:related_lam Vision-language-action models~ kim2025openvla, black2024pi0, shukor2025smolvla, ding2024quarvla scale with action-labeled robot data~ openx2024 . Latent action models offer a route beyond this dependence. An inverse dynamics model infers a pseudo-action between consecutive frames, and a forward model predicting the next frame from it keeps the latent informative~ schmidt2024lapo, bruce2024genie, bu2026whatmatters, garrido2026latent . LAPA~ ye2025latent , UniVLA~ bu2505learning , Moto~ chen2025moto , and villa-X~ chen2026villa pre-train policies on such latents from action-free video before fine-tuning on robot actions. LAWM~ tharwat2025latent replaces the pairwise inverse model with a forward instruction-conditioned policy and LAOF~ bu2026laof introduces optical-flow constraints. Closest to our setting, CLAM~ liang2025clam learns continuous latent actions with inverse and forward dynamics and jointly trains an action decoder on a small amount of labeled data. In these methods, however, the learned dynamics mainly serve representation learning. instead learns latent actions within a recurrent world model trained on human and robot play, and trains the action decoder separately, conditioned on the latent state; our ablations show both choices are critical for decodability. =-1 =2pt Improvement in Imagination: Reinforcement learning can refine skills acquired through behavior cloning~ wang2019exploringmodelbasedplanningpolicy, nematollahi2022robot, ren2025diffusion , but fine-tuning through physical interaction is costly. The Dreamer family~ hafner2020dreamer, hafner2021dreamerv2, hafner2025dreamerv3, hafner2025training replaces the environment with learned dynamics and learns behaviors from imagined rollouts. DITTO and LUMOS~ demoss2023ditto, nematollahi2025lumos learn imitation policies inside world models trained on robot data, and DiWA, World4RL, and World-Env~ chandra2025diwa, jiang2025world4rl, xiao2025worldenv post-train robot policies with reinforcement learning inside offline world models. D2R~ tharwat2026dream extends this to continual learning, rehearsing earlier tasks in imagination to prevent forgetting. All condition their dynamics on robot actions, requiring every training sequence to include them. DGAC~ chen2026dgac instead learns dynamics from human video, but improves the policy through real robot failures rather than imagined interaction. DreamDojo~ gao2026dreamdojo conditions a world model trained on human video on latent actions, but uses it to evaluate and plan rather than to improve a policy. instead conditions the world model on inferred latent actions, so human play trains the dynamics that later serve as the simulator, and the policy is pre-trained and fine-tuned entirely in latent action space. =-1 Problem Formulation sec:problem We study learning and improving robot manipulation skills when most of the available interaction data comes from humans and therefore carries no robot actions. title: Grana: Compositional Reward Modeling for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot reward modeling faces two challenges: generalizing across tasks and accurately tracking progress in long-horizon manipulation. General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored. Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions. We train a language-conditioned model to estimate progress in short-horizon tasks and individual subtasks of long-horizon tasks. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask's predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress. General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores. Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.
full_text: Method sec:method learns to select the unfinished subtask and predict its local progress, then combines these outputs into whole-task progress. The same language-conditioned model is pretrained on mostly short tasks and reused for longer compositions. Its progress targets account for both execution quality and the evaluated subtask's position in the task sequence. Predicting Progress through Subtasks sec:problem_formulation sec:local_reward_model sec:atomic_grounding sec:stage_composition Given camera observations, a task description, and the task's subtask sequence, selects the unfinished subtask and predicts its local progress (Fig.~ fig:rhoval-language-interface ). The supplied sequence specifies the user's preferred execution order and evaluation granularity. Subtask descriptions are language inputs to a shared predictor; their order and number are not hard-coded into the architecture. The same task can therefore be queried with different valid orders or coarser or finer decompositions. Training or adaptation uses supervision defined under the chosen specification, while inference conditions on the supplied list. Whole-task progress measures completion relative to this user-specified procedure. Let be the selected subtask's zero-based index, and let be its predicted local subtask progress. For a task with subtasks, we assign each subtask an equal share of global whole-task progress: Six completed subtasks and halfway progress through the seventh give in a nine-subtask task. If local progress falls to zero, the estimate becomes . This composition assumes that preceding subtasks remain completed after a local failure; an incorrect selection can still distort the estimate. Shared predictor sec:implementation-details In our model, subtask selection and progress prediction share a VLM that processes multiview observations sampled over time, providing context to distinguish a failed attempt from its recovery. A temporal transformer combines features for local-progress prediction through a shared head. Temporal aggregation can use later observations. In our policy-learning experiments, we score recorded trajectories offline. Supervision for Imperfect Execution sec:structured_supervision sec:target-construction 3pt 12pt r 0.49 fig:annotation-retry Selecting the right subtask does not reveal how much of it is complete. Elapsed time advances through both a successful insertion and repeated misalignment, yet these executions should receive different progress targets. We therefore combine subtask annotations with judgments of local action quality (AQ). Subtask annotations identify completed work. AQ judgments describe setbacks and recovery within the unfinished subtask. Annotators mark subtask boundaries and intervals of suboptimal or regressed execution; unmarked intervals are nominal. Nominal execution follows the task normally. Suboptimal execution is degraded without physical failure, such as a misaligned screw that remains held. Regressed execution loses local progress through physical failure, such as dropping the screw. Separately, each subtask receives a binary outcome: 1 for successful completion and 0 for failure. These outcomes describe how the subtask ends: a completed subtask can still contain regressed intervals followed by recovery. The annotations define a local progress target without requiring numerical scores for individual frames. Within each uninterrupted attempt, we distribute progress according to action quality, giving nominal frames larger increments than suboptimal frames. In a successful subtask with retries, regression resets local progress to zero, and a subsequent attempt rebuilds it. The binary outcome anchors the final local-progress target. Let denote the annotated subtask to evaluate. We construct the whole-task progress target using the same composition as at inference. In the insertion retry in Fig.~ fig:annotation-retry , the six completed subtasks retain their credit while insertion fails and recovers. Training Subtask Selection and Progress Prediction sec:reward_model_inference sec:progress-training-details sec:native-stage-training Because selects its own subtask, progress training must account for a description that is chosen incorrectly. For example, if insertion is only partly complete but the model selects fastening, fastening should receive zero progress rather than insertion's partial progress. We use task order to define the target for each queried subtask: earlier completed subtasks receive one, the annotated unfinished subtask receives its local progress, and later subtasks receive zero: Pretraining combines subtask selection with annotated-subtask and whole-task progress prediction. Selection learns to identify , while local-progress training teaches the predictor to evaluate its description. Whole-task prediction provides auxiliary supervision from available overall labels, allowing data without reliable subtask annotations to contribute. During adaptation, we also query the progress predictor with descriptions selected by the model itself. For each selected description, Eq.~ eq:focus-progress-target provides the corresponding local-progress target, including when the selected subtask is earlier or later than the annotated one. We implement the shared predictor with Qwen3.5-4B~ qwen2026qwen35 and LoRA~ hu2022lora , training the adapters, temporal transformer, and progress head while keeping the base VLM frozen. Selection and progress use cross-entropy objectives. For progress training, scalar targets are encoded as distributions over neighboring bins; the head predicts a distribution whose mean gives a continuous progress estimate. Both objectives place greater weight on predictions farther from the target. Pretraining and adaptation retain the same architecture and language interface. At inference, the model receives observations, the description, and the subtask list, without annotation inputs. We use these differences in two ways, holding the conversion procedure fixed across reward models in each comparison. Offline reinforcement learning Using the learned progress model , we assign each -step action chunk a reward equal to the discounted sum of predicted progress increments: \[ r_t(s_t,a_ t:t+H ) = _ j=0 ^ H-1 ^j , \] where is the per-step discount factor. Using these rewards, IQL~ kostrikov2022offline learns an action-value function and a state-value function . We use the resulting advantage estimates, , to update the policy with BPPO~ zhuang2023behavior . Progress-weighted behavior cloning Even successful trajectories can contain unhelpful actions, so we use progress changes to weight their contribution to imitation learning. We map these progress changes, , over each action step to high, intermediate, or low nonnegative imitation weights, using separate thresholds for human and policy actions. title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
comment: 8-page main paper with references and supplementary material (15 pages); 5 figures, 13 tables. Code: https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI Project page: https://starsholic.github.io/AeroRSI/
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.

Introduction sec:intro Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that follow natural-language instructions could inspect infrastructure, search for people, and deliver goods without a human pilot. Toward this goal, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models for aerial vision-language navigation (VLN)~ liu2023aerialvln,wang2025travelUAV,gao2025openfly,lee2025citynav,wang2025uavflow,jiang2026satnav directly map visual observations and instructions to flight actions~ zhang2026navfom,xu2026aerialvla,xu2026aerodpo,sun2026autofly,cai2025flightgpt , mirroring their success in robotic manipulation~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,octo2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 . Despite this progress, existing aerial agents~ zhang2026navfom,xu2026aerodpo,jiang2025longfly,xu2026aerialvla,wang2026refinefly still fail frequently in closed-loop flight, often due to collisions with obstacles. Since a single wrong action can terminate an entire flight, such failures severely limit their reliability. These failures stem from a well-known mismatch in imitation learning~ pomerleau1988alvinn,ross2010efficient,ross2011dagger , as a policy trained on demonstrations reaches states that the demonstrations never cover and accumulates errors along the flight. Correcting them requires repairs, namely actions that avoid a failure at the states the policy itself reaches, and existing approaches differ mainly in who judges such an action. Interactive imitation learning~ ross2011dagger,kelly2019hgdagger,laskey2017dart,hoque2021thriftydagger queries an expert for corrective actions, but human annotation is extremely expensive at scale, and rule-based planners~ khatib1986apf,zhou2021ego ignore the language instruction. Automatic correction methods~ xu2026aerodpo,yu2026correctnav,xiao2025pld avoid human labeling by deriving corrections from collision rollbacks, reference paths, or auxiliary teacher policies, yet they do not consider whether the policy can actually execute these corrections. Reinforcement learning~ wang2026refinefly,ju2026xfly,zhao2026worldvln,ma2026semantic instead relies on episode-level rewards, which indicate whether a flight fails but not which action should have been taken. As a result, annotation-free, action-level supervision that the policy itself can execute remains missing. Recursive self-improvement offers a promising route toward such supervision. It has recently achieved remarkable success in language models~ zelikman2022star,gulcehre2023rest,singh2024beyond,yuan2024selfrewarding,kumar2025training,deepseek2025r1 , where a model learns from its own verified outputs, and has begun to extend to robotics and navigation~ li2026rsinav,zhang2026recovery,wang2026adarsi,lang2026embodirsi,he2026criticality,liu2026mobiagent,xiao2025pld . However, closed-loop flight poses three challenges that answer-level self-improvement leaves open. First, an answer can be verified on its own, whereas the value of a flight action depends on the subsequent flight of the policy, which calls for step-level values as in process supervision~ wang2024mathshepherd,kazemnejad2025vineppo . Second, a language model learns from a fixed set of problems, whereas a flight terminates at its first failure, so later failures remain hidden until earlier ones are repaired. Third, self-improvement in language models mainly reinforces answers that the model can already produce~ huang2025sharpening,song2025mind , whereas a failing flight policy often cannot sample the action it needs, even though simple physical priors, such as climbing or detouring around obstacles, can readily propose one, as rationalization does in STaR~ zelikman2022star . These challenges lead to our key insight that a failing policy should judge its own repairs. By continuing its flight after each candidate action, the current policy estimates the value of the candidate under its own behavior, which is what approximate policy iteration requires~ kakade2002approximately,fern2006api,scherrer2012ampi . This self-verification turns weak sources into reliable supervision. Actions sampled from the policy often contain a repair, and rule-based proposals that degrade the policy under direct imitation become its most effective supervision once verified, whereas checking only the next few actions often favors candidates that fail later (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)). It also reveals how failures evolve. Verified repairs remain valid for subsequent policies, while new failures emerge elsewhere on the same routes (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)), so supervision must be renewed in every round. Moreover, actions learned from rule-based proposals in one round appear among its sampled actions in the next, indicating that the loop expands what the policy can do rather than reinforcing existing behavior. Based on these insights, we present , a recursive self-improvement framework that repeats three steps in every round. First, adaptive failure anchoring ( ) collects the states leading to each failure of the current policy at multiple time scales, so that supervision follows the failures as they are revealed. Starting from these states, continuation-verified repair ( ) builds candidates from actions sampled from the policy and from rule-based proposals, and accepts a candidate only if the original action fails again from the same state or falls clearly behind the best candidate, and the policy completes the candidate again in an independent re-flight. Finally, retentive repair learning ( ) distills these verified repairs into the policy while keeping its behavior on states that need no repair. Extensive experiments on the TravelUAV benchmark~ wang2025travelUAV demonstrate the effectiveness of . Starting from a supervised policy, improves the success rate from 46.4 to 67.5 in three rounds and reduces collisions by half (Fig.~ fig:teaser (c)), outperforming the previous state-of-the-art method~ xu2026aerodpo , which is trained from the same policy, by 10.6 points. When built upon the stronger policy of this method, further improves the success rate to 69.9 , establishing a new state of the art without additional human annotation or inference cost. In summary, our contributions are as follows. [leftmargin=*,topsep=2pt,itemsep=1pt] We identify three challenges of self-improvement in closed-loop flight and show that letting a failing policy judge its own repairs turns its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals into reliable supervision. We reveal that verified repairs remain valid while new failures emerge elsewhere on the routes, and that actions learned from rule-based proposals enter its sampled actions, which together make recursion essential. We propose , which anchors the failures of the current policy, verifies candidate repairs by its own continuation, and distills them while keeping its behavior elsewhere, achieving state-of-the-art results on TravelUAV with no extra annotation or inference cost. Vision-Language Navigation. title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

Introduction sec:introduction World--action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, linking environment modeling with control~ uva2025,dreamzero2026,openwam . They learn from large-scale visual experience to develop manipulation skills that generalize across scenes, object configurations, and execution conditions~ vpp2025,genie2025,geact2026 . This requires visual representations that support both environment prediction and policy learning. In WAMs, visual representations determine how observations are encoded and what the model predicts. Manipulation-centered representations of scene structure should capture spatial organization, visual appearance, and motion. Latents learned for video reconstruction preserve rich visual information, but reconstruction fidelity alone does not ensure that they capture manipulation-relevant structure and its relationship to actions~ videoldm2023,wan,lingbotva2026 . Recent work on representation alignment and generation with visual foundation model features shows that visual understanding complements generative modeling~ repa2025,rw_rae,dreamworld2026 . We therefore investigate how geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge from these models~ dino,omega,vjepa21 can be used to build scene representations for joint prediction of future states and actions. We introduce Phoenix, a WAM that learns generative representations of scene structure. Phoenix Encoder builds on DINOv3's general visual semantics and learns per-frame scene features through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE aggregates Phoenix Encoder features over causal temporal windows and compresses them into generative latents, preserving scene information and spatial layout. Phoenix jointly predicts these scene latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, learning how actions relate to scene changes. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser , after benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across six benchmarks: LIBERO-Plus~ plus , LIBERO-Pro~ pro , RoboTwin 2.0 C2R~ twin , RoboCasa-GR1~ casa , Bench2Dex~ dex , and RoboDojo-RealWorld~ dojo . These benchmarks assess manipulation generalization under environmental perturbations and across robot embodiments, spanning simulation and real-world settings. We further study how representations of scene structure affect manipulation performance and data efficiency across WAM pretraining and downstream adaptation. Ablations show that learning these representations and compressing them into generative latents both improve manipulation performance, accompanied by more faithful predictions of interaction dynamics. Scaling WAM pretraining data yields larger gains in success rate for Phoenix than for a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating improved pretraining data efficiency. These benefits extend to downstream adaptation, where pretrained Phoenix maintains high success rates with limited task-specific demonstrations, showing effective knowledge transfer in few-shot settings. Our main contributions are as follows: Representations of scene structure for world--action modeling. Phoenix Encoder builds on general visual semantics to learn features of scene structure through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses them into generative latents, preserving spatial layout. Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions. Improved WAM pretraining data efficiency. We compare visual representations across WAM pretraining scales using robot demonstrations and show that our representation yields larger performance gains from scaling data than a video-VAE-only baseline. State-of-the-art performance across six simulation and real-world benchmarks. Phoenix achieves SOTA results in perturbation robustness, cross-embodiment adaptation, and dexterous and real-world manipulation. Further experiments demonstrate strong few-shot adaptation with limited task-specific demonstrations. Related Work World--Action Models and Visual Representations. World--action models connect future prediction with control through predictive video features~ vpp2025 or joint video--action learning~ uva2025,rw_uwm,dreamzero2026 . Video co-training can improve policies even without future generation at inference~ fastwam , highlighting the role of the learned visual representation. Pretrained visual features enrich this prediction space with semantic knowledge. Such features have supported action-conditioned prediction and planning~ rw_dinowm,assran2025vjepa2 , and can guide generative learning through alignment~ repa2025 or serve as the latent space for generation~ rw_rae . Within WAMs, concurrent studies examine predictive feature learning and the integration of external representations~ rw_rewam,rw_r2wam . Recent approaches increasingly extend reconstruction-oriented visual representations with semantic knowledge, using pretrained semantic supervision~ geact2026,rw_repwam,lingbotva2026 or predicting semantic features alongside appearance~ dreamworld2026,rw_stwam . A controlled comparison of reconstruction and semantic latent spaces~ rw_reconstruction_semantics further shows that reconstruction fidelity alone does not determine planning quality, and that semantic latents can better preserve action-relevant information. Phoenix learns representations of scene structure by enriching general visual semantics with geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge through dual-teacher distillation. CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses these Phoenix features into compact generative latents while preserving spatial layout. The Phoenix WAM jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions. Embodied Pretraining from Heterogeneous Data. Large-scale pretraining pools data across tasks, scenes, and embodiments to support generalist robot policies~ openvla,pi05 . For world--action learning, heterogeneous human and robot recordings provide complementary visual and action supervision. VPP2~ rw_vpp2 develops a manipulation-video prior before visual-planner distillation and action learning. UWM~ rw_uwm and OpenWAM~ openwam study joint learning from heterogeneous data, while LDA-1B~ supp_lda uses recordings with different supervision to learn dynamics, visual forecasting, and policies. EgoWAM~ rw_egowam examines prediction targets for transferring from egocentric human videos to robot manipulation. Phoenix uses approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning, followed by world--action pretraining on robot demonstrations. We compare representations across pretraining scales to assess how effectively additional data improves manipulation performance. Method Phoenix predicts action chunks and future visual latents from current visual observations, robot state, and a language instruction (Fig.~ fig:method ). CS-VAE, a causal-semantic variational autoencoder, aggregates and compresses these Phoenix features into generative latents. Together with complementary Wan VAE appearance latents, they support scene prediction and action learning. Training proceeds through representation pretraining on heterogeneous recordings, WAM pretraining on robot demonstrations, and task-specific post-training.
