title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
summary: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer visual and linguistic knowledge to robotic control by building policies on pre-trained VLMs~ rt2, kim2024openvla, pi0 . Recent architectures extend this paradigm by coupling a VLM backbone with a continuous action expert~ pi05, gr00tn1_2025, psi02026 , combining multimodal reasoning with high-frequency action generation. In parallel, world action models (WAMs)~ dreamzero, motus, fastwam, rollingwam2026 adapt pre-trained video generators to jointly model future observations and actions, capturing physical dynamics at the cost of large video diffusion backbones. Recent methods avoid pixel generation by moving future supervision into latent space, yet either align intermediate policy features to compact embeddings~ flare2025, spatialforcing2026 without generating a future stream, or predict features of frozen target encoders~ dreamvla2025, vlajepa2026, unijepa2025 that decouple from the VLM's native feature space. We introduce , a unified model that brings joint future-and-action generation into the policy's co-evolving native visual space (Figure~ fig:teaser ). A VLM encodes observations into spatial visual tokens. By supervising future predictions against an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher of this same vision encoder, perception and prediction remain aligned throughout pre-training and downstream adaptation, without introducing a video generator or an external target encoder. As shown in Figure~ fig:method , couples the VLM stream with a foresight expert and a continuous action expert in a mixture-of-transformers (MoT)~ mixtureoftransformers . Conditioned on the VLM's instruction, state, and observation history, the foresight expert predicts future spatial tokens via flow matching while the action expert attends directly to these predicted features. During inference, both experts jointly denoise future visual tokens and actions, informing control with online latent dynamics at high efficiency. We train on egocentric human video and cross-embodiment robot trajectories, then adapt it across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid settings spanning LIBERO~ libero , RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin , SIMPLE~ wei2026simple , and six physical Unitree G1 tasks. achieves strong humanoid loco-manipulation performance, reaching 81.9 success on SIMPLE and 73.3 on the real robot (+9.6 and +20.0 points over the strongest baselines) at 110\,ms per action chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop manipulation benchmarks. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce , a unified VLA and latent world model that jointly denoises future spatial visual tokens and continuous actions within the VLM's co-evolving visual representation space. Through matched architectural controls and test-time interventions, we demonstrate the advantages of co-evolving native targets and joint denoising over implicit feature alignment and frozen external targets. achieves strong humanoid loco-manipulation results on SIMPLE and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks at 110\,ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop manipulation benchmarks. title: CausalDrive: Causal Decomposition for Data-Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Efficient use of expert demonstrations is essential for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, directly imitating expert trajectories couples nominal intention, which specifies where the vehicle should go, with multimodal driving styles, which determine how that intention is executed. Different combinations of these factors can yield similar expert trajectories, obscuring their respective causal contributions and forcing the policy to learn both from a single entangled target. This ambiguity limits how effectively the policy can exploit expert demonstrations. We propose CausalDrive, a causal decomposition framework for data-efficient driving policy learning that separates deterministic nominal intention prediction from probabilistic driving style modeling. Specifically, we construct counterfactual nominal trajectories from navigation command, map topology, and ego state by removing style dependent effects, providing a Nominal Intention Planner with supervision independent of expert trajectories. Conditioned on the predicted nominal intention and surrounding agents, a diffusion-based Style Execution Policy models diverse driving styles as a multimodal distribution over residuals between nominal and expert trajectories. This causally structured supervision reduces redundant learning of shared nominal behavior in routine scenarios, directing expert supervision toward informative execution variations and improving data utilization. CausalDrive achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Further experiments demonstrate strong performance with limited expert data and clear advantages in challenging interactive scenarios.

Introduction sec:intro End-to-end autonomous driving maps scene observations and driving context to future ego trajectories. Early studies established imitation learning for driving policy learning~ codevilla2018end,bansal2019chauffeurnet,chen2019learning,prakash2021multi,wu2022trajectory , while recent approaches introduced structured scene representations and planning-oriented architectures~ hu2022stp3,hu2023uniad,jiang2023vad,sun2024sparsedrive,11094944,LiWLYWA25,YuZZYW25,YangJLYYY25,JiaYZY25 . Despite these advances, most methods treat expert trajectories as monolithic supervision targets, entangling factors with distinct causal roles. Learning these factors jointly obscures their respective contributions and limits the effective use of expert demonstrations. We distinguish two factors underlying driving behavior: a nominal intention that specifies where the vehicle should go, and multimodal driving styles that determine how that intention is executed. Given the navigation command, map topology, and ego state, the nominal intention is represented by an intention-consistent trajectory~ paden2016survey,schwarting2018planning . Driving styles, in contrast, describe how the ego vehicle responds to surrounding agents, such as by following, yielding, or overtaking, while pursuing that intention. Different combinations of these factors can yield similar expert trajectories over a short planning horizon. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview , a vehicle intending to turn left and one intending to proceed straight with an aggressive execution style can exhibit similar lane-changing trajectories. The observed trajectory alone therefore provides no explicit signal for attributing the behavior to nominal intention or driving style. Directly imitating this trajectory requires the policy to infer both factors from a single entangled target, making their respective contributions ambiguous and reducing the sample efficiency of learning either factor. Existing approaches do not explicitly resolve this ambiguity. Conventional planners based on regression directly predict the complete expert trajectory, coupling nominal intention and driving style within a single target. Generative approaches~ zheng2024genad,liao2025diffusiondrive,zou2025diffusiondrivev2reinforcementlearningconstrainedtruncated,LiXGLYXZCSWMCYL26,YangCJLSZSY26,ZhaoFCGG25,WangZLXLMYCLCXZ26 instead model a multimodal distribution over complete trajectories, but typically leave the underlying sources of multimodality entangled. Meanwhile, methods based on causality~ Zheng_2026_CVPR,tang2026causalvad,moon2026causality,HuangQJLZ25,PourkeshavarzZR24,Moon2026CausalityAwareEA mitigate spurious correlations at the representation or training level. Our approach instead explicitly decomposes the supervision target, assigning deterministic nominal intention and probabilistic driving style to dedicated learning objectives. To this end, we introduce CausalDrive, a causal decomposition framework for data-efficient driving policy learning. First, we construct counterfactual nominal trajectories from navigation commands, map topology, and ego state by removing style dependent effects. Each trajectory represents how the ego vehicle would proceed under the specified intention in the absence of surrounding agents. These targets supervise a Nominal Intention Planner (NIP) independently of expert trajectories, and the NIP predicts a deterministic nominal trajectory. Second, conditioned on the predicted nominal trajectory and surrounding agents, a diffusion-based Style Execution Policy (SEP) models diverse driving styles as a multimodal distribution over residuals between nominal and expert trajectories. This decomposition provides causally structured supervision by aligning separate learning objectives with the distinct roles of nominal intention and driving style. In routine scenes, nominal trajectories already approximate expert execution. Residual modeling therefore reduces redundant learning of nominal behavior and focuses expert supervision on informative style variations. Moreover, large residuals identify demonstrations that contribute substantial execution adjustments beyond the nominal reference, which improves both data utilization and challenging scenario mining. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of CausalDrive. It achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on the more challenging NAVSIM v2, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Residual guided data selection yields strong performance with only 20 of the expert demonstrations, while further analyses show clear advantages in large residual interactive scenarios and more structured driving style distributions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify a causal ambiguity in direct imitation of expert trajectories: different combinations of nominal intention and driving style can yield similar trajectories, obscuring their respective contributions and limiting the effective use of expert demonstrations. We propose CausalDrive, a causally structured supervision framework that separates deterministic nominal intention prediction from probabilistic driving style modeling. A Nominal Intention Planner learns from independent counterfactual targets, while a diffusion-based Style Execution Policy models execution residuals, reducing redundant learning of nominal behavior and enabling residual guided mining of informative scenarios. CausalDrive achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong data efficiency with residual guided data mining and clear advantages in large residual interactive scenarios. Related Work sec:formatting End-to-End Autonomous Driving End-to-end autonomous driving maps sensor observations and driving context to future ego trajectories, enabling perception, prediction, and planning to be optimized toward a unified objective. Early approaches established imitation learning as an effective paradigm for driving policy learning and improved robustness through synthesized perturbations or privileged supervision~ bansal2019chauffeurnet,chen2019learning,TianLLYQLWGZWYC26,JiaGCYLL23,NguyenFJDIGC26,KeZDS024,WangHLXZMCYCZ26 . Subsequent work introduced structured scene representations and planning-oriented architectures. ST-P3~ hu2022stp3 learns spatial-temporal features for vision-based planning, UniAD~ hu2023uniad organizes perception and prediction around a planning objective, VAD~ jiang2023vad represents map elements and agent motion as vectors, and SparseDrive~ sun2024sparsedrive develops a sparse, object-centric driving framework. Complementary causality-aware approaches~ tang2026causalvad,moon2026causality,liang2026curve address spurious correlations through causal intervention or structured scene modeling. These advances improve scene modeling and policy learning, but generally retain the complete expert trajectory as the supervision target without separately supervising nominal intention and driving style. CausalDrive instead decomposes this target into independently supervised nominal intention and expert-derived style residuals, making their causal roles explicit and reducing the ambiguity that limits effective use of expert demonstrations. Generative and Diffusion-Based Planning Generative planners model uncertainty in driving by producing diverse trajectory hypotheses rather than a single deterministic prediction. GenAD~ zheng2024genad jointly generates agent motion and ego plans through latent generative modeling, while DiffusionDrive~ liao2025diffusiondrive employs truncated diffusion for efficient multimodal planning. DiffusionDriveV2~ zou2025diffusiondrivev2reinforcementlearningconstrainedtruncated further incorporates reinforcement learning to improve trajectory quality while preserving behavioral diversity. These methods model multimodality over complete trajectories without explicitly separating variation in nominal intention from variation in its execution. ResAD~ Zheng_2026_CVPR instead models normalized residuals relative to an inertial reference, simplifying trajectory generation. However, residual parameterization alone does not provide an independently supervised, intention-consistent reference or explicitly isolate driving style. In contrast, CausalDrive learns a deterministic nominal trajectory from style-free counterfactual targets and conditions diffusion on this trajectory to model multimodal style residuals. The distinction lies not merely in generating residuals, but in assigning nominal intention and driving style to separate supervision targets, reducing the burden of learning their entangled distribution from expert demonstrations. title: TrajWAM: Trajectory-Conditioned Future Learning for Vision-Language Driving
comment: 22 pages, including supplementary material. Code and model weights: https://github.com/FangWD520/TrajWAM
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Each driving record pairs an executed ego trajectory with its observed future, providing a factual outcome for learning this connection. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision-language driving through auxiliary bird's-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Together, these objectives train the shared planner to generate driving waypoints. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and eight successful routes.

Introduction sec:intro Autonomous driving requires recognizing the current scene and anticipating its evolution under ego actions. World Action Models (WAMs) connect observations and actions with future scene representations~ wang2026wamsurvey,ye2026dreamzero . Driving systems learn video, latent, or bird's-eye-view (BEV) futures to support planning~ wang2024drivewm,li2025law,li2025wote,zheng2025world4drive . When future prediction and planning share parameters, observed futures also supervise the driving policy during training. This coupling supports direct waypoint generation at deployment. Representation-space supervision provides a compact interface for this coupling. DeepSight supervises DINOv3-aligned BEV futures within a driving VLM~ zhang2026deepsight , and Latent-WAM trains auxiliary latent dynamics alongside a driving policy~ wang2026latentwam . We study how an explicit future-trajectory query can strengthen this auxiliary supervision. Trajectory-agnostic supervision predicts future features from scene states. A future-waypoint query explicitly links these predictions to ego motion (Figure~ fig:motivation (a)). The resulting training problem has asymmetric supervision: driving records supply the observed future for the executed trajectory, while alternative queries have unobserved outcomes. Our central question is: How can trajectory queries and observed futures jointly improve a vision--language driving policy? We introduce , a trajectory-conditioned WAM that trains a Qwen2.5-VL-3B driving planner with auxiliary BEV future supervision~ bai2025qwen25vl . A four-waypoint ego trajectory modulates the shared VLM's future-query states through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)~ perez2018film . A frozen readout maps these states to DINOv3-aligned features at the current anchor and four future times~ simeoni2025dinov3 . The trajectory enters the readout after planner-logit computation, and the auxiliary losses backpropagate into shared planner layers. Native inference retains the fixed future-query tokens and directly generates reasoning and waypoints. Our joint objective combines factual reconstruction and perturbed-query separation (Figure~ fig:motivation (b)). Factual reconstruction aligns the executed-query prediction with observed DINOv3 targets. One-sided separation uses this prediction as a detached reference and encourages a distinct prediction under the perturbed query. Both objectives update the shared planner, coupling observed-future supervision with trajectory-query sensitivity. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes~ jia2024bench2drive , achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45 Success Rate. It improves on schedule-matched planning-only continuation by 5.31 DS points and nine successful routes. Matched two-seed controls on 120 routes show gains from trajectory conditioning and separation. Correct trajectory pairing improves DS by 4.25 over shuffled pairing. Prediction diagnostics on newly collected episodes connect these controls to reconstruction quality and executed-query benefits. Our contributions are: Trajectory-conditioned auxiliary training for vision--language driving. An external waypoint query conditions shared future-query states, coupling BEV supervision with a policy that directly generates driving waypoints. Joint learning from factual and unlabeled trajectory queries. Factual reconstruction anchors the observed outcome, and one-sided separation trains the readout to respond to changes in the trajectory query. Closed-loop gains supported by matched training controls. Full-set evaluation establishes planning performance; two-seed controls quantify the gains from trajectory conditioning, separation, and correct query pairing. Joint planning--prediction diagnostics relate these gains to reconstruction quality and query responses. Related Work sec:related World action models and video-generative priors. title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
summary: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
full_text: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2 and improves SR and SPL by 15.8 and 30.9 , respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2 and improves SR and SPL by 5.6 and 23.2 , respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency. Introduction sec:introduction Language-goal aerial navigation (LGAN)~ lee2025citynav,fan2023aerial,liu2023aerialvln requires a UAV to reach a destination specified by a natural-language instruction, typically describing its appearance, surrounding landmarks, and spatial relations. Because the target often lies outside the current field of view, the policy must relate local observations to spatial evidence accumulated along the flight path. Existing approaches mainly follow two paradigms: LLM-driven egocentric planning~ zhang2024navid,zhou2024navgpt,cai2025flightgpt and map-based navigation policies~ zhang2025citynavagent,xu2026geonav,fan2026htnav , as illustrated in panels 1 and 2 of Fig.~ fig:teaser . The former reasons over observations that change with the UAV's viewpoint, making it difficult to maintain consistent spatial references over long trajectories. The latter preserves environmental information in maps, yet typically fuses map features implicitly within black-box policy networks without explicit spatial reasoning over long-range targets. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models~ rt2,openvla have offered a unified framework for learning perception-to-action mappings. However, applying VLA models to city-scale navigation still requires a way to retain spatial evidence across changing viewpoints and use it for long-range target prediction. The central challenge lies in connecting two complementary reference frames. In the egocentric frame, perception and actions are relative to the UAV's current position and heading, so the same landmark appears at different relative positions during flight. An allocentric map instead provides a fixed reference for organizing landmarks and accumulated observations. Yet a global map alone is insufficient: the UAV must identify the instruction-specified target and determine how to approach it from its current pose. Because this pose continuously changes, even a fixed map-frame target requires different body-frame commands. Navigation therefore requires a connection between first-person perception, global spatial reasoning, and local execution. To this end, we propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame VLA architecture for city-scale aerial navigation (Fig.~ fig:teaser , panel 3). Unlike prior map-based methods that rely on implicit feature fusion (Fig.~ fig:teaser , panel 2), our dual-frame design explicitly decouples allocentric spatial memory from egocentric execution, anchoring visual evidence to metric coordinates for explicit target grounding. Inspired by findings that navigational strategies shape hippocampal spatial representations~ gobbo2026navigational , our design assigns complementary roles to these frames: allocentric memory anchors environmental evidence to fixed locations for long-range reasoning, while egocentric context supports perception and action from the current UAV pose. To ground target prediction, we develop persistent allocentric memory with explicit metric grounding. A fixed north-up map is initialized with landmark priors, then accumulates newly observed RGB regions, exploration masks, and flight trajectories at corresponding map locations. Its position, orientation and scale remain fixed throughout an episode, making previously observed regions accessible even after they leave the current field of view. At each step, visual tokens from observed map imagery are aligned with navigation-map features on a shared spatial grid. Learned positional embeddings and metric coordinate encodings anchor cell to a fixed physical location, preserving visual evidence and spatial relations across viewpoint changes. A frozen pretrained multimodal backbone encodes the instruction, current observations, and accumulated map imagery. The resulting context feature is combined with UAV state and motion history to form a dynamic navigation query. Through cross-attention, the query retrieves relevant memory evidence and predicts the destination as a map-frame waypoint. To mitigate target fluctuations over long navigation horizons, we further introduce early goal commitment (EGC), a lightweight strategy that takes the coordinate-wise median of the first predictions as a fixed execution target, without introducing additional trainable parameters. A deterministic controller then transforms this target into body-frame commands based on the UAV's current position and heading, enabling adaptive egocentric execution while maintaining a stable global target. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2 and improves SPL by 26.1 on CityNav, with corresponding gains of 6.2 and 23.2 on refined CityNav, respectively, relative to the best prior results for each metric. Ablations highlight navigation-map features as the primary source of performance gains, with metric coordinates and EGC providing further improvements. Related Work sec:related_work -Goal Aerial Navigation. Continuous and city-scale benchmarks~ fan2023aerial,liu2023aerialvln,wang2025towards,xiao2025uav,lee2025citynav,gao2025openfly require UAVs to ground language-defined destinations in visual appearance and landmark relations~ miyanishi2023cityrefer . Existing approaches leverage VLM guidance~ spf2025,xu2026fly0 , learned policies~ singer2025,discretevla2025 , and structured reasoning~ cai2025flightgpt,ning2026lookasidevln to make flight decisions based on current observations, while some further exploit anticipated observations to guide action selection and trajectory planning~ zhang2026anwm,liu2026imagineuav,xu2026aerialvla . To extend spatial context beyond the current field of view, map-based approaches incorporate spatial memory and hierarchical planning, supporting long-range localization and subgoal selection~ zhang2025citynavagent,xu2026geonav,fan2026htnav . Nevertheless, maintaining spatial context does not necessarily enable direct use of accumulated visual evidence for final target prediction. How to anchor such evidence to fixed metric locations and leverage it for target prediction remains underexplored. CityNav-VLA addresses this gap by integrating persistent allocentric memory with metric-grounded target prediction. Memory and Reference Frames. Navigation in large environments requires retaining observations beyond the current step. Spatial memory has been realized as dense language-embedded maps that fuse visual-language features with 3D reconstructions~ huang2023vlmaps , volumetric grids~ liu2024ver , annotated semantic maps ~ zhang2025mapnav , and Gaussian-language representations~ zhang2026multi,xu2026map . Learned memories compress this history into dual implicit semantic-geometric channels~ zeng2025janusvln or jointly optimize map generation with action prediction~ lian2026mapdream . A recurring choice is the reference frame. Egocentric coordinates depend on the current pose, whereas allocentric maps anchor locations independently of it, and biological navigation exploits both systems in tandem~ gobbo2026navigational . LGAN exposes the fragility: agents suffer from navigation amnesia when critical evidence lies far behind the current observation~ wei2026memoryvln,lv2026himemvln . Explicit spatial structures must therefore be not only built but made reliably retrievable and coupled to control. CityNav-VLA addresses this by accumulating exploration history in a persistent map and encoding it into spatially aligned memory tokens at each decision. Metric coordinates anchor each token to a physical map location, so a query retrieves appearance and location together. Representations in VLA Models. VLA models adapt pretrained multimodal representations for action prediction~ rt2,openvla . SpatialVLA uses Ego3D position encoding for manipulation~ qu2025spatialvla . SeeR-VLA transforms point maps into a robot-centric frame to align geometry with control~ lee2026see . Action chunking and tokenization ~ zhao2023act, pertsch2025fast structure action prediction, while Qwen-VLA unifies manipulation and navigation across embodiments~ qwenvla2026 . Video-based VLAs such as NaVid predict actions from current and recent visual context without persistent spatial memory~ zhang2024navid . Current-step geometric grounding thus leaves open how past observations support later goal localization. In manipulation, SOMA shows persistent multi-view memory can localize out-of-view targets~ li2026soma . City-scale navigation must combine evidence from different poses into a destination estimate after landmarks leave view. AirAnchor maintains persistent object memory for zero-shot aerial VLN~ fan2026airanchor , and Fly0 projects image-grounded targets into 3D for geometric planning~ xu2026fly0 . CityNav-VLA uses instruction-conditioned egocentric context to retrieve history from persistent allocentric memory and predict a destination on the geometric consistency map. title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the WAM-AD Workshop, WACV 2027. Code: https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter
summary: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.

We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at . Introduction sec:intro World models have become a central component of autonomous driving research. By predicting future scene states conditioned on ego actions, they support counterfactual reasoning, closed-loop simulation and model-based planning. Recent driving world models synthesise future video conditioned on ego trajectories or high-level commands~ hu2023gaia,wang2024drivedreamer,gao2024vista , and planning-oriented approaches learn latent or occupancy dynamics jointly with a driving policy~ hu2022mile,zheng2024occworld . Existing evaluations of these models focus on the fidelity of the generated futures or on downstream planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. Over short horizons, however, ego motion is strongly autocorrelated, so the observed history already encodes much of the information carried by the future action. A model trained on logged driving data can therefore attain high forecasting accuracy while making little use of its action input, a failure mode analogous to the inertia and copycat problems reported for imitation-learned driving policies~ codevilla2019exploring,wen2020fighting,dehaan2019causal . An accuracy gain over a model without action input shows that the action is used, but not how strongly the forecasts depend on it, since on logged data the executed action and the action implied by the history largely coincide. How strongly action-conditioned forecasters trained on real driving data depend on the ego action, and whether this dependence holds across vehicle platforms, therefore remains largely unexplored. To address these questions, we study action dependence in semantic forecasting~ luc2017predicting , which predicts future semantic segmentation from past observations and has an established evaluation protocol on Cityscapes~ cordts2016cityscapes . Conditioning this task on future vehicle odometry has been proposed before~ bhattacharyya2019bayesian , but whether the forecaster uses the odometry was not examined. We condition on the ego action, represented by speed and yaw rate, and compare a U-Net forecaster with feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)~ perez2018film , input-level conditioning, and no action input. The rationale is that semantic forecasting has a compact output space and standard metrics, so each variant can be trained with several seeds at modest cost and its use of the action can be measured without new evaluation criteria. To assess whether the findings transfer across vehicle platforms, we define an equivalent protocol on BDD100K~ yu2020bdd100k , which differs from Cityscapes in camera, ego-motion sensing and driving environment. To measure action dependence, we evaluate each trained model under test-time action interventions, in which the executed future action is replaced by the action of a sample from another sequence, by zero yaw rate, by a stop command, or by the training-set mean action. All conditions are scored with the standard mIoU and MO-mIoU metrics~ luc2017predicting . Before applying this evaluation to real driving data, we validate it in a synthetic driving environment whose dynamics depend on the action by construction. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We present an action-conditioned semantic forecasting framework that compares FiLM, input-level and no action conditioning within a single U-Net forecaster under identical training. We develop a test-time intervention protocol that replaces the executed future action with shuffled, zero-yaw, stop and mean actions, and measures action dependence with established segmentation metrics only. We validate the interventions in a synthetic driving environment with action-dependent dynamics and a negative control trained on shuffled actions, which shows whether a model uses or ignores its action input. We provide a cross-platform evaluation on Cityscapes and BDD100K with GPS-derived ego actions, both within each dataset and across the two platforms. Related Work sec:related World models and action-conditioned prediction. Predicting future observations conditioned on actions originates in action-conditional video prediction for games~ oh2015action and robot manipulation~ finn2016unsupervised , and in world models that learn behaviour inside a learned simulator~ ha2018world,hafner2020dream . In driving, MILE~ hu2022mile learns a latent world model jointly with a driving policy, OccWorld~ zheng2024occworld forecasts 3D occupancy together with ego motion, and GAIA-1~ hu2023gaia , DriveDreamer~ wang2024drivedreamer and Vista~ gao2024vista synthesise future video conditioned on actions, trajectories or commands. A common theme across these works is that evaluation targets the fidelity of the predicted futures or the performance of a downstream planner. In contrast, we measure directly whether the prediction depends on the action, using a model small enough to be trained with multiple seeds. Semantic forecasting. Luc~ ~ luc2017predicting introduced the forecasting of future semantic segmentation on Cityscapes, with short-term (0.18\,s) and mid-term (0.54\,s) horizons that subsequent work adopted. Follow-up methods forecast with convolutional LSTMs~ nabavi2018future , recurrent flow-guided warping~ terwilliger2019recurrent , or in feature space followed by a segmentation decoder~ luc2018predicting,saric2021dense . These methods condition on past frames only. Bhattacharyya~ ~ bhattacharyya2019bayesian additionally condition a Bayesian forecaster on past and future vehicle odometry, but report no evaluation of how the predictions depend on it. Our work extends this line of research by measuring that dependence under the standard protocol, and by defining an equivalent protocol on a second platform. Shortcut learning in driving models. Driving policies trained by imitation are known to exploit the ego vehicle's past motion instead of the scene, which is referred to as the inertia~ codevilla2019exploring and copycat~ wen2020fighting problems, and more generally to rely on spurious correlates of the expert action~ dehaan2019causal . The forecasting counterpart of this failure mode is a world model that reproduces the observed motion and treats its action input as optional. Test-time input interventions provide a direct test for this behaviour, and we adopt them as our primary evaluation. title: NereidVLA: Learning to Understand and Navigate the Underwater World
summary: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation. ] Introduction sec:intro Language-guided underwater navigation requires robots to interpret a goal in the context of three-dimensional scene geometry. Following a pipeline requires understanding its direction and the obstacles nearby, while cave navigation depends on recognizing entrances and the geometry of traversable passages. These decisions involve changes in depth as well as horizontal motion: recognizing the target is only one part of determining how to reach it. Turbidity, light scattering, changing illumination, and occlusion further complicate these spatial judgments~ akkaynak2018underwater . Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual understanding and language to robot behavior~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,qu2025spatialvla , and recent work has begun to explore this connection in underwater environments~ wang2025underwatervla,gu2026usimu0,xue2025oceangym . Meanwhile, marine vision-language datasets provide rich annotations for objects, spatial relationships, and scene structure~ xu2025nautilus, zhu2026usibrain . These resources offer an opportunity to learn about the underwater world, but rarely include paired robot trajectories. Collecting underwater navigation demonstrations remains costly and difficult to scale, and spatial understanding alone does not specify how a robot should move. We therefore investigate a central question: Can spatial knowledge acquired from large-scale marine observations be transferred to language-conditioned 3D underwater navigation? We propose NereidVLA, an underwater VLA model that connects marine spatial learning with trajectory-supervised navigation adaptation (Figure~ fig:overview ). The first stage establishes spatial knowledge before learning robot motion. Using available annotations and question-answer formats from NAUTILUS~ xu2025nautilus and USI-Brain~ zhu2026usibrain , together with underwater simulation data, we construct approximately two million marine spatial-understanding examples. We use these examples to train Sea2Know, built on Qwen3-VL-8B~ bai2025qwen3vl , to learn target grounding, spatial relationships, and scene structure. This stage makes marine observations useful for navigation preparation without requiring paired robot-motion annotations. The second stage turns this spatially informed model into a trajectory predictor for closed-loop navigation. Using 573 simulated scenes in MarineGym~ chu2025marinegym , we collect 5,117 expert demonstrations and derive approximately 100,000 navigation examples spanning obstacle avoidance, target search, pipeline navigation, and cave navigation. An expert controller executes geometric reference plans under simulated vehicle dynamics, and the resulting robot motion supplies the trajectory targets. We use these demonstrations to adapt Sea2Know into NereidVLA, encoding local body-frame displacements as motion tokens. Given RGB histories and language instructions, the model autoregressively predicts local 3D trajectories, which a low-level feedback controller tracks as visual observations are updated and the trajectory is replanned. Our evaluation examines both the spatial knowledge learned in the first stage and its value for navigation. On a six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark strictly disjoint from the spatial training data, Sea2Know outperforms its backbone across all six dimensions. NereidVLA improves offline trajectory prediction over SimpleVLN~ hong2026simplevln in unseen scenes. Under matched downstream training and execution settings, Sea2Know initialization increases closed-loop simulation success from 72.4 to 84.4 compared with direct navigation fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-8B. On a BlueROVHeavy robot, NereidVLA achieves a 78.75 task success rate in laboratory-pool trials without fine-tuning on the test environment, compared with 47.50 for InternVLA-N1. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose NereidVLA, a two-stage underwater VLA framework that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned local 3D trajectory prediction and closed-loop navigation. We construct a diverse underwater navigation dataset from expert demonstrations executed under simulated vehicle dynamics, and introduce an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark. We demonstrate improvements in offline trajectory prediction and closed-loop navigation in simulation and on a real robot. Matched comparisons establish the benefit of marine spatial pretraining, while laboratory-pool trials demonstrate transfer to physical execution without test-environment fine-tuning. Related Work sec:related vision-language understanding. NAUTILUS introduces NautData for underwater captioning, visual question answering, grounding, and detection, alongside an imaging-prior-based visual feature enhancement module~ xu2025nautilus . USI-Brain develops spatial supervision covering object understanding, spatial relations, depth reasoning, degradation-aware perception, and scene understanding~ zhu2026usibrain . UWBench evaluates underwater captioning, grounding, and visual question answering, while MarineEval focuses on marine-domain knowledge and reasoning~ zhang2025uwbench,wong2026marineeval . These efforts advance underwater visual understanding and evaluation but do not provide paired robot-motion supervision. We use NAUTILUS and USI-Brain data to train Sea2Know and introduce an independent benchmark for navigation-relevant spatial judgments. -language-action learning and spatial reasoning. OpenSpatial generates spatial supervision grounded in 3D object boxes~ liu2026openspatial , while SpatialAxiom~ lou2026spatialaxiom and SenseNova-SI~ cai2026sensenova,opensensenova2026si13 advance general-purpose spatial reasoning. Zhu~ improve motion-grounded action understanding through action-centric video--text alignment~ zhu2026beyondscene . RT-2 represents actions as tokens and draws on vision-language and robotic data~ zitkovich2023rt2 , while OpenVLA provides an adaptable open-source VLA model~ kim2025openvla . SpatialVLA introduces Ego3D encoding and adaptive action grids for spatially grounded action prediction~ qu2025spatialvla , and FAST explores efficient action-sequence tokenization~ pertsch2025fast . For navigation, SimpleVLN adapts multimodal models using visual histories and action chunks~ hong2026simplevln , while InternVLA-N1 combines high-level goal planning with low-level execution~ internrobotics2025internvlan1 . We examine how domain-specific spatial knowledge acquired before navigation adaptation supports language-conditioned local 3D trajectory prediction. language-conditioned behavior learning. UnderwaterVLA combines high-level task reasoning with low-level control~ wang2025underwatervla . USIM provides automatically collected underwater demonstrations, while U0 incorporates relative-pose supervision for learning underwater behaviors~ gu2026usimu0 . AquaCap uses executable control programs and feedback-based replanning~ li2026aquacap , while AQUAACT contributes teleoperation demonstrations and closed-loop policy evaluation~ wu2026aquaact . OceanGym supports language-grounded perception and sequential decision-making in underwater environments~ xue2025oceangym . These approaches explore complementary aspects of underwater behavior and execution. NereidVLA focuses on transferring marine spatial knowledge to 3D trajectory prediction through dynamics-grounded demonstrations, followed by closed-loop navigation. navigation and simulation. Prior work investigates online 3D path replanning under motion constraints~ hernandez2019online and mapless obstacle avoidance through reinforcement learning~ yang2023collisionfree . HoloOcean provides underwater vehicle and sensor simulation~ potokar2022holoocean , while OceanSim advances underwater optical and sonar rendering~ song2025oceansim . MarineGym supports GPU-parallel simulation, hydrodynamic modeling, and domain randomization~ chu2025marinegym . Using MarineGym, we construct diverse navigation scenes and collect expert trajectories under simulated vehicle dynamics. Geometric paths guide the demonstrations, but the trajectory supervision comes from executed robot motion rather than the planned paths themselves. title: Target-Consistent Action Guidance via Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Drifting World Models
summary: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.

On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause. w Introduction sec:intro Action-conditioned world models predict how an environment changes in response to an agent's actions, so that a robot can imagine the outcome of a decision before executing it~ ha2018world,hafner2020dream . Built on large-scale video generation, they now simulate fine-grained robot--object interaction~ yang2024unisim,zhu2025irasim,guo2026ctrlworld and long-horizon plans~ du2024vlp,bruce2024genie,nvidia2025cosmos . They are used to rank candidate actions inside a control loop~ hansen2022tdmpc,qi2026gpc and to evaluate policies offline without hardware trials~ quevedo2025worldgym,team2025veo . Both uses need many rollouts, yet most world models are diffusion-based~ ho2020ddpm,ho2022vdm and spend many network evaluations on every frame. Drifting models~ deng2026drifting remove this cost by moving the iteration from inference to training: a drifting field attracts generated samples toward data and repels them from each other, and the one-step generator is trained until the field vanishes. Follow-up work relates drifting to score matching~ lai2026unified,turan2026secretly and to Wasserstein gradient flows~ he2026sinkhorndrifting,cao2026gradientflowdrifting . W-Flow~ han2026wflow derives the field as the Wasserstein gradient of a debiased Sinkhorn divergence, so that, under suitable assumptions, it vanishes only at the target, and UW-Flow~ jeon2026uwflow relaxes its marginal constraints with unbalanced transport. Both were developed for class-conditional image generation. DriftWorld~ lu2026driftworld brought drifting to action-conditioned world models with three adaptations: a conditional drifting field with a single positive, the recorded future, and an action-accentuated negative distribution; a drifting loss in a DINOv2/v3 feature space~ oquab2023dinov2,simeoni2025dinov3 ; and a U-Net that conditions each frame on its own action. To make the model follow the action rather than copy the current frame, DriftWorld also accentuates the action by pushing predictions away from that frame. Accentuation is borrowed from classifier-free guidance~ ho2022cfg , and it inherits guidance's extrapolation: the push does not stop at the recorded future. In image generation this overshoot strengthens a class, but a world model has only one correct future, and a push that persists there drives the accentuated predictions toward exaggerated motion. We call this the target bias of accentuation. It persists when accentuation is carried over to W-Flow, where every prediction receives the same constant push even when it is already correct, and unbalanced transport only weakens it. Removing accentuation is no remedy, since the model then tends to copy the current frame~ lu2026driftworld . The guidance should instead push a prediction only by the motion it is still missing. This is a property of the field; trained world models on our benchmarks show the opposite failure, under-reacting to the action, so we evaluate removing target bias and improving action response separately. We propose Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA), which corrects this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a competing destination rather than a negative: each prediction splits its mass between the recorded future and the current frame in one semi-relaxed transport problem, and the share sent to the current frame measures how much motion is missing. Subtracting the share that the correct future itself would send makes the guidance vanish at the target, and applying it as one shared translation leaves the W-Flow field otherwise unchanged. Our contributions are as follows. We show that action accentuation keeps pushing predictions at the recorded future in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced drifting fields, and a controlled toy confirms the overshoot of kernel and balanced accentuation ( ). We introduce MSA, a bias-corrected accentuation built on counterfactual semi-relaxed transport with a closed-form assignment ( ). We prove that the MSA field has the recorded future as its unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and, for any predictions, adds no relative deformation to the base field and is bounded by the prediction error ( ). On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, MSA improves action response and motion fidelity over latent-space DriftWorld and W-Flow baselines at no inference cost; the bias removal itself is verified in a controlled setting ( ). Related Work sec:related Action-conditioned world models. Predicting future observations from actions has a long history in model-based reinforcement learning~ ha2018world,hafner2020dream . Recent models instead adapt large video generators. UniSim, GAIA-1, Genie, and Cosmos treat the world as a video that unrolls under actions or text~ yang2024unisim,hu2023gaia,bruce2024genie,nvidia2025cosmos . Other work turns pretrained video diffusion models into interactive simulators~ rigter2025avid,huang2026vid2world , and robot-specific models such as IRASim, Ctrl-World, and UWM produce fine-grained, multi-view manipulation rollouts~ zhu2025irasim,guo2026ctrlworld,zhu2025uwm . Nearly all of these models sample with multi-step diffusion or autoregression. DriftWorld~ lu2026driftworld is the one-step exception and our starting point. We keep its architecture and change only how the training field encourages the model to follow the action. One-step generation. Diffusion models~ sohldickstein2015deep,ho2020ddpm,song2021sde and flow matching~ lipman2023flow,liu2023rectified,albergo2023stochastic,ma2024sit generate high-quality samples by integrating a stochastic or ordinary differential equation over many steps. Distillation compresses a pretrained multi-step teacher into a one-step student~ salimans2022progressive,luo2023diffinstruct,yin2024dmd,sauer2024add,zhou2024sid , but it requires the teacher and inherits its errors. Consistency-style methods train few-step models from scratch by enforcing self-consistency along a predefined diffusion or flow trajectory~ song2023consistency,song2024ict,lu2024scm,frans2024shortcut,geng2025meanflow,geng2025imf,boffi2025flowmap,zhou2025imm , so their training signal still comes from a trajectory designed for iterative sampling. Drifting~ deng2026drifting and its Wasserstein refinements~ han2026wflow,jeon2026uwflow instead define the training-time evolution of the generator directly, with neither a teacher nor a differential equation, and are competitive with multi-step models at one network evaluation. This makes drifting a natural backbone for world models, where each decision needs many rollouts. title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models
summary: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/

Introduction Embodied AI systems, like autonomous vehicles and drones, depend on robust perception models for navigating dynamic environments, making cross-domain generalization crucial. Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have sparked interest in applying them to autonomous driving for their improved robustness sikdar2025picazo,gandhamal2025ov . These models enhance multi-modal learning by integrating images and text, enabling better understanding of novel concepts, for example, CLIP, trained on 400 million image-text pairs. Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has emerged as a promising approach for scene parsing, leveraging large-scale vision-language models pre-trained on massive internet datasets with language supervision, which demonstrate strong generalization shi2024lca, radford2021learning . However, their reliance on image-level supervision limits performance on fine-grained tasks such as pixel-level segmentation zhou2022extract . Despite their potential, VLMs require thorough evaluation for fine-grained tasks, as cross-domain generalization challenges limit their effectiveness in embodied AI. Recent research has explored fine-tuning CLIP for fine-grained tasks and has explored improving OVSS models for segmentation using techniques such as mask proposal networks ghiasi2022scaling, yu2023convolutions and cost aggregation methods cho2024cat . However, pixel-level classification still struggles with unseen classes, particularly under significant domain shifts blumenstiel2024mess . This limitation worsens as the number of unseen categories increases ding2022decoupling , with open-vocabulary models being especially prone to overfitting during downstream task adaptation wortsman2022robust, kumar2022fine . Although OVSS models effectively capture open-set visual concepts for segmentation, their robustness remains largely unexplored.Their zero-shot generalization drops sharply under major category, distribution, or domain shifts, limiting open-vocabulary models’ real-world applicability zhang2024dept . Embodied AI systems require advanced perception capabilities to operate reliably in adverse weather and low-light conditions sikdar2025saga, chaudhuri2025domain . To address this, benchmarks such as the Multi-domain Evaluation of Semantic Segmentation (MESS) blumenstiel2024mess have been developed to evaluate model performance across a wider range of complex, domain-specific datasets. However, leveraging foundation models like CLIP radford2021learning for advanced perception presents three key challenges that remain unexplored in previous benchmarks: (1) fine-tuning on limited training dataset, for downstream segmentation tasks while preserving pretrained knowledge, (2) handling significant domain shifts arising from out-of-distribution data, and (3) accommodating substantial variations between seen and unseen classes, particularly those arising from differing viewing perspectives. These challenges are key to assessing model robustness across tasks. Reliable systems must work with visible (RGB) and infrared (IR) data, staying resilient to modality shifts and varying conditions like day-night cycles, fog, rain, and glare. Additionally, they must be capable of recognizing objects from multiple viewpoints, each offering unique semantic cues, despite often lacking the ability to choose the most informative perspectives seifi2021glimpse . However, current standard benchmarks primarily target in-domain tasks, offering limited insight into how models perform across domains. This limitation restricts our understanding of zero-shot segmentation models’ ability to generalize to unseen domains and handle diverse sensors or vocabularies. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Pixel2Perspective: a benchmark for multi-modal and multi-view generalization in vision-language models. It is an open-vocabulary RGB–Infrared segmentation benchmark designed for multi-angle object localization across drone, satellite, and ground-level perspectives, as shown in Figure fig:p2p . We evaluate state-of-the-art models such as CLIP for fine-grained object localization, alongside leading open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models across 13 datasets. These datasets are carefully curated to span diverse object classes, sensor modalities, and out-of-distribution domains, with an emphasis on varied viewpoints to comprehensively assess generalization. We also introduce Multi-Source RGB–IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), a benchmark framework that jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across co-registered RGB and IR modalities, enabling robust evaluation of OVSS models in diverse conditions. Our key contributions are as follows: (1) Pixel2Perspective Benchmark: We introduce Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for evaluating state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models. Leveraging a quantitative taxonomy of diverse segmentation datasets, it rigorously assesses out-of-domain object localization and OVSS performance across ground-level, aerial, and bird’s-eye perspectives, under varied weather conditions, and across multiple modalities including RGB and IR. (2) Systematic Evaluation of VLMs: We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of Vision-Language Models on object localization and open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, offering an in-depth analysis across diverse settings. (3) Multi-Source RGB–IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ): To handle uncertainties from both RGB and IR sensors, we propose MSRIQ, a framework that jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across co-registered RGB and infrared modalities. Related Works Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation Large-scale pre-training has revolutionized computer vision by training models on image-text pairs, enabling representation of visual and textual semantics in a shared space. Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) aims to bridge the gap between image-level and pixel-level understanding by enabling segmentation of unseen classes. OVSS models are generally categorized into two main types: (i) mask-proposal networks ghiasi2022scaling, ding2022open, xu2023open, xu2022simple, xu2023side, yu2023convolutions , and (ii) cost-aggregation networks cho2024cat . Mask-proposal approaches generate class-agnostic region proposals, which are then semantically aligned with CLIP-derived textual embeddings to facilitate open-vocabulary classification at the pixel level. For instance, OpenSeg ghiasi2022scaling leverages local image regions to form proposals, whereas models like ZegFormer ding2022decoupling and ZSseg xu2022simple adopt a two-stage architecture to address this task. CAT-Seg cho2024cat enhances robustness by using similarity scores to combine CLIP’s image and text embeddings into a cost volume, rather than relying on direct embeddings. OVSS models are commonly evaluated on standard datasets like ADE20K zhou2019semantic and Pascal VOC everingham2015pascal , which primarily feature everyday, in-domain images. However, such evaluations fail to capture real-world conditions with inherent domain shifts and environmental diversity. \\ Related Benchmarks OVSS models are typically evaluated on datasets composed exclusively of in-domain images zhou2019semantic,everingham2015pascal , which are considered the de facto standard for model evaluation ghiasi2022scaling, liang2023open . Few works have explored broader dataset diversity. The Segmentation in the Wild (SegInW) benchmark zou2023generalized includes 25 datasets, however, most of them still feature everyday, in-domain images, with only two notable exceptions. Robust benchmarks are crucial for advancing the vision community, providing standardized ways to evaluate performance across diverse tasks paul2022vision . Inspired by HELM liang2022holistic for LLMs, the MESS benchmark blumenstiel2024mess was introduced to assess OVSS models across domains such as medicine, engineering, earth observation, biology, and agriculture. However, a key limitation lies in the relatively low number of classes within these datasets, resulting in high random mIoU scores. To the best of our knowledge, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models have not been systematically evaluated on datasets that account for sensor shifts and variations in look-angle, as commonly encountered in drones and autonomous vehicles. This work presents the first comprehensive effort to address these challenges, aiming to provide new insights and advance the robustness of OVSS models in practical settings. Pixel2Perspective Benchmark Problem Formulation To evaluate the visual understanding of VLMs across different viewpoints and modalities, we focus on two key tasks: object localization and Open vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS). We define object localization as the task of determining an object’s location based on a given textual prompt, using both image and text encoders. For the OVSS task, let \(I\) represent an image associated with a set of classes \(C = \ C_ 1 , C_ 2 , , C_ N \ \), where each class \(C_i\) is defined by a textual label. OVSS models aim to assign a class label \(C_i\) to each pixel in image \(I\), where the set of candidate classes \(N\) can vary at inference time and may include novel categories not seen during training. Dataset Taxonomy Robustness challenges in real-world deployment of perception models are frequently overlooked in existing research. To tackle this, we introduce Pixel2Perspective-Benchmark, an open-vocabulary RGB–IR benchmark for multi-angle segmentation across drones, satellites, and ground perspectives. title: One Affinity, Two Axes: Bidirectional Slot Attention for Iterative Aggregation across the Structure--Detail Spectrum in Visual Retrieval
summary: Aggregating dense patch tokens into compact and discriminative global descriptors is central to visual retrieval. Although foundation models provide rich local features, existing aggregation heads still rely on single-pass mappings and lack an explicit mechanism to coordinate structural and fine-grained cues. Therefore, we propose Bidirectional Slot Attention (BiSA), which reformulates aggregation as an iterative coupled system. Cross-Axis Consensus (CAC) progressively refines learnable slots by interpreting a single shared token--slot affinity along two complementary axes. Along the competition axis, slots vie for each token under a temperature shared across all of them, determining token ownership and inducing a non-redundant scene decomposition. Along the selection axis, a slot-specific temperature governs the breadth of each slot's response, spanning a spectrum from broad layouts to sparse fine-grained details. Their consensus couples non-redundant decomposition with multi-granular slot specialization. Furthermore, the two axes expose intrinsic token-reliability cues at no extra cost: a token's claim strength under competition and its salience under selection. Progressive Token Filtering (PTF) converts these cues into a retention probability that down-weights unreliable tokens before the next CAC iteration, without any segmentation branch or external prior, forming a self-reinforcing loop of competitive decomposition, selective focusing, and feedback purification. Across all three retrieval tasks, BiSA leads on five of six place recognition benchmarks (+4.2 R@1 on Baidu Mall), tops all 16 metrics of drone--satellite geo-localization (+8.4 R@1 at 150 m), and improves instance-level retrieval on ROxford-Hard by 4.5 mAP points. Notably, the selection axis adds only 20 learnable scalars, yet improves average R@1 by 2.8 points.
