Introduction Visual retrieval aims to identify query-relevant images from large-scale databases using compact and discriminative descriptors. To do so, a descriptor must remain invariant to substantial appearance and geometric variations while discriminating against visually similar distractors. The former relies largely on stable, large-scale structural cues, whereas the latter often depends on sparse but discriminative local evidence, such as signs, entrances, decorations, and textures. This creates a fundamental tension between structural invariance and detail-level discriminability. As visual foundation models make patch tokens increasingly expressive, the principal challenge has shifted from extracting stronger local features to aggregating them into a compact descriptor that reconciles these two complementary requirements. Current aggregation heads fall short of this goal in two distinct ways. The first concerns the process of token-to-descriptor aggregation: across visual place recognition (VPR), cross-view geo-localization (CVGL), and instance-level retrieval (ILIR), dense local tokens are transformed and combined through assignment, spatial reweighting, or pooling to form the global descriptor. Representative methods instantiate this process through cluster assignment, feature mixing, or learnable queries in VPR arandjelovic2016netvlad,alibey2023mixvpr,izquierdo2024optimal,alibey2024boq , spatially aware aggregation in CVGL shi2019spatial,liu2026surfnet , and global pooling or object-aware selection in ILIR radenovic2018fine,ng2020solar,song2022glam,song2024cider . Despite these different formulations, they typically fix the complex token-to-descriptor mapping within a single forward pass, resulting in a unidirectional dependency: token assignments determine descriptor components without an explicit feedback loop to progressively refine the mapping. The second concerns the granularity of the evidence retained in the descriptor. SegVLAD, StructVPR and SURFNet reinforce structural representation via SAM-generated segmentation masks, distilled structural knowledge, and surface-aware priors respectively garg2024revisit,kirillov2023segment,shen2023structvpr,liu2026surfnet , whereas FoL strengthens detail representation by mining reliable discriminative local regions wang2025focus . Each of these designs, however, commits to either structure or detail, and none explicitly models within a single descriptor the full granularity spectrum that runs from broad layouts to sparse fine-grained details. To address both limitations, we propose Bidirectional Slot Attention (BiSA), which reformulates feature aggregation as an iterative coupled system by integrating Cross-Axis Consensus (CAC) with progressive token filtering (PTF). Within CAC, a learnable set of slots locatello2020slot serves as an evolving aggregation state for local token features and is updated by interpreting a shared token--slot affinity along two complementary axes under asymmetric temperatures. Along the competition axis, normalization across slots under a shared temperature establishes relative token ownership, encouraging different slots to cover complementary scene content. Along the selection axis, normalization across tokens with slot-specific temperatures controls each slot's support breadth, enabling the slot set to span the structure--detail spectrum, from broad layouts to sparse discriminative cues. CAC retains token--slot associations supported by both distributions, coupling non-redundant scene decomposition with multi-granular slot specialization. Crucially, the same axis-wise responses also expose complementary token-reliability cues at no extra cost: each token's claim strength under competition and salience under selection. PTF therefore combines these cues with the token features to suppress unreliable tokens and feeds the refined token pool back into the next CAC iteration. The next iteration thus recomputes competition and selection from a progressively cleaner token pool. Repeating this CAC--PTF feedback forms a self-reinforcing loop of competitive decomposition, selective focusing, and feedback purification. Since both decomposition and the reliability cues originate from the shared affinity, BiSA requires no external segmentation or semantic branch. As summarized in Figure~ fig:intro , BiSA consistently outperforms recent methods across VPR, CVGL, and ILIR, demonstrating its generality. To summarize, our work brings the following contributions: 1) We propose Bidirectional Slot Attention (BiSA), an iterative aggregation framework that coordinates structural invariance and detail-level discriminability across a continuous granularity spectrum without external priors. 2) We introduce Cross-Axis Consensus (CAC), which applies shared-temperature competition and slot-specific-temperature selection to a common token--slot affinity, coupling non-redundant decomposition with slot specialization across the structure--detail spectrum. 3) We introduce Progressive Token Filtering (PTF), which combines the axis-wise reliability responses with token features to predict per-token retention probabilities without additional supervision. The reweighted tokens re-enter CAC, coupling slot refinement with token filtering in a single evolving system. 4) The same aggregation architecture consistently leads across VPR, CVGL, and ILIR, including zero-shot cross-view transfer without target fine-tuning, supporting iterative structure--detail consensus as a task-general retrieval principle. Related Work Visual retrieval matches corresponding images from large-scale databases using compact descriptors. We consider three tasks--VPR, CVGL, and ILIR--differing in appearance, geometry, and matching granularity but share the need to preserve stable structure and discriminative local evidence. Place Recognition (VPR). VPR retrieves the same physical place under substantial appearance and viewpoint changes. Early aggregation heads match dense features against a fixed vocabulary of learned patterns, whether residual centroids in NetVLAD or mixing weights in MixVPR arandjelovic2016netvlad,alibey2023mixvpr . With foundation-model backbones, the head no longer needs such a vocabulary: aggregation becomes a matter of solving how tokens are distributed over a small set of units, by optimal transport in SALAD, learnable queries in BoQ, or compact VLAD-style assignment in SuperVLAD izquierdo2024optimal,alibey2024boq,lu2024supervlad . A parallel line instead intervenes outside the head, by selecting reliable regions (FoL-global), inserting retrieval tokens into the backbone (ImAge), or distilling into a deformable aggregator (D VPR) wang2025focus,lu2025image,zhang2026d2vpr . -View Geo-Localization (CVGL). CVGL matches geographic targets across ground, drone, and satellite viewpoints, where severe geometric variations make structural alignment important. Since SAFA's spatially aware aggregation shi2019spatial , progress has come mainly from adding structural priors around the aggregation head: position-aware partitioning in CAMP, domain and scene alignment in DAC, multilevel enhancement in MEAN, and surface-aware guidance in SURFNet wu2024camp,xia2024dac,chen2025mean,liu2026surfnet . -Level Image Retrieval (ILIR). ILIR retrieves images of the same object or landmark, requiring compact descriptors to retain fine-grained local cues that distinguish visually similar instances. Aggregation here evolves from a single pooling rule, as in GeM, toward global--local or spatial attention-based weighting in SOLAR and GLAM radenovic2018fine,ng2020solar,song2022glam . More recent designs add a second pathway for local evidence: DToP couples global and local branches over multi-layer features, and CiDeR localizes objects of interest within a single-stage pipeline song2023dtop,song2024cider . Across all three tasks, the aggregation head itself stays a one-shot mapping; structure and detail are coordinated, if at all, by modules placed around it. BiSA instead keeps both inside the head: one affinity, read along two axes under asymmetric temperatures, spans the granularity spectrum, while PTF uses the resulting axis-wise responses to down-weight unreliable tokens before the next iteration. title: Reliable Tree Recruitment from Scarce Annotations for Forest Inventory Expansion
summary: Species-level inventories of individual tree crowns (ITCs) from UAV imagery are limited by annotation cost: in tropical forests, many species are represented by only a handful of field-validated crowns. We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that expands a small annotated inventory by iteratively self-training a multi-task DeepLabV3 network, combining semantic segmentation with a crown-distance regression head, on RGB UAV orthomosaics. At each iteration, candidate crowns enter the training inventory only if they pass a confidence filter on class probability and distance map and a morphology filter on crown area and solidity, with at most five new crowns per species, keeping recruited samples consistent with the reference inventory. We evaluate the framework at two Brazilian sites: an Amazonian rainforest in Acre (17 species, 355 annotated crowns, 4 cm GSD) and a forest site in the Cerrado of Maranhão (4 species, 51 annotated crowns, 1.8 cm GSD). Over 20 iterations, the number of retained crowns grew from about 500 to 960 in Acre and from about 700 to over 3100 in Maranhão, while crown-level F1 exceeded single- and multi-task DeepLabV3 baselines (53.5% vs. 50.0% and 45.2%; 92.2% vs. 79.7% and 83.6%). The framework offers a low-cost route to expanding species inventories with consumer-grade UAVs and limited fieldwork.

Introduction Introduction Tropical forests are reservoirs of global biodiversity, hosting approximately two-thirds of all terrestrial species gardner2009prospects . Their vastness and inaccessibility have historically posed challenges for biodiversity monitoring, making it difficult to understand how global changes affect their capacity to harbor species. However, advances in high-resolution remote sensing are ushering in a new era of tropical forest monitoring fassnacht2016review . UAVs, capable of capturing imagery with centimeter-level spatial resolution, enable species detection at the individual tree crown (ITC) level ferreira2020individual, veras2022fusing . This detail transforms biodiversity assessment, allowing researchers to map and monitor tree species distributions, even in tropical forests' dense and complex canopies. Current approaches for tree species mapping are based on deep learning methods, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) standing out in this field kattenborn2019convolutional . CNNs are an artificial neural network designed to process and analyze image data by automatically learning spatial hierarchies of features through convolutional layers. These networks can capture species-specific crown structural properties in high-resolution images, enabling accurate species classification. ferreira2020individual is one of the pioneering studies to identify tree species in Amazonian forests using UAV imagery and CNNs. The authors employed images with a ground sample distance (GSD) of 4 cm and reported an average accuracy of 87.8 in distinguishing four palm tree species. Euterpe precatoria, known as Açaí, a palm of economic importance, was mapped with over 98 accuracy. veras2022fusing used a CNN for semantic segmentation and UAV images acquired across different seasons to classify Amazonian tree species. They found that combining multi-season images improved species classification, reaching an average accuracy of 90.5 in classifying eight tree species. Nonetheless, these studies were conducted in areas with relatively low tree species diversity and relied on datasets with more than 25 ITCs per species, which may have contributed to the high classification accuracies reported. However, obtaining sufficient reference ITCs for training remains a challenge in tropical forests due to the difficulties of field data collection and the high diversity of species. While successful studies in controlled environments or with more common species can benefit from hundreds or thousands of labeled samples per class, the reality for many species in tropical forests is the availability of only a handful of labeled ITCs. This scarcity is especially pronounced for rare species, which are typically represented by only a few training samples mellor2015exploring, fassnacht2016review . Increasing the set of samples from rare species may address this issue, but this alternative requires time and proves to be costly, as shown by graves2016tree1 . This data disparity limits the application of deep learning models that rely on large volumes of annotated data to achieve high performance and generalization zhu2017deep, ma2019deep . Some innovative approaches have been developed to address the scarcity of labeled data for tree species classification in tropical forests. For instance, cuerosa2021multi proposed a multi-task fully convolutional network (MTFCN) to classify tree species in dense tropical forests using sparse polygon-level annotations from hyperspectral UAV data. Their method incorporates a partial loss function to train the network with non-dense annotations. It introduces a complementary task for distance regression, which enforces tree crown boundary constraints and enhances classification performance. The MTFCN achieved an average user’s accuracy of 88.63 and producer’s accuracy of 88.59 , improving results for underrepresented species with fewer than three ITCs in the dataset. Another promising approach for improving tree species mapping is active learning settles2012active, tuia2011survey . In an active learning pipeline, the model is initially trained on a small annotated dataset and then used to make predictions on a larger pool of unlabeled data. It then makes predictions on a larger pool of unlabeled data, identifying areas or samples where additional annotations enhance model performance. Typically, the selected samples are those where the model exhibits the highest uncertainty or faces the most significant difficulty in making accurate predictions ren2021survey . The selected samples are then submitted to an oracle, an agent responsible for providing new annotations to enrich the annotated dataset and improve the initial model. Usually, the role of the oracle is performed by a human annotator with knowledge of the domain of the data. Then, the new labels are added to the training set to start a new cycle of the method. This iterative process gradually improves the model's performance until a stopping criterion is reached. In kellenberger2019half , the authors present a deep active learning strategy for object detection in UAV-obtained images, aiming to map wildlife in savanna areas. In contrast to traditional active learning techniques, in kellenberger2019half , the oracle is requested to label the set where the model is most confident about its predictions. This strategy aims to reduce the number of false positives common in scenarios with rare or unbalanced classes. It aims to minimize the annotator's efforts, who can focus on the most relevant cases. The authors show that the proposed technique achieves reasonable precision indicators, even with a lower annotation cost than conventional active learning methods. In tong2024active , the authors propose an active learning-based spectral-spatial classification (ALSSC) model for tree species classification in hyperspectral images. The ALSSC employs multiscale superpixels to extract spectral-spatial features and applies guided filtering to refine class probability maps while preserving edge information. Active learning is then integrated to iteratively select the most informative samples based on uncertainty, enriching the training set after each classification round. The proposed ALSSC achieved an overall accuracy of 94.86 . However, the ALSSC relies on hyperspectral imagery and performs classification at the pixel/superpixel level, rather than detecting and classifying individual tree crowns from the RGB UAV imagery used in our study. The examples above demonstrate the potential of active learning methods to address challenges in data-scarce scenarios and achieve high classification accuracy. However, these studies were conducted in environments with limited species diversity, such as savanna areas or controlled datasets. Despite their potential, active learning approaches have not been extensively tested in tropical forest environments, where the high species diversity and structural complexity, including dense and overlapping canopies, pose unique challenges for ITC level segmentation and classification. Thus, exploring the applicability of these methods in such biodiverse ecosystems remains an important area of research. Moreover, these approaches still rely on a human oracle to label the selected samples. When the scarce resource is botanical expertise in the field, a natural question is whether the model itself can act as the oracle, that is, whether reliable pseudo-labels can be selected automatically in a self-training fashion, without new manual annotation, to identify tree species at the ITC level. In this work, we address the problem of expanding forest species inventories from a limited number of annotated individual tree crowns (ITCs). We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that progressively enlarges forest inventories through the automatic incorporation of high-confidence tree crowns validated by crown morphology. The proposed framework is implemented through an iterative self-training (pseudo-labeling) strategy combining semantic segmentation, confidence estimation and morphology-aware pseudo-label validation. By progressively expanding the inventory, the proposed approach improves species detection and classification while substantially reducing manual annotation requirements. The main contributions of this work: We propose a framework for reliable tree recruitment that progressively expands forest species inventories from a small set of annotated individual tree crowns while preserving inventory quality. We introduce a morphology-aware recruitment strategy that combines confidence estimation and crown morphology validation to automatically identify reliable candidate trees. We implement the proposed recruitment strategy through a multi-task semantic segmentation framework and demonstrate consistent improvements across two tropical forest datasets. This approach supports scalable biodiversity monitoring by enabling the model to act as an automated oracle for label generation, reducing the reliance on manual annotation. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section Materials presents a detailed description of the proposed tree recruitment framework. Section Experimental Design describes the training and validation procedures as well as the datasets used in this study. Section Results reports the performance of the proposed method under different scenarios. Finally, Section Conclusion summarizes the main findings and outlines directions for future work. title: RAPID: Reconstruction Accelerated by Polarization-Informed Depth for 2D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Efficient and accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view images remains a fundamental challenge in Gaussian splatting. Many existing methods rely on sparse geometric initialization and iterative densification, resulting in substantial optimization overhead and difficulties in balancing rendering quality and geometric accuracy, particularly in reflective and weakly textured regions. To address these limitations, we propose RAPID, a geometry-first framework that uses multiview polarization cues to recover dense surface priors. We integrate surface normals into depth maps using sparse geometric anchors. These depth maps are then fused across views. Curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization then support efficient optimization. Experiments on the PISR dataset demonstrate an approximately \(5\times\) speedup over PhyGaP, which is a state-of-the-art Gaussian-based reconstruction method. RAPID reduces the average optimization time from approximately 21 minutes (PhyGaP) to 4 minutes while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of RAPID in accelerating Gaussian optimization from polarimetric multi-view inputs.

Introduction sec:intro Recovering accurate 3D surfaces from multiview images~ pmvs2010,mvsnet2018,volsdf2021,schoenberger2016mvs and reproducing object appearance from unseen viewpoints are fundamental problems in 3D vision. 2D Gaussian splatting (2DGS)~ huang2024_2dgs represents local surfaces using oriented disks distributed in 3D space and efficiently synthesizes novel views through rasterization. However, rendering speed after model construction and the time required to build the model are distinct measures of efficiency~ quicksplat2025,minisplatting2024 . Starting from a sparse point cloud still requires repeated adjustment of disk positions, orientations, and scales, along with densification to establish surface coverage~ kerbl2023gaussians,huang2024_2dgs . In reflective and weakly textured regions, color variations across views provide limited reliable geometric guidance for these adjustments~ cui2017polarization,pisr2024 . Reducing scene optimization time while preserving novel view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy therefore remains a challenge in Gaussian surface reconstruction. Polarization observations provide information about surface orientation, supporting geometric estimation beyond color observations~ cui2017polarization,pandora2022 . In neural implicit reconstruction, PANDORA~ pandora2022 uses polarimetric inverse rendering to jointly recover object shape and separate diffuse and specular reflection components. NeRSP~ nersp2024 combines Stokes vector rendering errors with multiview azimuth consistency to constrain the shape of reflective surfaces from sparse views. PISR~ pisr2024 incorporates per-pixel perspective viewing rays into polarization constraints to directly constrain implicit surface normals. In explicit Gaussian reconstruction, Sparse2DGS~ sparse2dgs2025 generates a dense initial point cloud from depth predicted by multiview stereo matching, then selectively updates primitives based on rendered geometry. PhyGaP~ phygap2026 uses polarimetric deferred rendering to estimate geometry and material properties, supporting reflection decomposition and relighting. PolarGS~ polargs2026 employs polarization information for depth completion and back-projects the completed depth to generate new Gaussians. Inspired by these methods, we focus on geometric initialization. We investigate how polarization observations can determine the initial positions, orientations, and spatial extents of 2D Gaussians before training to reduce subsequent optimization time. Our research faces two core challenges: The first challenge is recovering surface positions. Since polarization-derived normals specify tangent-plane orientations but not positions along viewing rays. Under perspective projection, normals constrain log-depth gradients, so integration recovers only relative depth~ normalintegration2018 ; we use sparse geometric anchors to fix its scale. Cross-view scale inconsistencies can place back-projected points on different depth layers despite accurate normals~ normalintegration2018,cao2021normalintegration , introducing position errors into Gaussian initialization and subsequent training. Depth anchoring and multiview surface alignment are therefore both necessary. A further challenge is the mismatch between depth sampling density and required primitive density~ luo2018density,minisplatting2024 . Assigning one Gaussian to each depth sample creates redundant coverage in low-curvature regions, while uniformly coarser sampling risks losing detail in curved regions. A single scale is also insufficient when curvature differs between the two principal directions. Initializing representative primitives from dense observations using curvature adaptive spacing and scales emerges as a viable option. During training, merging redundant primitives and subdividing inadequately represented regions constitutes a principled strategy~ gauhuman2024,bai2025memgs,rotabulo2024densification , so that the primitive count reflects local surface requirements. In light of these considerations, we propose Pol2DGS, a method that uses polarization-derived surface priors to accelerate 2D Gaussian optimization. Given calibrated multiview color images, polarization observations, and foreground masks, we first estimate polarization-derived normals and their confidence, and then we convert these normals into perspective log-depth gradients and recover depth for each view through least-squares integration with sparse geometric anchors. After multiview consistency checks, we fuse the depth maps using a truncated signed distance function (TSDF)~ curless1996volumetric and extract an initial surface. We then fit a quadratic surface in local tangent-plane coordinates. The two principal curvatures determine the sampling spacing along their respective principal directions. Sampled positions define Gaussian centers, while surface normals and principal directions determine disk orientations. Local sampling spacing initializes the two tangential scales. Training thus begins with a set of oriented disks that already provides surface coverage. The primitive distribution is then refined according to observations and local geometry. Our main contributions are as follows: We integrate polarimetric normals with sparse geometric anchors, then use anisotropic, curvature-adaptive surface sampling to initialize Gaussian positions, orientations, and scales without depth sensors. We replace the native 2DGS~ huang2024_2dgs primitive update strategy with insertion guided by surface geometry, deterministic splitting along major axes, merging subject to coverage constraints, and pruning based on opacity. Our Pol2DGS reduces average measured runtime from roughly 21 to 4 minutes (5× speedup) while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy. Related Work sec:related_work Novel View Synthesis and Mesh Extraction Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ nerf2020 synthesize novel views by integrating volume density and view-dependent radiance along camera rays. However, a density field can reproduce images without identifying a unique surface~ neus2021 . NeuS~ neus2021 addresses this ambiguity by representing the surface as the zero level set of a learned signed distance function. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussians instead rasterizes anisotropic Gaussians for real-time rendering, but the primitives do not directly define a mesh. Gaussian reconstruction methods differ in how they recover a surface from these primitives. SuGaR~ sugar2024 aligns Gaussians with the surface and applies Poisson reconstruction~ poisson2006 to sampled points. 2DGS~ huang2024_2dgs represents local surfaces as oriented disks and extracts a mesh by fusing rendered depth maps. Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF)~ gof2024 extracts an opacity isosurface on an adaptive tetrahedral grid. MILo~ milo2025 incorporates differentiable mesh extraction into training, allowing discrepancies between mesh and Gaussian renderings to guide optimization. Sparse2DGS~ sparse2dgs2025 exploits geometry at an earlier stage by initializing primitives from stereo depth maps and selectively updating them using rendered geometry. Inspired by this approach, we instead integrate polarization-derived normals and use curvature-adaptive sampling to initialize oriented primitives. Polarization-Guided 3D Reconstruction Polarization provides surface orientation cues in weakly textured regions, but orientation alone does not determine depth. The method in Ref.~ cui2017polarization employs polarization-derived azimuths to trace iso-depth contours and propagate reliable stereo depths. PANDORA~ pandora2022 incorporates polarization into neural inverse rendering to recover shape and illumination while separating diffuse and specular radiance. NeRSP~ nersp2024 combines supervision on rendered Stokes vectors with multi-view azimuth consistency for sparse-view reconstruction. PISR~ pisr2024 directly constrains implicit surface normals using the polarization angle and the viewing ray at each pixel. Gaussian methods exploit polarization at different stages. PolGS~ polgs2025 uses measured Stokes vectors to supervise diffuse and specular reflection, while PhyGaP~ phygap2026 uses polarimetric deferred rendering and self-occlusion-aware environment maps for reflection decomposition and relighting. PolarGS~ polargs2026 incorporates polarization into PatchMatch~ patchmatch2009 depth completion and back-projects the completed depths to add Gaussians. Our Pol2DGS uses polarization to establish surface coverage before Gaussian optimization. Sparse geometric anchors fix the depth scale during normal integration. On the fused surface, local normals and principal directions determine disk orientation, while principal curvatures guide sampling intervals and disk scales. Method presents the overview of Pol2DGS. The input, as illustrated, comprises multiview red-green-blue (RGB) images, angle of linear polarization (AoLP) and degree of linear polarization (DoLP) measurements, foreground and polarization validity masks, fixed camera calibration, and feature tracks. Second, under standard reflection models, diffuse and specular reflection produce orthogonal polarization directions. An additional ambiguity therefore arises when the reflection mechanism is unknown~ pmvir2023,miyazaki2012polarization . title: Multi-Band Galaxy Novel-View Synthesis with Radiative Gaussian Fields
summary: We propose a novel view synthesis tool for galaxies based on Gaussian Splatting (GS). Unlike RGB data, where GS has achieved success, galaxy observations consist of multi-band signals from a massive number of bodies, contain complex patterns of cross-band interactions, and capture light propagation in highly heterogeneous media. As a result, the underlying physical process poses great challenges in model representation and optimization, which have not been investigated in existing research. To this end, we propose a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method, GalaxyGS, which is equipped with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanism of different astronomical bodies and the light propagation between them. In the absence of directly comparable baseline methods, we adopt a wide range of possible alternative approaches. Comparisons conclusively demonstrate that GalaxyGS is better in accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics.
full_text: We propose a novel view synthesis tool for galaxies based on Gaussian Splatting (GS). Unlike RGB data, where GS has achieved success, galaxy observations consist of multi-band signals from a massive number of bodies, contain complex patterns of cross-band interactions, and capture light propagation in highly heterogeneous media. As a result, the underlying physical process poses great challenges in model representation and optimization, which have not been investigated in existing research. To this end, we propose a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method, GalaxyGS, which is equipped with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanism of different astronomical bodies and the light propagation between them. In the absence of directly comparable baseline methods, we adopt a wide range of possible alternative approaches. Comparisons conclusively demonstrate that GalaxyGS is better in accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian has become a versatile foundational component for 3D reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping~ keetha2024splatam , autonomous driving~ yan2024street , and 3D representations in generative models~ yi2024gaussiandreamer . So far, its applications have often focused on RGB and RGB-D data, sometimes with additional appearance or geometric information such as texture, lighting, and surface normals~ liang2024gsir . In other words, the synthesized novel view is often restricted to the visible spectrum of human eyes. Recently, 3DGS has been extended to data that go beyond the visible spectrum, such as thermal imaging~ lu2025thermalgaussian and hyperspectral reconstruction~ thirgood2025hypergs . Our research also extends 3DGS into a new domain, multi-band galaxy novel view synthesis, where the signals cover a wide range of wavelengths with light propagation through complex and heterogeneous media. Given sparse multi-band images of a galaxy, we reconstruct galaxies by predicting multi-band images at unseen viewpoints, extending 3DGS into a scientific research tool for astronomy. Galaxy reconstruction poses three coupled representational and optimization challenges, which demand a fundamental modeling innovation rather than a naive adaptation of existing 3DGS research. The first challenge is the heterogeneous media. A galaxy observation contains mixed multi-band signals from stars and dust of various sizes and properties. This gives compound signals which, if not untangled well, severely compromise novel view synthesis. These components have distinct emission mechanisms, manifested as different energy distributions across wavelengths, ultraviolet-to-near-infrared (UV-NIR), mid-infrared (MIR), and far-infrared to submillimeter (FIR/submm) ranges~ conroy2013panchromatic . The energy of stellar emission is concentrated in the UV-NIR range, while dust emission extends across the MIR and FIR/submm ranges~ draine2007dust . This is significantly different from existing methods where stellar and dust emission mechanisms are rarely explicitly considered, even in those designed for spectral signals~ thirgood2025hypergs,meyer2026mssplatting and astronomy~ levis2022bhnerf,jarolim2024sunerf,nolan2026astrosplat . The immediately following challenge is the complex light propagation in heterogeneous media. Stellar emission is strong but attenuated by dust through absorption and scattering, and absorbed energy heats the dust, which further re-emits energy mainly in the infrared range, producing a thermal dust continuum~ steinacker2013dust . At the same time, there are small dust grains that also absorb and re-emit energy, contributing strongly to emission in the MIR range~ draine2007dust . Existing 3DGS research, including spectral models, often simplifies the propagation process without modeling the behaviors of different media during propagation~ meyer2026mssplatting . In our case, not only do we need to model emission and its propagation, but we also aim to make them physically meaningful, attributing the correct amount of energy to different components when learning from mixed signals. Last but not least, heterogeneous media and complex light propagation jointly impose challenges on optimization, which needs to accurately synthesize views and simultaneously untangle the signals and attribute them to corresponding components. Such optimization cannot be achieved by simple stochastic gradient~ kerbl2023gaussian or sampling methods~ kheradmand2024mcmc alone, without a representation that distinguishes emission from attenuation, as shown later. To jointly address these challenges, we propose a new 3DGS method named Galactic Gaussian Splatting (GalaxyGS). GalaxyGS is physically inspired and consists of two key elements: structured primitives and staged optimization. We first create three Gaussian fields in 3D space: a stellar emission field, a dust attenuation field, and a dust emission field. We design three types of primitives for these fields. Next, the first two fields jointly model stellar emission and its attenuation, while the last field captures the dust re-emission. These physically inspired fields explicitly model light propagation and assign distinct emission and attenuation contributions to the observed multi-band signals. Having addressed the representational challenges, we find that jointly training all components easily suffers from local minima. This involves not only a highly nonconvex optimization problem but also solution ambiguity, multiple physical models can give the same observation~ denicola2020deprojection,kouros2024ambiguity . Therefore, we propose a new physically inspired strategy for staged optimization of the fields. We evaluate on two datasets: Auriga~ kapoor2021auriga and TNG50~ costantin2023ceers . Since there are no GS methods for galaxy reconstruction, we adapt six closely related methods, which cover a wide range of representations and optimization strategies. Evaluation conclusively demonstrates the performance of across galaxies of different types, formation mechanisms, . universally outperforms the best baseline method by in reconstruction accuracy and in physical fidelity. Our contributions include: the first 3DGS method for multi-band galaxy novel view synthesis, to the best of our knowledge. a physically inspired 3DGS representation that explicitly models energy emission mechanisms. a physically inspired light propagation model for 3DGS. a staged optimization strategy to enable 3DGS to disentangle mixed signals. Related Work sec:related Multi-band view synthesis extends appearance modeling beyond RGB through wavelength-dependent radiance or shared spectral features. HS-NeRF~ chen2024hsnerf conditions radiance on wavelength, while ThermalGaussian~ lu2025thermalgaussian couples RGB and thermal Gaussians through multimodal regularization. Using shared spectral features, HyperGS~ thirgood2025hypergs renders in a pretrained autoencoder's latent space and decodes the result into spectra. MS-Splatting~ meyer2026mssplatting instead decodes shared per-Gaussian features into band radiance before rendering. For direct spectral modeling, DD-HGS~ narayanan2025ddhgs conditions spherical harmonic coefficients on wavelength and denoises rendered spectra with diffusion. Material-based approaches give a physical interpretation. UnMix-NeRF~ perez2025unmixnerf models diffuse spectra as nonnegative mixtures of learned material spectra, and SpectralGaussians~ sinha2024spectralgaussians separates spectral reflectance and illumination for relighting. These methods advance spectral modeling from appearance prediction toward physical interpretation, but do not explicitly distinguish objects with different emission mechanisms. The observed image depends on source spectra and light propagation through the scene. FitSKIRT~ degeyter2013fitskirt estimates parametric stellar and dust distributions by comparing SKIRT radiative-transfer simulations with galaxy images. Astronomical neural renderers incorporate domain-specific propagation. BH-NeRF~ levis2022bhnerf recovers emission near black holes using gravitationally bent rays, while SuNeRF~ jarolim2024sunerf models solar-coronal emission and absorption. For small-body surfaces, AstroSplat~ nolan2026astrosplat instead ties Gaussian intensity to surface orientation and sunlight through planetary reflectance models. SeaThru-NeRF~ levy2023seathrunerf and SeaSplat~ yang2025seasplat similarly separate scene appearance from wavelength-dependent attenuation and backscatter in water. These neural renderers model specialized propagation effects, but not the distinct emission mechanisms and attenuation that coexist in galaxy images. Other than gradient-based optimization with adaptive cloning and splitting~ kerbl2023gaussian or sampling~ kheradmand2024mcmc , existing research uses bespoke optimization for different scenarios. Under sparse views, LGDWT-GS~ salehi2026lgdwt adds global and patch-wise image wavelet losses to regularize scene fitting. 3DSatellites~ chang2025satellites couples Gaussian reconstruction with camera-pose estimation. Estimating physical properties introduces a different difficulty, because material and illumination changes can compensate in the rendered image~ kouros2024ambiguity . GS-IR~ liang2024gsir organizes this estimation in stages, reconstructing geometry and caching occlusion before fitting material properties and illumination. In our research, separating mixed radiative signals requires controlling compensation between emission and attenuation. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries A typical galaxy observation ( left) is a multi-band image , where , , and denote the image height, width, and number of bands (channels), respectively. This is a discretized representation in both space and wavelength. The raw data at a pixel form a continuous spectrum of wavelengths. It is then discretized into bands. At each pixel, band contains light signals over a range of wavelengths and is labeled by a representative wavelength . Furthermore, we divide the bands into three band groups: UV-NIR below , MIR from to , and FIR/submm beyond ~ hickox2018obscured . Galaxy observations are more complex than the RGB data in standard GS, and novel view synthesis for galaxies requires physical fidelity on top of visual realism. As a result, cross-band interactions need to be explicitly considered and physically meaningful measures of light distribution are required, none of which is needed in standard GS. Next, different astronomical bodies show distinctive behaviors in light emission and attenuation. Their emissions can span the whole spectrum but concentrate on different band groups, shown in~ left. First, stellar emission dominates the UV-NIR group. Its spectral shape varies with stellar age and metallicity~ bruzual2003stellar . Hotter stars, for example, emit a greater fraction of their light at shorter wavelengths. Dust absorbs and scatters stellar light, causing dimming. This intensity of the dimming depends on the optical depth~ steinacker2013dust and the wavelength, also described by a function called an extinction curve~ fitzpatrick1999extinction . Furthermore, dust is heated by absorbed light and then emits in the IR groups, where small grains contribute strongly in the MIR group, while larger grains dominate the FIR/submm group~ draine2007dust . Methodology sec:method We propose , a physically inspired model of light propagation in galaxies ( ). It represents stellar emission, dust attenuation, and dust emission with separate Gaussian fields, fitted through a specially designed optimization. One key design is to constrain the learning of different Gaussian fields within physically meaningful spaces spanned by appropriate basis functions. title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models
summary: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

Introduction sec:introduction Interactive world models are evolving from open-world exploration toward fine-grained embodied interaction. Advances in generating action-controllable environments have established a foundation for predicting visual experience under user intervention~ bruce2024genie,parkerholder2024genie2 . In embodied tasks, this prediction must capture how an agent's actions change the objects it engages with. Hand--object interaction brings this requirement into focus: hands support varied contacts and transformations, connecting egocentric experience to dexterous manipulation. This connection has motivated growing interest in hand-centric world models. A growing body of work extends world modeling from locomotion and robotic-arm manipulation to hand-centric interaction. Recent methods use meshes, joints, and poses to control hand motion~ wang2026hand2world,zhang2026jointcontrol,gao2026pam,fang2026worldscapemoe . Contact and scene modeling support object interaction and continued manipulation~ li2026egohoi,kim2026dwm,hao2026egosim , with applications to data synthesis and digital teleoperation~ gao2026pam,zhao2026rynnworldteleop . Yet these advances are largely assessed through model-specific tasks and validation targets, making progress across methods difficult to compare. This growing field still lacks a unified benchmark for systematic evaluation across tasks and embodiments. Existing video and world-model benchmarks evaluate visual quality, interaction and navigation control, and embodied utility~ huang2024vbench,ying2026wbench,fang2026iworldbench,li2026worldarena2 . Manipulation-focused benchmarks further assess physical executability, human-to-robot transfer, and agreement with real executions~ jiang2026robowm,rong2026h2r,duan2026worldoracle (Table~ tab:comparison ). These benchmarks provide evidence about interaction quality and task outcomes; comparing hand-centric models further requires resolving how the prescribed motion produces those outcomes. Small finger contacts can determine an operation's outcome, while occlusion requires object states and previously observed details to remain consistent when they reappear. Coordinated finger motions also make control fidelity consequential: similar overall hand movements can differ in joint configuration, contact location, and object response. Evaluation must distinguish errors in following the supplied control from errors in the resulting interaction, using correspondences between native control inputs and generated motion. These judgments must extend across human hands and simulated and real dexterous hands with different morphologies and kinematics, as well as operations with different completion and persistence requirements. Existing protocols have yet to organize these requirements into a common evaluation of hand-centric world models. We introduce , a unified benchmark for hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands. Our data curation pipeline yields 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. From this corpus, we manually select 500 clips spanning seven task families to form the evaluation set. To compare methods across embodiments, we establish shared structural semantics and spatiotemporal correspondences, then adapt the resulting controls to each model's native interface. Task annotations connect action requirements to evidence of object-state changes, subsequent persistence, and the preservation of previously observed details. Our six-dimensional protocol combines visual and geometric measurements with these task-specific judgments to evaluate generated interactions under shared scoring criteria. Our evaluation of eleven models shows that stronger hand-pose control can coexist with weak object-state evolution and persistence. Several specialized hand-control models also underperform general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks. These findings identify a gap between motion control and interaction prediction: realizing a prescribed movement does not ensure that its consequences are modeled coherently, and specialization in hand control does not ensure robust performance across embodiments. Our contributions are: A unified benchmark. establishes common interaction tasks and six evaluation dimensions for comparing world models across human hands and simulated and real dexterous hands. A data curation pipeline and corpus. We construct high-quality interaction data through quality screening and signal-alignment checks, producing 20,500 clips from which we manually select 500 for evaluation. A systematic evaluation. We systematically evaluate 11 representative models under a unified protocol, characterizing their performance across hand-centric tasks and embodiments. 1 Related Work sec:related Hand-centric world models. Controllable hand--object generation combines motion constraints with scene modeling. Projected meshes, sparse joints, and pose-based rendering provide explicit motion constraints within visually conditioned generation~ wang2026hand2world,zhang2026jointcontrol,gao2026pam . The interaction model determines how this prescribed motion affects objects: contact-aware embeddings encode geometric and kinematic priors, while scene-conditioned generation anchors the interaction to surrounding geometry~ li2026egohoi,kim2026dwm . Explicitly updating the underlying scene state carries these effects into later interactions~ hao2026egosim . HandWorldBench sec:benchmark We construct HandWorldBench by curating egocentric interaction data across embodiments (Section~ sec:dataset ), organizing model inputs through unified control interfaces, and establishing task annotations (Section~ sec:annotations ). We evaluate the generated interactions with seventeen metrics across six dimensions (Section~ sec:metrics ), then aggregate these measurements into category scores and for model comparison (Section~ sec:aggregation ). Dataset Construction sec:dataset Figure~ fig:data_pipeline (a) outlines data curation from our in-house human-hand recordings, HandsOn~ luo2026handson (simulated dexterous hands), and our own real dexterous-hand recordings. Starting from over 600 hours of footage across the three embodiments, we validate video readability, timestamps, and alignment with available hand and camera signals. Screening checks camera stability, hand visibility, and image quality. Visual checks assess blur, exposure, and hand size. We extract continuous clips of frames ( ), screen for overlapping sources and visual duplicates, and check exported frame counts and signal correspondence. Source intervals and available validity masks accompany each clip throughout processing. From 20,500 curated clips, we manually select 500 for evaluation using the criteria in Appendix~ ; 20,000 remain for non-test use. Evaluation cases cover seven task families and 22 task categories (composition, durations, and coverage in Appendices~ -- ), including material shaping, tools and mechanisms, and object handling (Figure~ fig:data_pipeline , right). Control Interfaces and Annotations sec:annotations We unify control through native-signal parsing, structural normalization, spatiotemporal alignment, and model-specific encoding (Figure~ fig:data_pipeline (b)). Human-hand inputs provide native 3D keypoints, left/right validity, camera calibration, and visual-inertial odometry poses. For dexterous hands, forward kinematics uses joint states, palm poses, and robot assets to obtain landmarks and surfaces, which are transformed into camera coordinates. Each hand follows a fixed 21-point order: one wrist or palm anchor and four landmarks per finger, with hand identity and validity retained alongside native kinematics and surface geometry. Human meshes are fitted to keypoints or visually reconstructed as required. Coordinates use meters, explicit world-to-camera transforms, and image-matched projection and viewport mappings. Source frame indices, timestamps, and shared inference windows align images, geometry, and cameras. Adapters encode these assets as skeletal videos, 3D joints, surface renderings, or scene conditions for each model. The common interface establishes structural and spatiotemporal correspondence while preserving each model's conditioning format. Shared operation categories, global task descriptions, and segmented action descriptions establish task semantics across embodiments (Figure~ fig:data_pipeline (c)). Evaluation annotations anchor action requirements and state checkpoints to the same manipulated object and its before, during, and after windows, distinguishing minimum change from full completion. Persistence checks follow state establishment to identify unsupported reversals.
